_about: Cross-book name authority for the whole translation shelf. Consult BEFORE romanizing anything in a new book; one rendering per referent ACROSS BOOKS unless a book records a deliberate deviation in its own glossary note. Feed every new book's decided renderings back in on completion. Statuses: 'agreed' (multiple books, one form), 'agreed-article-varies' (only the leading article differs), 'single-book' (observed once so far; 'provisional': true marks an uncertain romanization), 'decided' (a real cross-book conflict adjudicated; the 'decided' field is the binding form for new books, and other listed renderings stand as those books' recorded deviations), 'context-dependent' (the hanzi names different things in different books or takes different renderings by sense; the note carries the rule), 'reconcile' (a live disagreement not yet adjudicated). Adjudicated shelf-wide 2026-08-29 from all fourteen branches carrying the file; adjudication rationale is in each entry's note.

207师.note: A division of the Youth Army, formed 1 January 1945.

264旅.note: The Nationalist brigade of the 88th Division in which Su Lina's husband, Zhou Chukang, serves at the front.

76号.note: The Wang Jingwei regime’s “Secret Service General Headquarters” at No. 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai, notorious for torture; run by Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun.

White night酒吧.note: A Chongqing bar, once a foreign correspondents' club. Fictional; the source keeps the English name.

おちゃちゃ.note: The eldest of Katsuie and Oichi’s three daughters (Oichi’s by Azai Nagamasa), seventeen at Kita-no-shō; the future Lady Yodo (see the Lady Yodo).

おつね.note: Kondō Isami's wife, a silent, gloomy woman and, by Toshizō's account, a poor cook.

おのぶ.note: Toshizō's elder sister, wife of Satō Hikogorō.

おゆう.note: A kunoichi (woman shinobi) of Tarao, planted by Hattori Hanzō among Nobunaga's waiting-women at Azuchi. She feeds rumor to Nobunaga's page Ranmaru and works the smitten Soda Yoichiro.

おらしょ.note: The Christians' set prayers (from Latin oratio), memorized and handed down by rote.

お佐絵.note: Younger sister of the Saruwatari chief priest of Fuchū; the woman Toshizō meets in the festival dark. Apparently the novelist's invention. Romanization mine.

お咲.note: A meshimori-onna at the Jōshūya inn in Fuda, a thin-lipped Jōshū woman; a minor figure. Romanization mine.

お市.note: Nobunaga's sister, widow of Azai Nagamasa; married to Shibata Katsuie in the anti-Hideyoshi cause. Mother of the Lady Yodo.

お雪.note: Oyuki (given name Yuki) is Shiba’s invention; see the note at her first appearance. She recurs to the end of the novel as the woman who draws out Toshizō’s private self.

かまり.note: A stealth-scout or skirmisher; the Taikōki's word for Yomoda's disguised reconnaissance troops.

がらさ.note: Grace (Portuguese graça), a loanword of the mission.

くノ一.note: The ninja's cant word for a female agent, from breaking the character 女 (woman) into the strokes ku-no-ichi (く-ノ-一). Footnoted at first appearance.

さんまい.note: Under the dual-grave custom, the desolate field where corpses alone are buried, apart from the gravestone-site.

すね次.note: Another of Kohagi's rappa, posted in the streets around the Jurakudai. Reading a project call (すね次, unglossed).

ちぬの海.note: The old poetic name for the stretch of sea off Sakai and Izumi, much sung in the ancient verse.

でうす.note: The Kirishitan word for God, from Latin/Portuguese Deus.

ねね.note: Hideyoshi's principal wife, later honored as the Kōdai-in; recipient of Nobunaga's teasing 'bald rat' letter.

まあ.note: Maeda Toshiie’s third daughter, twelve, held as a hostage at Kita-no-shō and betrothed to Sakuma Jūzō; later a favorite of Hideyoshi.

イルマン.note: Irmao (Portuguese 'brother'): a Jesuit lay brother or catechist, below the padre.

ウグイス張り.note: A floor built to chirp underfoot and betray an intruder; the trap sprung on Goemon at Yodo Castle.

エテギ.note: A hugely fat young ninja of Oyamada, twenty-four, good-natured and hopeless at stealth; taken into Ieyasu's service on the Tarao crossing.

オルガンチノ.note: Gnecchi-Soldo Organtino (1533–1609), Italian Jesuit, for many years superior of the Kyoto mission.

カシイ.note: A young Iga shinobi, Tamo's companion, who died shielding her when Iga was destroyed.

カスミ.note: An Iga ninja master, uncle to both Kashii and Etegi, who taught them the arts; died at the Momochi fort in 1581.

カズエ.note: Maki’s younger sister. (Her stated age differs between two passages; see the note.)

ガスパル・クエリョ.note: Portuguese Jesuit, vice-provincial of the Japan mission.

ガスパル・ビレラ.note: Portuguese Jesuit, among the first to work in Kyoto (cited here for a report on the peasants).

タモ.note: A young beggar-woman, burned and half-crippled, taken under Organtino's protection at the Nanban-ji.

チカ.note: The unhurried, big-boned woman, neither wife nor caretaker, who keeps Hanzō's Chigachi manor at Yono.

ネジリ.note: A warped, malevolent ninja of the earlier volume, killed before this book opens; recalled here as having witnessed the fall of Odani.

バテレン.note: Bateren, from Portuguese padre: a Jesuit priest. Rendered 'padre'.

フランシスコ・ザビエル.note: St Francis Xavier (1506–1552), who opened the Japan mission at Kagoshima in 1549.

マキ.note: Goemon's wife, a poor fisher-and-farmer's daughter from the hills above Saiga in Kishu; guileless, devoted, and the still center of his new life in Sakai. She is the physical double of Hatsuko, though the two are of no kin.

ヤソ教.note: Yaso-kyo, from 'Jesus'; the ordinary period Japanese term for Christianity. Rendered 'the Christian faith' / 'Christianity' throughout.

ルイス・フロイス.note: Luis Frois (1532–1597), Portuguese Jesuit and the mission's great chronicler.

ルソン.note: The chief island of the Spanish Philippines; destination of the overseas slave-trade in women. Cf. Ruson Sukezaemon (ch02).

レオン・ロッシュ.note: Léon Roches (1809–1900), French minister to Japan 1864–68, who tied France to the shogunate’s cause with loans, arms, and the Yokosuka arsenal.

ロレンソ.note: Lourenco Ryosai (c.1526-1592), the blind biwa-player of Hizen converted by Xavier at Yamaguchi, and one of the first and most gifted Japanese Jesuit brothers; the beggar-woman Tamo's one confidant.

ワリニヤーニ.note: Alessandro Valignano (1539–1606), Jesuit Visitor to the Indies; organized the seminaries and the Tensho embassy.

一向宗.note: A militant strand of Jodo Shinshu (True Pure Land) Buddhism whose peasant leagues warred with the warlords.

一橋慶喜.note: Tokugawa Yoshinobu (Keiki), head of the Hitotsubashi house and, at this date, Superintendent of the Defense of the Imperial Palace; he became the fifteenth and last shogun in 1866. His personal notice of Kondō marks how high the farmer's son had risen.

一百单八将.note: The 108 heroes of Water Margin; the nickname for the 101 trainees plus 7 instructors of the first public-security class.

丁默村.note: 1901–1947. Former Nationalist Zhongtong man who became director of the Wang Jingwei “Secret Service General Headquarters” at No. 76; executed as a collaborator after the war.

丁默邨.note: Co-founder and director of the puppet Special Operations Headquarters (No. 76) with Li Shiqun; tried and executed as a traitor after the war.

七方出.note: The shinobi art of transforming into seven social types (monk, yamabushi, komūsō, mendicant conjuror, sarugaku player, merchant, ordinary man). Self-explained in the text. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: translate the term (lang-ja: no bare romaji common noun); 'shichihode' stands as the-stealthy-ones' recorded deviation.

七里研之助.note: The chief personal antagonist of the novel's early and middle chapters. An iai master of the Araki-ryū, trained first in the Maniwa Nen-ryū; reading from the source's furigana (しちりけんのすけ).

万国公墓.note: The Shanghai cemetery for the dead of all nations (万国公墓, ‘Cemetery of All Nations’), Chinese and foreign alike, on Hongqiao Road in the western outskirts (founded 1909); Stephen is buried here (ch28–ch29).

万国殡仪馆.note: The best-known funeral home of Republican Shanghai (opened 1926). Historical.

万墨林.note: Du Yuesheng's household steward and chief factotum; ran Du's Shanghai affairs during the war and was seized by the puppet secret service.

万梅山庄.note: Ximen Chuixue’s estate, named for its plum trees; in the fourth month it stands flowerless while the peach and azalea bloom on the slopes around it (ch05–ch06).

万福丸.note: Oichi’s son by Azai Nagamasa; hunted down after Odani fell and executed by impalement at Kinomoto in 1573.

万葉集.note: Japan's oldest anthology of verse, compiled in the eighth century.

三八式.note: The standard Japanese Arisaka bolt-action rifle. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: 'Type 38' is the handle; 'Type 38 rifle' at first use where the reader needs it.

三好三人衆.note: The three Miyoshi captains who contested control of the Kinai after 1564; Matsunaga's war with them burned the Great Buddha.

三月亭石巴.note: Toshizō’s grandfather, a haiku poet well known in the Hino country in the Bunka–Bunsei years; the source of the family’s haiku tradition.

三条.note: The Third Avenue of Kyoto; the site of Gohei's official residence.

三条小橋.note: The “little bridge” on Sanjō, over the Takase canal; the Ikedaya stood at its west end.

三民主义.note: 三民主义; Sun Yat-sen's doctrine of nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood, made the Nationalist creed. See the note at first appearance.

三法師.note: Nobunaga’s infant grandson and legitimate heir, later Oda Hidenobu (Chūnagon of Gifu); Gen’i was charged to protect him.

三浦義勝.note: A Sagami warrior whose reinforcements turned the Battle of Bubaigawara for Nitta.

三潭印月.note: A celebrated West Lake scene, an islet ringed by three small stone pagodas standing in the water.

三炮台.note: 三炮台, the Chinese name for the Wills brand Three Castles, a premium foreign cigarette of Republican Shanghai.

三田尻.note: Chōshū's chief port on the Inland Sea, in Suō province (the modern Hōfu), from which the domain shipped its expeditionary force toward Osaka.

三番町.note: An Edo quarter to which the Saitō hall (Renpeikan) moved after a fire.

三野.note: One of the People's Liberation Army's field armies in the civil war. Attested English name.

三青团.decided: the Three People's Principles Youth Corps
三青团.note: The Nationalists' youth organization, founded in 1938 and folded back into the Kuomintang in 1947. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: standard scholarly form; short handle 'the Youth Corps' after first use.

三马路.note: 三马路; the colloquial name of Hankou Road (汉口路), the financial street of Chinese Shanghai where the securities exchange stood. See the footnote at first appearance. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: majority form, parallel to Fourth Avenue for 四马路; colloquial name of Hankou (Hankow) Road, gloss once.

上官木.note: The original name of Huo Xiu, one of the four ministers of the Golden Roc (ch04).

上官谨.note: The Great King’s maternal uncle and one of the four ministers; the only one to stay loyal, he raised the exiled king in China and has since died (ch04).

上官雪儿.note: The little cousin of Princess Danfeng and younger sister of Shangguan Feiyan; a girl of twelve who lies without a blink and leads Lu Xiaofeng in circles. She fears her vanished sister has been murdered (ch03–ch04).

上官飞燕.note: A thief-girl of Jiangnan; Shangguan is a two-syllable surname and Feiyan means ‘flying swallow’ (Prologue).

上州屋.note: Rihei's inn at the Fuda station on the Kōshū Highway.

上海.note: China’s largest city and the seat of the Party Central and its underground in this period.

上海师专.note: The teacher-training college where Yanzhi first finds Qin Shuji.

上海泰晤士报.note: An English-language daily of treaty-port Shanghai. Historical.

上海职工运动委员会.note: The labor-movement organ Dai Li ordered set up in 1940, with the notables Yu Qiaqing and Zhao Zigang as figurehead members; it never really took shape.

上清寺.note: A district of Chongqing where Wang lodged.

上石原.note: A village of the Fuda Five Stations on the Kōshū Highway (now part of Chōfu); Kondō Isami's birthplace.

上野.note: The chief town of Iga; the Hattori village lies just north of it.

上野彦馬.note: A samurai of the Ōmura domain (1838–1904) and a pioneer of photography in Japan, who kept a famous studio at Nagasaki. His portraits of Bakumatsu figures survive; the photograph of Kondō is historical.

下京.note: The southern, mercantile half of Kyoto.

下呂正兵衛康次.note: The false name Gohei adopts after deserting Iga, claiming descent from a retainer surname of the old Ichijō house of Tosa. Furigana げろ on 下呂; reading of 康次 (Yasuji) a project call.

下柘植次郎左衛門.note: 下柘植 glossed しもつげ (Shimotsuge). In the opening he is 老人, 'the old man'.

下長者町.note: A street bounding the Jurakudai on the south; Jūzō approaches by its eastern corner.

不战而屈人之兵.note: Sun Tzu's dictum; the received translation is used.

与兵衛.note: The keeper of the night saké-shop that gives the chapter its name.

东亚协同体.note: A related Japanese slogan (東亞協同體) for the merging of Japan, 'Manchukuo,' and China.

东亚同文书院.note: The Tōa Dōbun Shoin, a Japanese academy in Shanghai (founded 1901) that trained Japanese “China hands” and doubled as a nursery of intelligence officers; a Communist Party branch also grew up inside it.

东亚同文会.note: The Tōa Dōbunkai, the semi-official Japanese society that founded and oversaw the academy.

东亚新秩序.note: Japan's slogan (東亞新秩序) for a Japanese-led East Asian bloc, from Konoe's statement of 3 November 1938.

东亚旅馆.note: A Shanghai hotel named in the story. Rendered by sense.

东交民巷.note: The walled diplomatic quarter of Beiping, extraterritorial under the 1901 Boxer Protocol. Noted at first appearance in the introductions.

东京帝国大学.note: The pre-war name of the University of Tokyo. Historical.

东京日日新闻.note: A major Japanese daily (1872–1943), forerunner of the Mainichi Shimbun; the paper that ran the propaganda feature on Jiang.

东北人民解放军.note: The Chinese Communist field army in the Northeast, commanded by Lin Biao with Tao Zhu as political-department director; the target of the chapter's intelligence operation.

东方汇理银行.note: The Bank of Indochina, the French colonial bank of issue in Hanoi.

东方通讯社.note: A news agency Lin heads in cover in postwar Shanghai.

东方饭店.note: The Shanghai hotel (东方, 'the East') where Fourth Madam stages the storytelling that opens A-Chu's origins to him; rendered by pinyin, since the source's 东方饭店 does not map cleanly onto any one attested Republican-era English hotel name. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: real venues keep their period English names (shelf canon: Jessfield Park, Bubbling Well Road, the Paramount).

东条英机.note: 1884–1948. The Japanese army general who became prime minister in October 1941 and led Japan into the Pacific War; executed as a war criminal in 1948.

东湖.note: The large lake east of Wuchang, across which Jiang rows the escaping Guo Bingyan.

严副官.note: Guo Bingyan's aide-de-camp. Fictional; fuguan is a military adjutant.

严立本.note: The original name of Yan Tieshan, one of the four ministers of the Golden Roc (ch04).

中京.note: The central district of Kyoto, between the upper and lower city.

中仙道.note: The inland highway between Edo and Kyoto, running through the central mountains; longer than the coastal Tōkaidō but free of its river-crossings.

中储银行.note: The note-issuing bank of the Wang Jingwei regime.

中华日报.note: The chief newspaper of the Wang Jingwei regime.

中华路.note: A street in central Chongqing; the White Night bar stands at its junction with Linjiangmen.

中原.note: The Central Plains (Zhongyuan) Liberated Area, linked to Chongqing by a secret line Liu Shaowen laid (ch41).

中原司令部.note: The novella's name for the Japanese army command in the Wuhan region, where Jiang serves as a military doctor. Zhongyuan means “the Central Plains”; not a standard historical designation.

中国.note: The western provinces of the main island (NOT China); rendered 'the Chūgoku provinces' to avoid confusion with 大明.

中国人民反法西斯大同盟.note: The anti-Japanese, Communist-linked front Ji Hongchang helped organize at Tianjin in 1934.

中国民权保障同盟.decided: the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights
中国民权保障同盟.note: Civil-liberties body founded in Shanghai, December 1932 (Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei, Yang Quan). Chapter 29 (footnoted). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: majority (three books) and the fuller standard translation.

中土.note: Literally ‘the central land’: China proper, the settled heartland, as named from the vantage of the frontier kingdom of the Golden Roc (ch04).

中央党部.note: The central headquarters of the Nationalist Party; Jiang carries its credentials, cover for his intelligence work.

中央情报部.note: Established September 1941 as the unified strategic-intelligence organ of the Party Center and the Military Commission, known within the Party as 中情部 (Zhongqingbu); one body with the Social Affairs Department under two signboards, run in practice by Li Kenong.

中央政治局.note: R1 register pass (2026-08-22): 中央政治局 and bare 政治局 both render "the Politburo" — the standard term in English-language CCP scholarship (reader-ease over decode). "Political Bureau" was collapsed to "Politburo" book-wide and the redundant "Central" dropped, matching the form already used in ch19–ch20. 中央政治局常委 = "the Politburo Standing Committee".

中央日报.note: The Nationalist party's official newspaper. Attested English name.

中央特科.note: The CCP's clandestine intelligence/security organ (established 1927-28) that Gu Shunzhang helped run under Zhou Enlai. English 'Central Special Branch' is the form used by Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Special_Branch); 'Special Services Section' and 'Central Department for Special Tasks'  Adjudicated 2026-08-29: majority and the newest canon (short handle: the Special Branch); zhou-enlai's 'Central Special Section' stands as its recorded deviation.

中央社会部.note: The CCP’s central intelligence and security organ from February 1939, headed by Kang Sheng; known within the Party as 中社部 (Zhongshebu). The bland name “Social Affairs” was itself a cover.

中央警校.note: The Central Police Academy (Nanjing, 1936), the Nationalists' police-officer school; Dai Li ran it as superintendent and used it to recruit for the Juntong.

中央训练团.note: The Nationalist party-and-government training organ at Chongqing; Chen attended the Third Term of its Party-Government Training Class.

中央调查研究局.note: The high-standing intelligence-and-research bureau Mao Zedong set up in 1941 and headed himself; its remit, “investigation and study” (diaocha yanjiu), was Mao’s own doctrine of intelligence analysis.

中央银行.note: The Nationalist government's central bank; not to be confused with the Wang regime's Central Reserve Bank. Attested English name.

中山舰事件.note: Chiang Kai-shek's March 1926 move against Communist influence in the Nationalist Party and army.

中山陵.note: The tomb of Sun Yat-sen on Purple Mountain, Nanjing.

中川清秀.note: Also Nakagawa Sebei. Held Mount Ōiwa for Hideyoshi and fell defending it against Morimasa’s night raid.

中村半次郎.note: Nakamura Hanjirō (1838–1877), later Kirino Toshiaki: a Satsuma swordsman of the Jigen-ryū reckoned one of the ‘four man-cutters’ of the Bakumatsu, close to Saigō Takamori. He rose to general in the imperial army and fell with Saigō at Shiroyama in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.

中村文荷斎.note: A favorite of Katsuie’s, more tea-master than warrior, entrusted with escorting the three daughters out of the burning castle.

中汇银行.note: Du Yuesheng's own bank (the China & Overseas Bank), a pillar of his finances. Rendered ‘Zhonghui Bank’ across the collection.

中统.note: The Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Central Organization Department, the KMT's civilian/party secret service; grew out of the 1928 Investigation Section under Chen Lifu.

中美合作所.note: The Sino-American Cooperative Organization, a 1943 joint U.S. Navy–Nationalist (Dai Li) intelligence and training body at Chongqing; its Geleshan compound is bound up with the Baigongguan and Zhazidong prisons where many Communists were held and killed. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: full form 'the Sino-American Cooperative Organization (SACO)' at first use, SACO thereafter.

中西功.note: 1910–1973. A Japanese Communist and China expert who worked for the South Manchuria Railway’s research arm while spying for the CCP under Pan Hannian’s system; obtained strategic intelligence on Japan’s southern advance. Arrested by the Tokkō, tried, and freed at the war’s end; later a Japanese Communist Party member of the Diet.

中西登.note: A pupil of Itō who later cast his lot with the Satsuma domain.

临时政府.note: The Japanese-sponsored 'Provisional Government of the Republic of China' at Beiping (North China), headed by Wang Kemin.

临江门.note: A gate and district on the Jialing side of old Chongqing.

丸太町.note: An east–west street of the capital, north of the Jurakudai.

丹凤公主.note: Danfeng (丹凤) means ‘scarlet phoenix’; her surname is Shangguan. She teases that she is Princess Danfeng, not Princess Xiaofeng (‘little phoenix’), which is Lu Xiaofeng’s own name (ch03).

丹桂戏园.note: A long-established Shanghai opera house. Attested romanization.

丹羽長秀.note: Oda commander on the Yamashiro road in the 1581 invasion; his HQ at Ōyado is the target of the fire-raid.

丹虎.note: A Kiyamachi restaurant kept by Shikokuya Jūbei, the second suspected meeting-place; the object of Toshizō’s party on the night of the raid.

丽都花园.note: A Shanghai entertainment garden/ballroom Du frequented.

久坂玄瑞.note: Historical, 1840–1864. A leading loyalist of Chōshū, disciple and son-in-law of Yoshida Shōin; died the next year in the Chōshū attack on the Forbidden Gate. Reading from the source’s furigana.

九国公约.note: The 1922 Washington treaty guaranteeing China's sovereignty and the Open Door.

九州.note: The Nine Provinces of legend, a classical name for the whole of China. See the note at the epithet ‘One Blade Quells the Nine Provinces’ (Prologue). Two referents: in a Chinese source, the classical Nine Provinces (China); in a Japanese source, Kyūshū. Both renderings correct in their books.

九度山.note: A fortified height above the Kino River at the foot of Mount Kōya. Long after Goemon’s day Sanada Yukimura raised his fort here; the author flags it as the central stage of his sequel, The Sanada Ninja Band.

九条尚忠.note: Historical, 1798–1871. Head of the Kujō regent house and leader of the pro-shogunate nobles at court; hated by the loyalists, he shaved his head and withdrew after the terror of 1862. Reading from the source’s furigana (ひさただ).

九江.note: 九江; the Yangzi river-port in Jiangxi, below Mount Lu.

九鬼嘉隆.note: Nobunaga's admiral, who built the iron-plated warships that broke the Mori navy off the Kizu River in 1578.

乱波.note: A Kantō term for a shinobi/spy; used interchangeably with 忍び in the text.

予野.note: A hidden hamlet in the Iga hills, two ri south of Ueno; site of the Chigachi manor, Hanzō's home seat.

二帖半敷町.note: A block in central Kyōto; the crossroads that gives the chapter its name. The name reads literally “two-and-a-half-mat town.”

二月堂.note: The Hall of the Second Month at Tōdai-ji.

二条.note: The Second Avenue of Kyoto; here its eastern edge and the Nijō riverbank (二条河原) by the Kamo, where Kohagi meets Gohei.

于右任.note: 1879–1964; Nationalist elder statesman, calligrapher, and president of the Control Yuan.

云南路.note: 云南路; a Settlement road near the racecourse; older English Yunnan Road.

五一口号.note: The Communists' May 1, 1948 slogans, whose call to convene a Political Consultative Conference and found a coalition government opened the road to the People's Republic.

五四运动.note: The 1919 nationalist and cultural movement; Chen ties it to the entry of Communism into China.

五奉行.note: The five administrators Hideyoshi set over the government of the realm.

五平.note: Bare given name of Kazama Gohei.

五徳.note: Nobunaga's daughter, married to Nobuyasu; her twelve-article accusation set his ruin in motion.

五畿内.note: The five provinces around the capital (Yamashiro, Yamato, Kawachi, Izumi, Settsu).

五相会议.note: Inner council of the Japanese cabinet (premier, war, navy, foreign, finance ministers), set up 1938.

五遁の術.note: The ninja's arts of evasion, grouped into five (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) and their inner counterparts.

井上源三郎.note: Historical, 1829–1868. One of the founding Tama members of the Shinsengumi; killed at Toba-Fushimi.

井伊直政.note: One of Ieyasu’s generals, whose red-lacquered troops were the famous ‘Red Guard.’

交警总队.note: The Transport Police Corps (交通警察总队), the postwar rebadging of the Loyal and Patriotic Army as 'transport police'; in Chen's account it was in fact given over to the suppression of the Communist rising.

交通银行.note: One of China's major government banks.

交际花.note: 交际花, lit. 'a flower of society'; a fashionable woman of the demimonde who moves among wealthy men, here Xu Manli. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: 'society flower' is a calque; wang-yaqiao's form stands as its recorded deviation.

亨利路.note: French Concession road (Route Paul Henry), today's Xinle Road.

京都守護職.note: The shogunal office created in 1862 to keep order in Kyoto, held by Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu; the Shinsengumi served under its authority.

人丹.note: Small refreshing medicinal pellets; 人丹 is the Chinese brand answering the Japanese Jintan (仁丹).

今井信経.note: Sōkyū's claimed grandfather, said to have been lord of Imaichi Castle in Ōmi.

今井宗久.note: Sakai merchant and tea master high in Hideyoshi's favor; the secret paymaster of the plot.

今井宗薫.note: Son of Imai Sōkyū; formal name Tatewaki Saemon. A tea master and merchant in his own right.

今井武夫.note: 1898–1982. A Japanese army officer who ran Operation Kiri, the secret 1940 peace channel to Chongqing, and later negotiated the Japanese surrender in China.

仏光寺.note: A large Shin-sect temple in central Kyōto; its gate-front was a landmark and a stand for hired palanquins.

代官.note: A shogunal officer administering a district of the Tokugawa house's own lands in place of a resident lord.

以天仰山.note: The eccentric monk-abbot of the Chinnō-in who buries himself in the bamboo grove; a fictional figure. Reading of 以天 not independently confirmed.

仰山.note: Bare name of the abbot Iten Gyōzan.

仲村信夫.note: A Japanese intelligence officer in Shanghai. A fictional character; Japanese reading of 仲村信夫.

仲良.note: Xu Zhongliang (徐仲良), the postman's son and the story's protagonist. The given name pairs 仲 (“second-born”) with 良 (“good, upright”). A fictional character; pinyin.

任应岐.note: A former Zhili-clique general drawn into Ji Hongchang's circle; extradited and executed alongside Ji in 1934, though, as Chen notes, not himself a Communist.

任远.note: Jidong intelligence station chief captured and later escaped from the Japanese.

伊勢.note: Province held by Takigawa Kazumasu; Hideyoshi’s first target in the spring campaign.

伊勢屋嘉兵衛.note: The Kyōto shopkeeper's cover identity Jūzō assigns to Kuroami at the end of ch01.

伊東甲子太郎.note: Born Suzuki Daizō in Hitachi; a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept and Mito-school loyalist ideologue who kept a dōjō at Fukagawa in Edo. He joined the Shinsengumi at the end of 1864, meaning all along to turn it into a topple-the-shogunate party. His faction would later break away as the Kōdai-ji guardsmen and be destroyed.

伊藤一刀斎.note: Founder of the Ittō-ryū line of swordsmanship.

伊藤近二.note: The Japanese agent, planted as a postal inspector at the Jing'an office, who has lived twenty years in Shanghai and been exiled to it for defeatist talk. A fictional character; Japanese name in Hepburn romanization.

伊賀.note: The 'hidden country', home province of the ninja.

伊賀ノ乱.note: The Tenshō Iga War; Nobunaga's 1581 invasion (Tenshō 9).

伊香保.note: A hot-spring town in Kōzuke (Jōshū), site of the shrine tablet affair between Chiba Shūsaku and the Nen-ryū.

伍豪.note: An alias of Zhou Enlai, from his code name in the Awakening Society; the pivot of the fake ‘renunciation’ notices and their rebuttal. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: two-syllable pseudonym, spaced like a name (Zhou Enlai's alias).

伏見城.note: Hideyoshi's great castle southeast of Kyoto, built from 1592.

众坊街.note: A street in Yau Ma Tei, Hong Kong. Attested official English name.

会合衆.note: The council of thirty-six townsmen who governed Sakai; the ten strongest were the naya-shu (warehouse men).

会审公廨.note: The Shanghai concessions' pre-1930 joint tribunal, abolished by the two reproduced retrocession agreements and replaced by the Chinese Special District Courts.

会津.note: The Matsudaira domain of the mountainous northeast, staunchly loyal to the shogunate; its lord was Kyoto Protector and the Shinsengumi's patron, and it fought the Restoration to a bitter end in 1868.

会田源右衛門.note: The false name Jūzō gives in Sakai, posing as a gōshi of Kanbara in Echigo.

伝習隊.note: The shogunate's French-drilled infantry corps. Full note at ch44.

传记文学.note: Zhuanji Wenxue, the Taipei monthly in which Nameless Heroes was serialized.

佐々成政.note: Lord of Toyama, a staunch Shibata man who submitted to Hideyoshi after Katsuie’s fall.

佐々木唯三郎.note: Historical, 1833–1868. A shogunal swordsman, later of the Mimawarigumi; killed Kiyokawa Hachirō in 1863 and is widely thought to have led the killing of Sakamoto Ryōma in 1867. Shiba writes the given name 唯三郎; he is also recorded as 只三郎.

佐々木承禎.note: A defeated commander (of the Rokkaku/Sasaki line) sheltered at Erin-ji, as the novel has it.

佐久間十蔵.note: A boy samurai of Katsuie’s, betrothed to Maa; killed in the last assault on Kita-no-shō.

佐久間盛政.note: Katsuie’s nephew (styled Genba-no-jō), a renowned horseman; his raid on Mount Ōiwa and refusal to withdraw opened the disaster at Shizugatake.

佐尔格.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet military-intelligence master spy who worked first in Shanghai and then in Tokyo, where he reported on Japanese and German intentions. Arrested by the Japanese in 1941 and hanged in 1944.

佐川官兵衛.note: Aizu senior retainer, nicknamed the Aizu ogre; captain of the han's Bessentai. Full note at ch44.

佐渡.note: The island whose gold mines Hideyoshi engrossed.

佐藤彦五郎.note: Historical, 1827–1902. Headman (nanushi) of Hino, married to Toshizō's elder sister; his household kept the Tennen Rishin-ryū training hall where Kondō and Toshizō trained.

佐藤贤了.note: Japanese officer; deputy chief of staff of the South China Expeditionary Army, who helped Wang Jingwei's Shanghai activity.

佐野七五三之助.note: A comrade of Itō who died by his own hand before the Restoration.

何庆宇.note: Enemy-work section chief of the Eighth Route Army’s Shandong Column.

何应钦.note: 1890-1987; senior Nationalist general, at this time acting head of the Military Affairs Commission's Beiping Branch.

余吾湖.note: The small lake below Shizugatake, around which the decisive fighting turned.

余延智.note: Fifth Action Brigade commander (surname perhaps Chu), killed with Xu Shouxin at No. 76 in December 1939.

佟麟阁.note: Later a Nationalist general and a celebrated martyr of the 1937 defense of Beiping.

侯宝林.note: 1917–1993. The most celebrated xiangsheng (comic-dialogue) performer of his day.

保安处.note: The security office within the Police Administration Department; Yang Qun's posting.

保定.note: The Hebei provincial city on the Ping-Han line; seat of the First Command Room's Baoding Group and a hub of the line's pacification work.

保密局.note: The Ministry of National Defense's Bureau of Confidential Investigation, the reorganized successor to Juntong after Dai Li's death in 1946, under Mao Renfeng. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: majority and parallel to Juntong/Zhongtong handles; full translated gloss at first use.

保田安政.note: Brother of Sakuma Morimasa; the source names him both Yasuda (folio 205) and Sakuma (folio 223) Yasumasa.

保皇党.note: The Emperor-Protection party of Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, opposed to the revolutionaries.

俞作柏.note: Deputy commander-in-chief of the Loyal and Patriotic Army, addressed in one of Dai Li's quoted telegrams.

俞飞鹏.note: A Chiang confidant who headed wartime transport.

俞鸿均.note: Yu Hongjun (俞鸿钧, 1898–1960; O.K. Yui), mayor of Shanghai at the time of the 1937 Japanese invasion. Historical. The source prints the name 俞鸿均; the attested figure is 俞鸿钧.

信孝.note: Oda Nobutaka (1558–1583), Nobunaga's third son, joint commander of the projected Shikoku campaign.

信康.note: Ieyasu's eldest son and heir, forced to commit seppuku in 1579 at the age of twenty-one, with Hanzō as his second.

信忠.note: Oda Nobutada, Nobunaga’s heir, who took his own life at Nijō castle during the Honnō-ji revolt.

信玄.note: Takeda Shingen (1521–1573), the great warlord of Kai, Katsuyori's father.

信長.note: Oda Nobunaga (1534–1582), the warlord who had brought most of central Japan under his power.

信雄.note: Oda Nobunaga's son, adopted into the Kitabatake house of Ise; led the failed first Iga campaign.

傅作义.note: 1895–1974. Nationalist commander in North China; his 1949 surrender gave the Communists Beiping without a fight, and he served the People's Republic as water-resources minister.

傅式说.note: Former president of Daxia University who joined the Wang regime; New Group One recruited two of his secretaries. The source misprints his surname 傅 as 传.

傅筱庵.note: 1872–1940. Mayor of the Japanese puppet Shanghai municipal government; assassinated in 1940.

储备券.note: 储备券, the banknotes of the Wang regime's Central Reserve Bank; the currency of occupied Shanghai.

僧兵.note: The ‘warrior-monks’ kept in arms by the great temples to fight rival lords and hold down their own tenantry; the Negoro-ji fielded them in the thousands.

儀助.note: Maki’s elder brother, farming the family plot at Nagao; twenty-two in Tenshō 13.

元遗山.note: Jin-dynasty poet Yuan Haowen (styled Yishan), a couplet of whose ci Wang echoed in his last poem.

兆丰公园.note: 兆丰公园; the large park in the western part of the International Settlement, known in English as Jessfield Park (today Zhongshan Park, 中山公园), with a lake and a small zoo. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: concession-era proper names keep their period English forms (shelf canon).

先斗町.note: A narrow lane of teahouses and geisha between the Kamo River and Kiyamachi in central Kyoto.

先施公司.note: Sincere Co., opened on Nanjing Road, Shanghai, in 1917; one of the 'four great' pre-war department stores. Cited in ch05 as commercial camouflage for moving parcels. Attested in histories of Nanjing Road commerce.

光复会.note: A rival revolutionary body (Guangfuhui) set up by Zhang Taiyan and Tao Chengzhang.

光复军.note: The armed force of the Korean Provisional Government; historical.

光秀.note: Akechi Mitsuhide, Nobunaga's killer at Honnō-ji, defeated by Hideyoshi at Yamazaki. Bare surname-reading used in ch05 narration; see 明智光秀.

克鲁格.note: Father Kruger (克鲁格), the fair-haired German priest who succeeds Father Brown as the church's intelligence contact and later strikes his own bargain with Zhongliang. A fictional character; the source's transliteration of a German surname (Kruger/Krüger).

児玉民部.note: A Chōshū commander who led the assault on the Shimodachiuri Gate in the Hamaguri Gate battle.

入定.note: 'Entering samadhi': the eternal meditation into which Kobo Daishi is said to have passed, neither living nor dead.

兪叶封.note: Variant-glyph spelling (兪 for 俞) of Yu Yefeng, the collaborator sanctioned at the Gengxin Stage in January 1940 (ch24).

八仙桥.note: A district of the French Concession (lit. 'Eight Immortals Bridge'). Book form 'Baxianqiao', consistent across ch08/13/14/16.

八办.note: Short for 八路军办事处. The open liaison offices the Communists were allowed to maintain in Nationalist cities during the wartime alliance; rendered “the Eighth Route office(s)” or, where the author uses the bare abbreviation, “the offices.”

八十八师.note: A German-trained elite infantry division of the National Revolutionary Army, sent to the 1937 Battle of Shanghai. Historical.

八木源之丞.note: A rural samurai of Mibu whose house lodged the corps; the Yagi residence survives as a site of Shinsengumi history.

八王子.note: A town west of Fuchū on the Kōshū Highway.

公安部.note: The People's Republic's ministry of public security (police), founded in 1949 out of the Military Commission's Public Security Department.

公用方.note: A domain's political-liaison bureau, handling its dealings with the court, the shogunate, and other domains in Kyoto.

六国饭店.note: 六国饭店, the 'Six Nations Hotel' in the Legation Quarter; the site of the Zhang Jingyao killing. Noted at first appearance in Section 1.

六波羅.note: A district on the east bank of the Kamo below Higashiyama, once the seat of the Taira and of the Kamakura shogunate's Kyoto office.

六車宗伯.note: A swordsman of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, deputy master at Fuchū, whom Toshizō kills in this chapter. The surname is read Rokusha on the source’s own furigana (ろくしゃそうはく), echoing the Rokusha Myōjin shrine he serves; hence the chapter title, ‘Cutting Down Rokusha.’

兰心大戏院.note: A Shanghai theatre (the historical Lyceum Theatre); He Yashu says they saw a Shaoxing opera there (Chapter 25). Romanized 'Lanxin' to match the Lanxin Western Restaurant. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the venue's own period name; proper names are exempt from the American-spelling locale.

关东军.note: The Japanese army in the Northeast; staged the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931. Chapter 28.

关中.note: ‘Within the passes’: the region around the ancient capital Chang’an (modern Xi’an), in the Wei River valley. The Yan jewel-house is seated there (ch03–ch04).

关特演.note: The Kantokuen (関特演), a huge July 1941 mobilization of the Kwantung Army against the Soviet Union after the German invasion; never carried out, as Japan chose the southern advance.

关露.note: 1907–1982. Born Hu Shoumei; a celebrated poet and left-wing writer sent by Pan Hannian to work inside the Wang Jingwei and Japanese secret services, at the cost of a lasting public reputation as a “collaborator.” Imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case; rehabilitated shortly before her suicide.

兴亚院.note: The Asia Development Board, a Japanese cabinet organ set up in 1938 to run affairs in occupied China, with a special-service department that drew the secret services under one hand. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: one romanization, no hyphen (newest book's form).

兵工署.note: The National Government's ordnance directorate, which oversaw the arsenals and paid the arsenal workers' death benefits.

兵糧丸.note: A shinobi’s ration-ball of dried rice, buckwheat, bonito, loach, pickled plum and pine bark, said to sustain a man ten days.

冀东.note: The eastern part of Hebei, seat of the Japanese-sponsored puppet 'East Hebei' government.

内山书店.note: Real. Uchiyama Kanzo's Hongkou bookshop (from 1917; moved 1929 to Scott Road), stocking Japanese and banned left-wing books; Lu Xun's haunt.

内海二郎.note: A pupil of Itō who later cast his lot with the Satsuma domain.

内藤新宿.note: The first post-station out of Edo on the Kōshū Highway.

内野.note: The Uchino, the open ground in the northwest of the capital (the old palace site) on which Hideyoshi raised the Jurakudai.

冈村宁次.note: Commander-in-chief of the Japanese China Expeditionary Army, who surrendered at Nanjing on 9 September 1945.

军事三人小组.note: The three-man committee of Marshall, Zhang Qun for the government, and Zhou Enlai for the Communists, that directed the 1946 truce negotiations.

军事调处执行部.note: The tripartite body (American, Nationalist, and Communist) set up at Beiping in 1946 to enforce the cease-fire brokered by the Marshall Mission.

军委二局.note: The Central Military Commission’s Second Bureau, the CCP’s radio-interception and cipher-breaking service.

军委会.note: The Nationalist supreme military command, chaired by Chiang Kai-shek.

军统.note: The Kuomintang's Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (secret police). The name is strictly of 1938; its use for 1931 is a mild anachronism. See the note at Chapter 4. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the shelf handle (article varies by sentence); full 'Military Statistics Bureau' gloss at first use.

冢田.note: The Eleventh Army commander named in Jiang's cover story.

冯传庆.note: Juntong main-station radio officer turned secret Communist; member of Zhang Luping’s branch, executed 1945.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the ‘Christian General’ and warlord, at this time an anti-Japanese figure.

冯雪峰.note: 1903–1976; poet, literary theorist and CCP cultural figure, liaison to Shanghai’s writers.

冷藏间谍.note: An agent planted deep in the enemy camp and kept dormant, doing no active work, until a decisive moment; the book uses it interchangeably with 战略间谋 “strategic spy.”

凌云.note: 1917–2018. A Social Affairs Department trainee; the first Minister of State Security of the People's Republic.

出羽守宗慶.note: Sōkyū's claimed father, who drifted from Ōmi into Yamato.

刀ざらえ.note: The confiscation of swords and other arms from temples, townsmen and peasants; the Negoro edict of Tenshō 13 was a prelude to the general sword-hunt (刀狩) Hideyoshi decreed in 1588.

刀疤强.note: Old Mo's nephew and one of the last surviving marsh bandits; his byname 刀疤 is the knife-scar on his left cheek.

分倍橋.note: A small bridge south of Bubaigawara, the appointed place of the fight.

分倍河原.note: A district on the old Tama-River flats near Fuchū, a road-junction long fought over; site of the 1333 battle and of the duel of this chapter.

分水亭.note: A lakeside pavilion at a fork in the channel; the place Qin Shuji names for their meeting, and where their lives divide.

刑部左衛門.note: Bare name of Mochizuki Gyōbuzaemon in dialogue.

刘宗铭.note: General Rong's name in his native place; he and Old Pan served together in the Nineteenth Route Army. Pinyin.

刘少奇.note: 1898–1969; PRC head of state, purged and hounded to death in the Cultural Revolution.

刘绍唐.note: 1921-2000; founder and, for some four decades, editor of the Taipei monthly Biographical Literature, the foremost venue for Republican-era memoir and first-hand historical recollection, in which the whole of Chen's memoir was serialized.

刘钊.note: Pan Hannian’s secret courier in the Jiangnan area and Zheng Wendao’s Party sponsor.

刘麻子.note: Zhu Qi's sworn brother and a rival marsh chief; his nickname means 'pockmarks' (see note).

判官笔.note: Iron writing-brushes used as weapons; the traditional arms of the underworld clerks called panguan. The Iron-Faced Judge carries a pair (ch02).

利助.note: A newly hired servant of the Masuya who informed on the arms cache. Romanization mine.

利家.note: Maeda Toshiie, one of Hideyoshi's most senior generals and a boyhood comrade.

利顺德饭店.note: The Astor House Hotel in the British concession; glossed at first appearance.

制裁.note: The service's euphemism for the targeted killing or execution of an enemy or traitor; kept as the book's own term.

前川十郎左衛門.note: A squad-leader (kumigashira) of the Kyoto magistracy, Gohei’s immediate superior.

前川屋敷.note: One of the requisitioned residences at Mibu that served as Shinsengumi barracks; Yamanami was confined and died here.

前田.note: The Maeda house of Maeda Gen'i (distinct from the Kaga Maeda).

前田利家.note: Shibata general and lord of Noto (1538–1599); his withdrawal at Shizugatake decided the battle for Hideyoshi. Later one of Hideyoshi’s Five Elders.

前田利長.note: Toshiie’s eldest son, lord of the castle at Fuchū (Takefu) in Echizen.

前田玄以.note: Hideyoshi's magistrate of Kyoto (Kyoto shoshidai/bugyō), a former monk who administered the capital and its temples; Gohei's new master, at 200 koku.

副長.note: Fukuchō, second to the commander; Hijikata’s chosen post, from which he worked the corps.

力行社.note: The 'Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People' (三民主义力行社), a secret Whampoa-clique organization of 1932, popularly the 'Blue Shirts.'

劝业场.note: A famous multi-story commercial arcade in the Tianjin French concession.

加田進次郎.note: Oyuki’s late husband in the novel, an Edo-resident foot-guard of the Ōgaki domain; like Oyuki, a fictional figure.

加納道之助.note: An old comrade of Itō, later known as Kanō Washio; he went over to the Satsuma side.

加納鵰雄.note: A corporal of the Shinsengumi in Itō’s faction; 鵰雄 is a roster variant for the same man written 道之助 elsewhere (see ch27).

加藤嘉明.note: One of the Seven Spears of Shizugatake; later a daimyo and admiral under Hideyoshi.

加藤清正.note: Katō Kiyomasa (1562–1611), boyhood name Toranosuke; one of Hideyoshi's foremost captains, later daimyo of Higo.

加藤肥後守.note: Katō Kiyomasa, under his court title Governor of Higo; the Iga man Kuranawate-no-Shishiji was killed for entering his service.

加賀.note: The great domain on the Sea of Japan (modern Ishikawa), held by the Maeda house; its levy took the Tengu Party’s surrender.

助勤.note: A line officer of the corps, adjutant in quarters and platoon-leader in the field; the term borrowed from the student self-government of the shōgunal college.

励志计划.note: The plan under which the Ministry of National Defense raised, trained, and tasked the Pacification Corps; 励志 means to steel the will or better oneself.

励志训练班.note: The training class at the Central Training Corps in Nanjing through which the cadres of the Pacification Corps were passed; see the note on the Lizhi Plan.

勝家.note: Shibata Katsuie, Nobunaga's senior general, passed over by Hideyoshi after Yamazaki. Bare given name; see 柴田勝家.

勝海舟.note: Katsu Kaishū (1823–1899), the far-sighted shogunal official who built the first Japanese navy and, in 1868, negotiated the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle.

勝猛.note: Given name of Shima Sakon; he refers to himself by it.

勝頼.note: Takeda Katsuyori (1546–1582), son and heir of Shingen; the last lord of the Takeda.

勾魂手.note: The Iron-Faced Judge’s partner from the Blue-Robe Tower; famed for a pair of silver hooks and for a snakeskin whip that can crack a walnut on three cubes of bean-curd (ch02).

北ノ庄.note: Katsuie’s castle (modern Fukui), built 1575 with a famous nine-storied keep, where he and Oichi died.

北伐.note: Real. The Nationalist-Communist military campaign (1926-28) from Guangzhou to unify China; its approach to Shanghai in 1927 is the backdrop to Cui Wentai's story.

北光丸.note: The Yamashita Steamship Company cargo vessel that carried Wang Jingwei from Vietnam to Shanghai in 1939.

北四川路.note: 北四川路; a main road running north from the Settlement into the Hongkou district; older English North Szechuen Road.

北平.note: The name of Beijing under the Nationalist government (1928–49); site of the Tongyi Company’s largest creditors.

北平军分会.note: The Beiping Branch of the National Military Affairs Commission (军事委员会北平分会), the top Nationalist military organ in North China, headed at this time by acting deputy chairman He Yingqin.

北政所.note: Title of the principal wife of a Regent; here Hideyoshi's wife.

北极阁.note: A height at Nanjing; Wang climbed it on the Double-Ninth for his last ci.

北添佶麿.note: Tosa loyalist, cut down at the head of the Ikedaya stairs. The given name 佶麿 is read Yoshimaro.

北辰一刀流.note: The great Edo sword school of Chiba Shūsaku, at the height of its fame in these years; Tōdō Heisuke’s school.

十九路军.note: Real. Cantonese army that fought the Japanese at Shanghai in 1932, later sent against Communists in Fujian.

十人团.note: the 1928 ten-man Liaison Group of Dai Li lore, retrojected to 1927 by the book

十津川.note: A mountain district of Yamato (modern Nara) whose rural samurai were fierce imperial loyalists; see the note here.

千人町.note: The Hachiōji quarter named for the Thousand Guardsmen settled there; site of the Hiruma hall.

千利休.note: The supreme tea master; the same man recorded elsewhere under his lay name 千宗易 Sen no Sōeki.

千宗易.note: Sen no Rikyū, the great tea master; here under his lay name Sōeki.

千葉周作.note: Historical, 1792/94–1855. Founder of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and of the Genbukan hall in Edo; his school’s ties to the Mito house made it a seedbed of revere-the-Emperor politics.

千葉栄次郎.note: Historical, 1833–1862. Second son of Chiba Shūsaku and a swordsman prodigy of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, nicknamed the Little Tengu of Chiba.

千鳥の香炉.note: The incense-burner that, by popular legend, cried out and betrayed Goemon at Hideyoshi's pillow; a 'surface' fiction of the kabuki plays.

半山.note: The hillside residential quarter of Hong Kong Island.

半造.note: Son of Hiruma Yohachi and head, from a hall in Senninmachi at Hachiōji, of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū; married to Sen, daughter of the abbot of the Senjubō.

华东局.note: The Chinese Communist Party's regional bureau for East China. Attested English name.

华兴洋行.note: A silk-and-tea export firm; the Juntong's Shanghai intelligence relay in cover.

华北五烈士.note: Also called the Beiping Five Martyrs: Xie Shiyan, Ding Xing, Zhu Jianguo, Zhao Liangzhang, and Shi Chun, Communist agents inside the Nationalist Eleventh War Zone, arrested in 1947 and executed in 1948.

华北剿匪总司令部.note: The North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters, the Nationalist theater command that conferred the First Brigade's code-name 'Unit 0760'; built on the keyed 剿匪 'bandit-suppression'.

华南情报局.note: The Communist intelligence bureau Pan Hannian ran from Hong Kong, coordinating the various networks of the region.

华懋饭店.note: Victor Sassoon's Cathay Hotel on the Bund (今和平饭店), the most fashionable hotel of 1930 Shanghai.

华格臬路.note: A street in the French Concession, today's Ninghai West Road; site of Du Yuesheng's chief residence.

华润公司.note: Founded in Hong Kong in 1948–49 out of the Party's trading firms; today one of China's largest state-owned conglomerates.

华清池.note: A Ganzhou bathhouse named for the Tang imperial hot springs. Fictional locale.

卓琳.note: 1916–2009. Born Pu Qiongying, daughter of a wealthy Yunnan ham merchant; Deng Xiaoping's wife from 1939 to the end of his life.

单不移.note: Zhongtong boss at Luochuan (the surname 单 is read Shàn).

南京.note: The Nationalist capital until 1937; later seat of the Wang Jingwei regime. Historical.

南华日报.note: The Hong Kong Chinese daily run by the Wang Jingwei faction, which floated the 'Blue Shirt Society' theory of the Hanoi killing.

南委.note: The Communists’ Southern Work Committee, under the Southern Bureau, responsible for the underground in the southeast and south; wrecked by Zhongtong in 1942.

南宁.note: The capital of Guangxi, in the region where Ho Chi Minh was jailed by the Nationalists. Attested pinyin.

南市.note: The old South City district of Shanghai, site of the Nanshi Refugee Zone.

南汇.note: A rural county on the coast southeast of Shanghai.

南汉宸.note: Communist figure, co-organizer of the 1934 Tianjin alliance; later the founding governor of the People's Bank of China.

南洋兄弟烟草公司.note: One of China's largest cigarette makers, founded by the Jian brothers.

南禅寺.note: A great Zen monastery in eastern Kyoto whose gate-tower is bound up with the Goemon legend.

南蛮.note: “Southern Barbarian”: the Japanese term for Europeans and their goods.

南蛮寺.note: The Jesuit church in Kyoto (Our Lady of the Assumption), completed c. 1576.

南通.note: The Jiangsu city on the north bank of the Yangtze, Zhang Jian's base.

卡尔登公寓.note: A Shanghai apartment building, home of Chen's friend Hu Yongquan.

卢小嘉.note: Son of the Zhejiang military governor Lu Yongxiang; his quarrel with Huang Jinrong over the actress Lu Lanchun led to Huang's arrest and Du's rescue of him.

卢汉.note: Yunnan-army general who took the Japanese surrender in Hanoi and later governed Yunnan; he declared for the Communists in 1949.

卢绪章.note: 1911–1995. The Communist businessman who ran Guangda Huaxing as a Party front and money-maker; after 1949 a founder of the state foreign-trade system.

卫立煌.note: 1897–1960. Nationalist First War Zone commander; won over enough to give the Eighth Route Army ammunition, he was later suspected of Communist sympathies and eventually returned to the mainland.

原田.note: Mr. Harada (原田先生), the aged proprietor of the Japanese pawnshop on Fourth Avenue who keeps Qin Zhaokuan's sealed box against the day the ring appears. A fictional character; Japanese surname.

原田左之助.note: Historical, 1840–1868. A spearman of the Hōzōin line; died in the fighting around Edo.

双十协定.note: The “Summary of Conversations” signed 10 October 1945 (the Double Tenth, the ROC national day) at the close of the Chongqing negotiations; its terms were soon overtaken by civil war.

双重政权.note: The wartime coexistence of a Nationalist-appointed and a Communist-appointed government in the same Border Region county; the “nails” of the chapter title.

反战同盟.note: The Japanese People’s Anti-war Alliance (日本人民反战同盟, formed 1939 under Kaji Wataru from Japanese prisoners of war); Itō claims membership to explain his survival. Historical.

反省院.note: A Nationalist ‘Three People’s Principles’ re-education facility to which unconvicted political prisoners could be transferred, used as a rescue channel. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: lowercase as the generic institution; capitalize only in the proper name of a specific one.

古琴.note: The seven-stringed zither of the Chinese scholar, an emblem of cultivation. See the note at first appearance (Prologue).

古高.note: A loyalist agent (1829–1864) who, under the merchant alias Masuya Kiemon, ran an arms depot for the Chōshū-aligned plotters. His arrest set off the Ikedaya raid.

台儿庄.note: Town in southern Shandong, site of the Chinese victory of spring 1938.

史良.note: 1900–1985; lawyer, the only woman of the Seven Gentlemen; first Minister of Justice of the PRC.

史量才.note: 1880–1934; owner of the Shenbao, assassinated 1934 on Chiang Kai-shek's orders.

叶剑英.note: 1897–1986. A Communist general and later marshal; in charge of liaison for the Southern Bureau, and decades on a decisive figure in the arrest of the Gang of Four.

叶孤城.note: The Lord of White Cloud City, of Flying-Immortal Isle in the Southern Sea; named in passing by Lu Xiaofeng as one of the few peerless swordsmen of the age, beside Ximen Chuixue (ch04).

叶秀珠.note: The third of the Four Beauties of Emei, and the honest, plain-spoken one of the four (ch09).

叶鸿英.note: 1860–1937; a Shanghai merchant and philanthropist, target of a boycott-era squeeze.

司徒雷登.note: American ambassador to China 1946–1949; the conventional English form is used.

司空摘星.note: The king of thieves, who steals only on a wager and never what is truly valuable; being robbed by him is counted an honour. He once matched Lu Xiaofeng at somersaults on the summit of Mount Tai, and takes the likeness of Zhao the Pockmarked in ch08.

吉村貫一郎.note: Historical inspector of the corps, a Nanbu (Morioka) man; later the subject of Asada Jirō's novel Mibu Gishi Den.

吉田稔麿.note: Chōshū loyalist (1841–1864), a favored pupil of Yoshida Shōin; killed at twenty-four in the Ikedaya fight.

吉田良道.note: The Kyoto painter under whom the fictional Oyuki is said to study; part of Shiba’s invented history for her.

吉祥天女.note: The Buddhist goddess of beauty and good fortune (Sanskrit Lakṣmī / Śrī); a byword for a lovely face. Footnoted at first appearance.

吉章简.note: Nationalist gendarmerie officer, commander of the Fourth Regiment and leader of Chen's Lixingshe cell; later a general. The source's stray '古章简' is the same man.

吉野.note: Mountainous district south of Nara, celebrated since antiquity for its cherry blossoms; the setting of Hideyoshi's 1594 flower-viewing progress.

吉鸿昌.note: 1895–1934; Northwest Army general, figure in the 1933 Chahar anti-Japanese army; executed by the Nationalists. Honored as a Communist martyr in the People's Republic.

同盟会.note: The Revolutionary Alliance founded by Sun Yat-sen at Tokyo in 1905, forerunner of the Nationalist Party.

名主.note: The headman of a village, lowest office of Tokugawa rural administration: a leading farmer, not a samurai.

名古屋.note: Japanese city where Wang Jingwei died of illness in 1944.

名張.note: A town in northern Iga; the home Goemon invents for his false self, 'Tahei.'

名張ノ耳.note: 名張ノ耳; 耳 (Mimi, 'ear') is a by-name from his keen hearing. A former Iga ninja of the Tsuge faction turned beggar, then Kōga informer; footnoted at first appearance in ch13.

名護屋.note: The staging base on the Higashi-Matsuura peninsula in Hizen, north Kyūshū, raised for the invasion of Korea. Not to be confused with Nagoya in Owari.

后三杰.note: Xiong Xianghui, Chen Zhongjing, and Shen Jian, the trio that penetrated Hu Zongnan’s headquarters; named in deliberate parallel to the “Three Heroes of Longtan” of the early 1930s (see ch. 1).

向松坡.note: Xiang Haiqian; see the note at his first appearance.

向海潜.note: 1888–1974; also called Xiang Songpo; a leader of the Hongmen (the ‘Five Lakes’ lodges) and a veteran of the 1911 Revolution.

吕正操.note: Communist commander of the Central Hebei Military District, which held the Beiping-Tianjin-Baoding triangle from 1938; later a PLA general.

启东.note: A county at the Yangtze mouth on the Beisha line.

启德机场.note: Hong Kong's airport. Attested English name.

吴三桂.note: 1612–1678; the Ming general who opened the Shanhaiguan pass to the Manchus in 1644, letting the Qing conquest through.

吴世宝.note: Alias Yunfu (云甫); an underworld figure and first commander of No. 76's guard corps, later poisoned.

吴乃宪.note: Second chief of the Shanghai District, styled Jinfu, of the first class of the Whampoa Military Academy; later a National Assembly delegate. Figures in 'Rooting Out Traitors in the North.'

吴南山.note: The Qingyang schoolteacher who graduated the Hanzhong class, came forward to the Communists, and became the Border Security’s long-hidden field operative in Longdong; the case began with him.

吴开先.note: A leading member of the CC Clique in Shanghai.

吴德峰.note: 1896–1976. A founder of the Party's courier and intelligence systems; ran the hidden Xi'an intelligence station under a family cover and later held senior legal posts.

吴成方.note: A Communist intelligence officer under Pan Hannian who ran the Japanese cell in Shanghai; imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case and rehabilitated in 1982.

吴敬恒.note: The formal given name of the Kuomintang elder better known by his courtesy name, Wu Zhihui; the same man. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: known in English by his hao (Wu Zhihui / Wu Chih-hui); note 敬恒 is the ming.

吴樾.note: Revolutionary whose 1905 attempt to bomb the five ministers sent to study constitutions inspired Wang's own plot.

吴泰勋.note: Courtesy name Youquan, called 'the Fifth Master'; son of the Manchurian general Wu Junsheng, and a wealthy patron of Dai Li's work. Chen honors him as a 'nameless hero.'

吴淞口.decided: the mouth of the Wusong River
吴淞口.note: 吴淞口; the mouth of the Huangpu where it meets the Yangtze estuary, the seaward gate of Shanghai; older English Woosung. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the plain form (never send the reader to a dictionary; 'bar' is nautical jargon); 'Woosung' stands as midnight's period deviation.

吴石.note: 1894–1950. Nationalist lieutenant general and deputy chief of the general staff; the highest-placed Communist agent in Taiwan, executed in Taipei in 1950.

吴稚晖.note: 1865–1953; veteran Kuomintang elder and calligrapher; also written 吴敬恒.

吴绍澍.note: Du's disciple turned rival; postwar vice-mayor of Shanghai who publicly broke with him.

吴醒亚.note: A CC-clique Nationalist official; head of the Shanghai Bureau of Social Affairs in the 1930s.

吴铁城.note: Kuomintang statesman; former Guangdong governor and later overseas department minister.

吾市.note: The son born to Goemon and Maki in Tenshō 12; his name plays on the ‘Go’ of Goemon (written ‘five’), remade with the character for ‘I,’ plus ‘ichi,’ a market.

呂宋.note: The northern Philippines, newly under Spanish rule from Manila.

告罗士打酒店.note: 告罗士打酒店; the Gloucester Hotel, a landmark Hong Kong hotel.

周三.note: Doorman of the Jing'an post office and Zhongliang's Communist controller. 周三 means “Zhou Three,” a plain number-name of the sort given a laborer's son. A fictional character; pinyin.

周佛海.note: A leading figure in Wang Jingwei's peace movement and later regime.

周作.note: Founder of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and of the Genbukan hall in Edo; father of Eijirō. One of the great sword-reformers of the age.

周信芳.note: 1895–1975; the great Peking-opera actor known by his stage name Qilintong (麒麟童), who took Huang Jinrong as master for protection against Gu Zhuxuan.

周兴.note: 1905–1975. Head of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office (the “Border Security”) through the Yan’an years; later a deputy minister of public security.

周大庸.note: A famed old physician of the county town whom Yanzhi consults over her daughter's deafness.

周平.note: Kondō Shūhei, Kondō Isami’s adopted son, one of the five who charged into the Ikedaya.

周恩来.note: 1898–1976; then the real director of the Party’s underground work in Shanghai; the author’s superior.

周楚康.note: Su Lina's husband, a lieutenant colonel of the National Revolutionary Army who returns to the front. A fictional character; pinyin.

周祥生.note: Founder of the Johnson (Xiangsheng) Taxi Company in Shanghai.

周至柔.note: Nationalist air-force general; dean of studies at the Air Force Officers' School.

周锡良.note: A counter-espionage operative inside No. 76, killed there in December 1939; the puppet verdict writes his name with a different middle character (周希良), alike in sound.

和平建国军.note: The Wang regime's armed forces, in full the Peace National Construction Army.

和泉守兼定.note: A celebrated sword-signature. The blade Hijikata carried through his life bore it; see the note at its first appearance.

咏梅.note: The title of the poem used as a contact signal; a 七律 (regulated verse).

哈同花园.note: Aili Garden, the vast Nanjing Road estate of the Baghdadi-Jewish tycoon Silas Hardoon.

哈柴.note: Emil Hácha, president of rump Czecho-Slovakia, who in March 1939 signed his country to Germany and stayed on as puppet 'State President' of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.

唐先生.note: Tang Ya's father, an engineer at the Hanyang Arsenal, drowned when his boat was sunk on the westward evacuation. Fictional.

唐太太.note: Tang Ya's frail mother, who dies in the Jiaochangkou tunnel disaster. Fictional.

唐官屯.note: The town in Jinghai county on the Jin-Pu line where the assault-team command was handed from Wang Hongzhu to Chang Shaozeng, and where the Second Command Room's Third Group was stationed.

唐少爷.note: The soy-works heir who becomes the town's collaborationist headman.

唐有壬.note: A soft, 'feminine' associate of Wang's clique, named as already dead; assassinated in 1935.

唐津.note: A domain in Hizen, in northwest Kyushu; Ogasawara was its daimyō’s heir.

唐绍仪.note: 1862-1938; first premier of the Republic, assassinated in Shanghai.

唐雅.note: A Chinese-literature student turned Chongqing bailiff and executioner; the woman Jiang is ordered to kill. Fictional; her given name Ya means “refined, elegant.”

商丘.note: 商丘; a city in eastern Henan.

商山二老.note: Two aged and revered masters of the Heaven’s Bird sect, reckoned the polestar of the martial world; Huo Tianqing is their junior martial-brother (ch08).

善海.note: Abbot of the Senjubō, the Shinshū temple in Hachiōji where Toshizō lodged in his peddling days. Romanization mine.

善耆.note: Prince Su, the Qing Minister of the Interior who examined Wang and spared his life out of regard for his talent.

喜六.note: A farmer of Ishida village, Toshizō's eldest surviving brother and head of the house.

嘉禾县.note: The Jiangnan county in which Xietang lies.

嘉陵宾馆.note: The premier hotel of wartime Chongqing.

嘉陵江.note: The river that joins the Yangtze at Chongqing. Attested English form.

四国.note: One of the regions levied for corvée labor for the invasion.

四国屋.note: Shōkuōya Jūbei, keeper of the Kiyamachi restaurant Tantora, a known haunt of the Chōshū and Tosa men.

四方田但馬守.note: An Akechi general (Soda Yoichiro's lord); the Shinsho Taikōki makes his deeds and death at Yamazaki a set-piece. A kinsman-fighter, Yomoda Matabei, figures in the Honnō-ji account.

四明公寓.note: A 1932 lane compound in the French Concession, built as staff housing for the Siming Bank (四明邨/四明公寓). Historical.

四杂街.note: The Hankou street where the Iwai clinic and the little church stood. The name's first character means “four”; it is not a count.

四条.note: The Fourth Avenue of Kyoto (and its riverbank, 四条の河原, and bridge, 四条大橋, over the Kamo).

四野.note: The Fourth Field Army (第四野战军) of the PLA, Lin Biao’s army grown out of the Northeast forces; so renamed in 1949. Historical.

四马路.note: A busy, crowded Shanghai street (present-day Fuzhou Road), rendered by its old foreign-settlement name (Chapter 26). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: six books agree; 'Sima Road' stands as the-sword-roars' recorded deviation.

国友.note: A village of Ōmi whose swordsmiths, brought under Nobunaga after the fall of the Azai, became famous gun-makers.

国司信濃.note: A young Chōshū elder councillor (karō), only twenty-five, given overall field command of the Kyoto expedition. He was ordered to commit seppuku after the defeat.

国家总动员法.note: Japanese law of April 1938 placing the economy on a war footing.

国家政治保卫局.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic's political-security organ (1931–1935), modeled closely on the Soviet GPU; renamed the Northwest Political Security Bureau after the Long March.

国広.note: Horikawa Kunihiro, a celebrated swordsmith; here the maker of the blade Jūzō leaves to be polished.

国民党.note: Rendered ‘Kuomintang’ throughout (not ‘Nationalist Party’); the conventional English name.

国民参政会.note: The wartime advisory body; Dong Biwu and Deng Yingchao launched there a motion against the secret imprisonment of patriots (ch21). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: standard scholarly form, majority.

国民大饭店.note: The Tianjin French-concession hotel where the shooting took place on 9 November 1934. Chen also writes it simply 国民饭店.

国防线.note: The Japanese-imposed frontier along the Great Wall between occupied North China and “Manchukuo,” which a traveler could cross only with a passport, sealing the Northeast off from the resistance inside the Wall.

国防部情报局.note: The postwar successor organization to the Juntong.

国际饭店.note: 国际饭店; the Park Hotel on Nanjing Road, then Shanghai's tallest building.

土佐.note: The province on the south of Shikoku; the old Ichijō house whose retainer-surname Gohei borrows had ruled part of it.

土地庙.note: A small shrine to the local earth-god (Tudi), the humblest deity of Chinese folk religion; here a hiding place for a wireless set.

土方歳三.note: Historical figure, 1835–1869. Japanese name order, surname (Hijikata) first; the given name Toshizō carries a long final vowel. Called Toshi by his intimates.

圣玛丽公学院.note: The elite Episcopal girls’ school in Shanghai (properly 圣玛利亚女校, St. Mary’s Hall, so named 1881); Su Lina’s school. The source’s 圣玛丽公学院 is a non-standard form. Historical.

圣类思中学.note: A Catholic mission school in Xietang where Lin teaches (类思 renders the Christian name Aloysius).

坂垣征四郎.note: 1885-1948; general of the Japanese Kwantung Army, an architect of the 1931 Manchurian seizure; hanged as a war criminal. The source writes 坂垣 for the standard 板垣.

坂本.note: Akechi Mitsuhide's castle town on Lake Biwa.

坂本竜馬.note: Historical, 1836–1867. Of Tosa, a Hokushin Ittō-ryū swordsman of the Chiba hall; later the great broker of the Restoration, assassinated in 1867.

坂東.note: The old name for the eastern provinces (the Kantō), 'east of the passes'.

城隍庙.note: The City God Temple in the old Shanghai city.

基隆.note: The port at the northern tip of Taiwan, a way-station on Wang Jingwei's sea passage to Shanghai.

堀川国広.note: A short-sword of the Kyoto smith Horikawa Kunihiro (c.1531–1614); Toshizō’s companion blade to the long Izumi-no-kami Kanesada (see ch12, ch17).

堀秀政.note: Hideyoshi commander holding the Higashino fort on Kineyama, facing Katsuie at Kitsunezuka.

堺.note: The merchant port; home of Imai Sōkyū.

堺町.note: A street/quarter of the capital (not the port city of Sakai); one of the crossings watched by Kohagi's rappa.

塘沽.note: The port at the mouth of the Hai River, the sea-gate of Tianjin.

塚原卜伝.note: A sword-saint of the sixteenth century.

塩飽.note: Island group in the Inland Sea, home of noted seafarers.

士林布.note: Cotton dyed with Indanthren, the German synthetic vat-dye prized for not fading; ubiquitous in 1930s–40s China. Historical.

士道.note: Shidō, the way of the warrior; the governing idea of the corps, and of this chapter. In the Shinsengumi it hardened into a written code whose central charge, “failure in the warrior’s code,” carried death.

壬生.note: A village in the western outskirts of Kyoto, the first quarters and base of the corps that became the Shinsengumi (called, in derision, the Mibu-rō, the ‘Mibu wolves’).

复兴岛.note: An island in the Huangpu where Chiang Kai-shek stayed and received callers on the eve of the fall of Shanghai.

复兴社.note: founded spring 1932; the book has Dai Li organizing its Special Services Section in 1931 Adjudicated 2026-08-29: five books agree; 'the Fuxingshe' stands as chinas-secret-war's recorded deviation.

夏目成美.note: Real haiku poet (1749–1817), a wealthy Asakusa money-changer and a leading master of his day, patron of the young Issa.

夏見ノ耳次.note: A masterless Iga rappa Kuroami singles out at the muster. 夏見 (Natsumi) is a place in Iga; reading of 耳次 (Mimiji) unglossed in the scan and a project call.

夏超.note: 夏超; a Zhejiang provincial police chief and later provincial chairman, killed in 1926.

外島機兵衛.note: A liaison officer (kōyōgata) of the Aizu domain in Kyoto, the corps’s channel to its patron the Kyoto Protector. Reading from the source’s furigana (とじまきへえ).

外滩.note: 外滩; the riverfront boulevard of the International Settlement (外滩公园, the park on the Bund).

外白渡桥.note: The steel bridge at the mouth of Suzhou Creek, known in the foreign settlements as the Garden Bridge. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: concession-era proper names keep their period English forms (shelf canon); pinyin Waibaidu glossed once. Earlier pinyin books stand as recorded deviations.

多喜右近.note: Nineteen, a Koga seminary pupil; reserved and methodical, he reasons from stored-up fact and is usually right. One of the three who will contend with Goemon.

多宝塔.note: The Daitō of the Negoro-ji, a two-storied tahōtō raised by Kakuban in 1129 after the Konpon Daitō of Mount Kōya. It survived the burning of the temple and stands today, a National Treasure; its walls still carry the marks of Hideyoshi’s musket-balls.

多羅尾越え.note: Ieyasu's flight across Iga after Nobunaga's death; also called the Iga-goe.

多羅尾道可.note: Lay-monk and chief of the Tarao, one of the fifty-three houses of Koga; sheltered and guided Ieyasu on the Tarao crossing.

多聞院.note: A cloister of Kōfuku-ji whose diary, the Tamon-in nikki, records the 1567 fire.

大世界.note: The famous many-storeyed amusement palace at the edge of the French Concession (opened 1917); a dance hall behind it is the scene of ch31.

大东书局.note: A major Shanghai publishing house; Du Weiping was its deputy general manager.

大久保一蔵.note: Ōkubo Toshimichi (1830–1878), the Satsuma statesman who, with Saigō and Kido, drove the Restoration and then built the Meiji state; Ichizō was his earlier name. He was assassinated in 1878.

大久保忠世.note: Tokugawa retainer, lord of Futamata Castle, where Nobuyasu died.

大仏.note: The colossal Buddha of the Hōkō-ji in Higashiyama, Kyōto’s Daibutsu; “behind the Great Buddha” names the district around it.

大光明电影院.note: 大光明 ('great brightness'); a famous Shanghai cinema. Here only a passing reference (the girls touting at its door).

大公报.note: A major, respected Chinese newspaper. Attested romanization.

大兴.note: The Hebei county north of Beiping into which the North-Suburb Group extended its pacification work; Lishuiqiao lay within it.

大冶.note: County (now city) in Hubei where the author was sent on leaving Qincheng in 1975, her daughter's family being posted there with a geological team (ch40, ch42).

大华洋行.note: Qin Zhaokuan's front company. A fictional firm; 洋行 rendered “Trading Company.”

大司刑.note: The Taiping Society's office for purging its own ranks. Fictional.

大国魂神社.note: The head shrine (sōja) of Musashi Province, at Fuchū; also called the Rokusha Myōjin or Rokusho-gū. Its grand festival is the Kurayami (Darkness) Festival.

大坂.note: Site of Hideyoshi's great castle from 1583; the port to which Sakai's trade was drawn off. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: established conventional English form (lang-ja: like Kyoto, Tokyo), no macron.

大坂城.note: Hideyoshi's great stronghold, to which he had removed from the Jurakudai, leaving the Kyoto palace lightly guarded.

大垣.note: A fudai castle-town and domain in Mino (modern Gifu), ‘Ōgaki of the guns’ (see ch25).

大宮.note: A north–south avenue of the capital; the eastern bound of the Jurakudai.

大屋戸.note: Crossroads hamlet north of Kashiwara; Niwa Nagahide's HQ in 1581.

大屿山.note: The large island west of Hong Kong. Attested English form.

大岩山.note: Hill east of Lake Yogo, held by Nakagawa Kiyohide; Morimasa’s storming of it began the battle.

大島新五右衛門.note: An eighteenth-century rural samurai of Kōzuke (died 1779) famous for a trick-drawing feat of the Araki-ryū iai.

大徳寺.note: The great Rinzai Zen monastery in Murasakino, north Kyoto, closely tied to the tea masters; site of Nobunaga's funeral.

大明.note: Ming China, the ultimate object of Hideyoshi's continental war.

大智.note: ‘Great Wisdom’: the other hermit oracle, who can find a way through any question set to him — save one. Fifty taels of silver a question (ch05).

大津.note: The first post-town east of Kyoto on the Tōkaidō, on the south shore of Lake Biwa.

大生纱厂.note: Zhang Jian's cotton mills at Nantong, a landmark of early Chinese industry.

大策反.note: The chapter title. Cefan means to turn an enemy soldier or unit to one's own side; da cefan, the "great turning," is the mass defection of Nationalist forces in 1948–49, which the author treats as the highest art of the secret war.

大美晚报.decided: the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury
大美晚报.note: Real. The Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury, American-owned and foreign-registered; Chinese edition from 16 Jan 1933. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the paper's real English masthead; Da Mei Wan Bao glossed once.

大蔵卿.note: Titular Minister of the Treasury; Sōkyū's honorary court office.

大谷刑部.note: Ōtani Yoshitsugu (1559–1600), Hideyoshi’s trusted general, renowned for the handling of large forces; see the note here.

大通.note: ‘Great Penetration’: one of the two hermit oracles of the jianghu, who knows at least a little of every strange thing that ever happened. No one has seen his face; only Master Sun can find him (ch05).

大金鹏王.note: The aged, fallen monarch of the kingdom of the Golden Roc, carried into China as a child when his realm was overrun; Princess Danfeng’s father. He seeks justice from the three ministers who betrayed the old King (ch04).

大高又次郎.note: Banshū loyalist and leather-armorer; killed at the Ikedaya.

天下布武.note: “Cover the realm in arms”, Nobunaga's seal motto from 1567.

天津.note: North China treaty port; seat of the Party’s Northern Bureau.

天灯巷.note: A Chongqing lane, site of Anderson's safe house.

天然理心流.note: The country school of swordsmanship, founded by Kondō Kuranosuke and headed in this book by Kondō Isami; the school of Hijikata, Okita, and the Tama men. Known for overwhelming an opponent’s spirit and for close, practical fighting rather than polish.

天狗党.note: The radical revere-the-Emperor faction of the Mito domain, which in 1864 rose in open revolt and was crushed.

天王山.note: A hill commanding the Yamazaki defile on the road between Kyoto and Osaka, proverbial in Japanese for a decisive position. Maki Izumi and his men made their last stand here. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the battle-site hill, usually in the idiom of the decisive contest; keep the Japanese name.

天目山.note: A range in northwest Zhejiang; a New Fourth Army base area in the war against Japan. Two referents: in a Chinese source, the Tianmu Mountains (Zhejiang); in a Japanese source, Mount Tenmoku. Both correct in their books.

天禽老人.note: Founder of the Heaven’s Bird sect sixty years ago; he took a wife and got an heir only at seventy-seven, and that heir is Huo Tianqing (ch08).

天禽门.note: The school founded by the Old Man of Heaven’s Birds; Huo Tianqing is its sole bloodline heir, so its several hundred disciples would die to a man before they let harm come to him (ch08).

天竜寺.note: A great Rinzai Zen monastery in Saga, in the western reaches of Kyoto, head temple of its own branch; founded in 1339 to placate the spirit of the late Emperor Go-Daigo. Its walled compound made a natural fortress.

天竺.note: Tenjiku, the old Japanese name for India — shorthand for the farthest edge of the known world; footnoted.

天遁の術.note: The ninja 'heaven-hiding' art: using cloud, wind, rain, and the alternation of light and dark to slip a watcher's eye.

太古公司.note: The British 'Taikoo' trading and shipping firm.

太君.note: Occupation-era address for a Japanese soldier or officer (see note).

太平会.note: A secret fraternity of Christian merchants and officials, presented as legend. Fictional.

太平洋调查会.note: The IPR, an American-founded international academic body that met by turns around the Pacific rim, and whose views could sway the relevant governments.

太平記.note: The fourteenth-century war-chronicle of the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts, a storytellers' staple.

太田城.note: The Saiga peasants' marsh stronghold near Wakayama, taken by Hideyoshi's water-attack in 1585.

太田市之進.note: A Chōshū samurai of the Saga wing who rallied the wavering Fushimi force at Fujinomori; later known as Mihori Kōsuke.

太田次郎左衛門尉.note: The local strongman who commanded the peasant defenders of Ōta Castle.

太閤検地.note: Hideyoshi's nationwide cadastral land-survey, which fixed the tax base of the realm.

奥沢新三郎.note: The one Shinsengumi corpsman killed outright at the Ikedaya.

如意ヶ岳.note: A low mountain in the Higashiyama range east of Kyoto, later famous for the 大文字 bonfire; its western slope is Daimonji-yama.

妙兵衛.note: One of the rappa in Kohagi's employ, disguised as a timid shop-clerk; guides Watanabe to the ambush.

妙国寺.note: A temple of Sakai. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: Hepburn with macrons (lang-ja).

委员长.note: For Chiang; 'Chairman' would collide with the CCP usage a reader expects.

姜泳洙.note: Jiang Yongnan's elder brother, a follower of the Korean independence leader Kim Ku. Fictional; pinyin.

姜泳男.note: Protagonist of Potassium Cyanide: a Korean surgeon, Kyoto-trained, pressed into the Japanese army after the fall of Wuhan and turned Nationalist agent. A fictional character; his Korean name would be read Kang Yong-nam, but the Chinese text and this translation give the Mandarin reading throughout.

姫路.note: The castle town of Banshū (Harima), west of Osaka.

子璐.note: Miss Lan's son, killed in a stray-bullet crossfire. Pinyin of his given name.

孔令侃.note: H. H. Kung's son and chairman of the Yangtze Company; Chiang Ching-kuo's cousin.

孔祥熙.note: H. H. Kung (1881–1967); financier and premier, husband of Song Ailing. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: established conventional English form, consistent with the Soong family set; pinyin books stand as recorded deviations.

孙传芳.note: Warlord of the five southeastern provinces.

孙哲生.note: Sun Ke / Sun Fo (孙科, 1891–1973), son of Sun Yat-sen; 'Zhesheng' is his courtesy name.

孙秀青.note: The second of the Four Beauties of Emei; big-eyed, thin-lipped and sharp-tongued, and taken despite herself with Ximen Chuixue (ch09).

孙科.note: 1891–1973; son of Sun Yat-sen and a president of one of the Nationalist government’s Five Yuan.

孙老爷.note: A tiny, big-headed wastrel whose one talent is that he alone can find the oracles Datong and Dazhi; he pawns himself to pleasure-houses between windfalls. See the note on his ‘full style’ (ch05).

孝明天皇.note: Reigned 1846–1867. Fiercely opposed to opening the country to foreigners, he lent the loyalist cause an imperial sanction the shogunate could not command.

孟安南.note: An agent Gu Shenyan planted in Hong Kong years earlier; a member of the Indochinese Communist Party in cover. Pinyin.

孤山.note: An islet-hill in West Lake beside which the Yu Mansion stands.

孤岛.note: The name for the foreign-concession enclave of Shanghai between the Japanese occupation of the surrounding city in 1937 and the seizure of the concessions after Pearl Harbor in December 1941, during which the concessions kept a precarious neutral status.
