学習院.note: Not the later peers’ school of the same name but a court institution of 1863: a hall within the Imperial Palace where sympathetic nobles met loyalist activists to debate policy toward the shogunate.

宁汉分裂.note: The 1927 rupture between the Nanjing (Ning) and Wuhan (Han) Nationalist governments.

宇土.note: Uto, in Higo (modern Kumamoto), Konishi Yukinaga's castle-town and fief.

安南.note: An old name for Vietnam; here French Tonkin, in Indochina.

安国.note: The Hebei county whose Temple of the Medicine King was the object of the raid meant to seize Mao Zedong.

安土.note: Nobunaga's castle town on Lake Biwa, seat of the seminary.

安德森.note: An American diplomatic attaché, killed by Jiang in the back alley of the White Night bar. Fictional; the source's transliteration.

安次.note: The Hebei county garrisoned by the First Directly Subordinate Section (its seat, Langfang lies on the Bei-Ning line).

安溪.note: A county in Fujian, Yang Qun's birthplace and the home of Tieguanyin tea.

安藤早太郎.note: A Shinsengumi corpsman who died soon after of wounds taken at the Ikedaya.

宋哲元.note: 1885-1940; commander of the Twenty-Ninth Army in North China. See the note in this section.

宋子文.note: Real. Nationalist finance minister 1928-1933; evoked (unnamed) by the hint that 'Mr. Song's' elder brother is a great personage and the bank does Ministry of Finance bond business. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: established conventional form, spaced initials.

宋子良.note: The name the “Nationalist” negotiator used in Operation Kiri. Song Ziliang was a real member of the Soong family (a brother of T.V. Soong and Soong Mei-ling), but the man at the negotiating table was an impostor, an agent of Dai Li’s Juntong.

宋庆龄.note: conventional form; Sun Yat-sen's widow Adjudicated 2026-08-29: family-consistent conventional form (with T. V. Soong, Soong Mei-ling, H. H. Kung); the four pinyin books stand as recorded deviations.

宋教仁.note: Tongmenghui leader and architect of parliamentary Nationalism, assassinated in 1913 on Yuan Shikai's order.

宋美龄.note: 1898–2003; Madame Chiang Kai-shek, youngest of the Soong sisters. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: family-consistent conventional form.

宋霭龄.note: Eldest of the Soong sisters, wife of H. H. Kung and mother of Kong Lingkan.

宍戸備後助.note: A borrowed domain-elder’s name under which Chōshū sent a stand-in envoy to the Hiroshima interrogation.

宗義智.note: Lord of Tsushima; Hideyoshi's go-between with Korea before the invasions.

宗薫.note: Bare given name of Imai Sōkun.

宝生.note: The tailor's apprentice Yanzhi marries at her dying father's charge; Bai Tailai's heir.

宝葫芦.note: The popular name for the Guanzhong sub-district, a Communist salient thrust toward Xi’an; Hu Zongnan called the same ground the “pouch” (nangxing didai).

宝鏡寺.note: A Rinzai imperial convent (ama-monzeki) in Kyōto whose abbesses were imperial princesses; also called the Momo-no-gosho.

审干.note: Short for 审查干部, the vetting of cadres’ political histories; the phase of the Rectification that shaded into the Rescue Campaign.

宣侠父.note: 1899–1938. A Whampoa first-class graduate and secret Communist working the Xi'an united front; his 1938 assassination on Chiang Kai-shek's order is the subject of section 6.

宣祖.note: 宣祖 (Korean Sŏnjo, Japanese reading Senso), the reigning king of Chosŏn Korea (r. 1567–1608). The rumor that Yakurō was in league with his 'mother Hei' is Shiba's own baseless street-talk; footnoted.

室町.note: A north–south street in central Kyōto.

宮本武蔵.note: The famous seventeenth-century duelist, author of The Book of Five Rings.

宮部鼎蔵.note: Higo loyalist (1820–1864), a leading strategist of the cause; died at the Ikedaya.

家康.note: Tokugawa Ieyasu; crossed Iga in 1582 fleeing the Honnō-ji Incident.

家茂.note: Tokugawa Iemochi (1846–1866), the fourteenth Shōgun; a boy still, married to Princess Kazunomiya and made the living token of the union of court and shogunate.

富山弥兵衛.note: A corporal of the Shinsengumi who went over to Itō’s faction.

富阳.note: A district of Hangzhou, Zhejiang; Lin's claimed native place under his alias. Attested pinyin.

察哈尔.note: A former province north-west of Beiping, abolished in 1952.

察哈尔民众抗日同盟军.note: The anti-Japanese coalition Feng Yuxiang raised in Chahar in 1933, which Chen treats as Communist-penetrated; renamed, after Feng's withdrawal, the 'Anti-Japanese, Chiang-Chastising Army.'

寺島忠三郎.note: A young Chōshū loyalist, close to Kusaka Genzui, with whom he killed himself at the Takatsukasa mansion when the attack failed.

専修坊.note: The Shinshū temple in Hachiōji of the winter episode. Reading from the source's own furigana; romanization mine.

尊皇攘夷.note: The rallying slogan of the late-shogunate loyalists: reverence for the Emperor joined to the demand that the foreigner be driven out. Its logic pointed, in the end, past the shogunate itself.

小一.note: Koichi of Higashi-Yubune, the small man who carried the orphaned Karasumaru on his back through six happy years of childhood.

小云.note: One of the courtesans attending Ximen Chuixue (Prologue).

小仏峠.note: The pass west of Hachiōji by which the Kōshū Highway crosses into Kai.

小凤仙.note: The sing-song girl of Republican legend who helped Cai E flee Yuan Shikai's Beijing in 1915; a stock figure of stage and screen.

小北京.note: The waiter at the Dragon-Soaring Inn who serves as the Blue-Robe Tower’s eyes and hands in Chapter 1; his nickname (‘Little Peking’) is a servant’s stage-name, not a home town.

小原仁兵衛.note: Deputy commander of the Ōgaki troops, pen-name Tesshin; a noted strategist and student of Western gunnery.

小坂次郎.note: A Japanese newspaper correspondent whose feature on Jiang makes him a propaganda figure. Fictional; the name read in Japanese.

小德肋撒堂.note: A real Catholic church dedicated to St. Thérèse of Lisieux. 德肋撒 is the Catholic transliteration of Thérèse/Teresa. Historical.

小松谷.note: A wooded hollow at the eastern foot of Amidagamine, named from Taira no Shigemori's old mansion; site of Sōkyū's Kyoto villa, where Kohagi lives.

小林大介.note: A second secretary at the Japanese consulate in Shanghai who trades intelligence with Lin. Japanese reading.

小桜.note: A bell-shaking shrine maiden (miko) at the Ōkunitama Shrine in Fuchū; a minor character. Romanization mine.

小灵峰.note: A vital pass in the Siming Mountains on the outer ring of Xikou, guarded by the brigade; the subject of Feng Zhijun's garrison record.

小牧.note: Komaki-yama, the hill north of Nagoya Ieyasu fortified as his front against Hideyoshi at Gakuden; the campaign is named for it and Nagakute.

小玉.note: One of the courtesans attending Ximen Chuixue (Prologue).

小石川小日向柳町.note: The Edo neighborhood where Kondō’s training hall (the Shieikan) stood.

小笠原壱岐守.note: Ogasawara Nagamichi (1822–1891), heir of the Karatsu domain and a rōjū of the shogunate, prominent in the Chōshū war and the treaty question; Iki-no-kami is his court title.

小红.note: One of the courtesans attending Ximen Chuixue (Prologue).

小翠.note: One of the courtesans attending Ximen Chuixue (Prologue).

小萩.note: The taciturn Nara courtesan who is in fact Imai Sōkyū's guide-agent, sent to meet Jūzō; a Kōga woman, Jūzō suspects.

小西行長.note: Ryūsa's son, made Settsu-no-kami and a daimyō; a great Christian lord, executed after Sekigahara.

小西隆佐.note: Sakai merchant risen from a face-powder shop, favored by Hideyoshi as Sōkyū's rival; father of Konishi Yukinaga.

小谷城.note: Azai Nagamasa's stronghold in northern Ōmi. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: capitalize Castle in the proper name.

小豆島.note: Large island in the Inland Sea.

尤可常.note: The Chinese name taken by the former Japanese agent Itō Kinji after the war, when he stays on as the post office doorman. A fictional character; pinyin.

尾崎庄太郎.note: A left-leaning graduate of the East Asia Common Culture Academy and member of Nakanishi Kō’s network; a different man from the Sorge-ring spy Ozaki Hotsumi.

尾崎秀实.note: 1901–1944. Asahi Shimbun journalist, China expert, and adviser to Prime Minister Konoe, and the key Japanese member of the Sorge ring; arrested in 1941 and hanged with Sorge in 1944. Not to be confused with Ozaki Shōtarō.

尾形俊太郎.note: A jokin of the Shinsengumi and one of its few lettered men, employed by Kondō on documentary and liaison work.

局中法度.note: The written law of the Shinsengumi, breach of it punishable by seppuku. See the note in the chapter on its debated historicity.

局長.note: Kyokuchō, the title of a corps-captain in the Shinsengumi; three were made at the founding, to balance the Serizawa and Kondō lines.

居合.note: The art of drawing the sword and cutting in a single motion; a specialty distinct from ordinary fencing.

居正.note: 1876–1951; veteran Tongmenghui revolutionary and jurist, president of the Judicial Yuan.

山下株式会社.note: The Japanese shipping firm Yamashita Kisen K.K.

山东.note: 山东; the northern coastal province; older English Shantung.

山东纵队.note: The Eighth Route Army’s Shandong Column, the main CCP field force in Shandong.

山东肃托.note: The anti-Trotskyist purge that swept the Shandong base area from 1939, of which the Huxi killings were the worst.

山南敬助.note: Historical, 1833–1865. Held the full transmission at the Chiba hall; later general secretary (sōchō) of the Shinsengumi, second only to Kondō, until an attempt to leave the corps forced him to commit seppuku.

山岡鉄太郎.note: Historical, 1836–1888. A shogunal overseer of the Rōshigumi; later famous as Yamaoka Tesshū, a great swordsman, statesman, and Zen adept who helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle.

山崎.note: Japanese colonel, chief of staff of the Third Air Group; Jiang Yongnan's target in Wuchang.

山崎烝.note: Historical, died 1868. Son of an Osaka acupuncturist and the Shinsengumi’s ablest inspector and spy, skilled with the staff; mortally wounded after the sea-fight of Miyako Bay.

山田信道.note: Matsuda Jūsuke’s younger brother, later governor of Kyōto Prefecture, who raised the memorial to the Ikedaya dead.

山田弘一.note: The Japanese staff-officer alias Jiang Yongnan uses to reach Yamazaki.

山県半蔵.note: The real name of Chōshū’s sham envoy: Shishido Tamaki (1829–1901), a middle-rank samurai chosen for his glib tongue, after the Restoration a viscount and member of the House of Peers.

山西雁.note: The great hero of Guanzhong, famed near forty years for his twin iron palms; by martial generation the nephew of Huo Tianqing, though decades his elder. One of the Heaven’s Bird sect (ch08).

山路正国.note: Also called Yamaji Shōgen. A Katsutoyo officer who betrayed Hideyoshi for a promise of Maruoka castle; his family was crucified, and he was killed at Shizugatake (by Goemon in the novel).

岐阜.note: The Mino castle town, held by Nobutaka; the infant heir Sanbōshi was kept there.

岡田総右衛門.note: Founder of the Ryūgō-ryū of Warabi, the shin-cutting country school.

岩井.note: Dr. Iwai, the Japanese surgeon whose Hankou clinic Jiang tended; deported when China took back the Japanese concession. Fictional; the surname is read in Japanese as Iwai.

岩井公馆.note: The “Iwai Mansion” (Japanese Iwai Kōkan), the Japanese foreign-ministry intelligence organ Iwai Eiichi ran in Shanghai.

岩井英一.note: 1899–1980. Japanese deputy consul-general in Shanghai and head of a foreign-ministry intelligence organ, the “Iwai Kōkan.” Pan Hannian ran a channel into his operation.

岸和田.note: The castle-town on the Izumi coast south of Osaka; the Saiga and Negoro forces built their three forward forts (Sengokubori, Shakuzen-ji, Hama castle) to bar Hideyoshi’s road here in Tenshō 13.

岸淵兵輔.note: A Mito clansman, once a visitor at Kondō’s Edo dōjō, here made the bearer of the first warning about the Masuya. Romanization mine.

峨嵋.note: Mount Emei in Sichuan, one of the sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism and the seat of a great martial sect; here its sword-school, whose master is secretly the traitor Dugu Yihe (ch04). See also the later Four Beauties of Emei (ch09).

峨嵋四秀.note: The four young women disciples of the Emei sword-school (secretly headed by Dugu Yihe): Ma Xiuzhen, Sun Xiuqing, Ye Xiuzhu and Shi Xiuxue. Their given names all share the generation-character xiu (秀, ‘graceful, comely’), marking them as martial-sisters of one generation, whence ‘the Four Beauties’ (四秀). They are the counterpart of the Three Heroes (三英) among the Seven Swords of Emei (ch09).

島原.note: Kyoto’s licensed pleasure quarter, in the southwest of the city; the courtesan district that was to Kyoto what the Yoshiwara was to Edo.

島左近.note: Shima Sakon (Kiyooki, also read Katsutake; d. 1600), a famed warrior whom Ishida Mitsunari coaxed out of retirement by giving him nearly half his own stipend to serve as chief retainer. He commanded the Ishida vanguard and fell at Sekigahara in 1600. In this chapter he governs the Fushimi mansion in Mitsunari's absence.

島津久光.note: Historical, 1817–1887. Father of the young lord of Satsuma and the domain’s effective ruler in these years; it was his procession the English crossed at Namamugi.

島田左近.note: An agent of the Kujō house and of the shogunal side; cut down in Kiyamachi in the seventh month of 1862 by Satsuma’s Tanaka Shinbei, the first of the loyalist “Heaven’s punishment” killings.

島田魁.note: A Shinsengumi inspector, one of the biggest men in the corps; served on the surveillance of the Masuya.

崔一洞.note: A blade-bully disarmed by Hua Manlou; his given name means ‘One Hole’ (Prologue).

川东师范.note: A teachers' college in Chongqing; in the story, the Zhongtong's public front.

川合贞吉.note: A Japanese member of the Sorge ring, introduced to Sorge by Agnes Smedley.

川岛芳子.note: 1907–1948. Born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, a Qing princess raised in Japan who became a Japanese agent and cavalry commander in Manchuria; executed by the Nationalists as a collaborator in 1948. Her younger brother Xiandong was a member of the Communist Northeast intelligence group.

川樾.note: Kawagoe Shigeru, Japanese ambassador to China 1936–38, who negotiated with Foreign Minister Zhang Qun in 1936.

川沙.note: A rural county east of Shanghai, in what is now Pudong.

巡捕房.note: The police stations of the foreign concessions (Shanghai's International Settlement and French Concession). Their Chinese informers were 包打聽. Render by sense: 'the concession police' for the force, 'police station' for a station house; a specific named station keeps its period name (the Louza police station).

左右田与一郎.note: A young retainer of the Akechi general Yomoda Tajima-no-kami; Tarao-born and Oyu's childhood friend, hopelessly in love with her, and so a channel by which she reaches the Akechi camp.

左权.note: 1905–1942. Deputy chief of staff of the Eighth Route Army, killed at Shiziling; the highest-ranking Communist commander to die in the war.

左秋明.note: Lin's classmate from the training class; a liaison officer. Pinyin.

左近.note: Bare name of Shima Sakon, used throughout the narration and dialogue.

巨籁达路.note: A French Concession street lined with plane trees, today's Julu Road. Attested French name.

市井七侠.note: Seven sworn brothers who go disguised as street pedlars (a bun-seller, a quack, a pockmarked innkeeper and the rest), also called the Seven Righteous of Shanxi (山西七义); all of the Heaven’s Bird sect (ch08).

布朗神父.note: The English priest of St. Thérèse's Church. A fictional character; 布朗 is the source's transliteration of “Brown.”

布田.note: The central station of the Fuda Five Stations on the Kōshū Highway, in present-day Chōfu.

布谷鸟在歌唱.note: A recognition signal Su Lina passes up the line. The story's own tradecraft.

布鲁.note: A White-area underground veteran; reconnaissance chief of the Border Security and head of its first Qilipu training class.

师哲.note: 1905–1998. Security-office bureau chief; later Mao Zedong’s Russian-language interpreter.

常州.note: A city in southern Jiangsu on the Shanghai–Nanjing line. Two referents: in a Chinese source, Changzhou (Jiangsu); in a Japanese source, Hitachi province. Both correct in their books.

常春恒.note: A wenwu-laosheng Peking-opera actor shot dead by gunmen at the Dangui’s door on Gu Zhuxuan’s order, in a theatrical rivalry and salary dispute at the Tianchan Stage (about 1931).

常陸.note: An eastern province (modern Ibaraki), seat of the Kashima Shrine and the Kashima sword tradition.

平山五郎.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction, killed alongside Serizawa in the assassination of 1863.

平津保三角地带.note: The dozen-odd counties of central Hebei, bounded by Beiping, Tianjin, and Baoding, held by the Communists' Central Hebei forces from 1938.

平独鹤.note: The original name of Dugu Yihe, one of the four ministers of the Golden Roc (ch04).

平重盛.note: 1138–1179; eldest son of Taira no Kiyomori, whose mansion once stood at Komatsudani (hence his sobriquet, the Komatsu Minister).

平間重助.note: A Mito follower and inner pupil of Serizawa Kamo. Romanization mine.

广大华行.note: A Shanghai pharmaceutical trading firm founded in 1932 and run from 1937 as a secret Communist enterprise, funding and covering the Party's intelligence work in Nationalist territory.

广州湾.note: A French-leased territory on the Guangdong coast, today's Zhanjiang. Attested romanization.

广田.note: Hirota Kōki (广田弘毅, 1878–1948), Japanese foreign minister and later premier; author of the 1935 'Three Principles.'

広沢兵助.note: Hirosawa Saneomi (1834–1871), a Chōshū official who became a councillor of the Restoration government and was assassinated in 1871; Hyōsuke was an earlier name.

広沢富次郎.note: An Aizu official (later known as Hirosawa Yasuto) who dealt with the Mibu corps at first hand; author of the record the Ōshōroku, quoted here.

庐山.note: A mountain resort in Jiangxi where Chiang Kai-shek was staying. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: Mount X pattern; Lushan glossed once.

庚申.note: The kōshin folk-cult and its emblematic monkey; the 'kōshin monkey' simile is footnoted at first appearance.

府中.note: The old provincial seat of Musashi, on the Kōshū Highway; site of the Ōkunitama Shrine.

府内.note: The capital of Bungo (modern Oita); site of a Jesuit college.

庞京周.note: A prominent Shanghai physician, Du Yuesheng's personal doctor.

康世昌.note: A younger Yan'an-born cadre; deputy chief and, on the recapture of Yan'an, chief of the municipal public-security bureau.

康生.note: 1898–1975. Born Zhang Zongke; “Zhao Rong” was a working alias.

廖承志.note: 1908–1983; son of Liao Zhongkai and He Xiangning, CCP leader; arrested in Shanghai in 1933 and among those the author’s circle worked to rescue.

延安.note: The Communist base in northern Shaanxi; Ronghua’s wireless link runs between Shanghai and Yan’an. (The Party’s seat only from 1937; its use in the novel’s earlier setting is a mild anachronism, as with ‘Juntong.’) Adjudicated 2026-08-29: pinyin with ASCII apostrophe in source files (the builder typographizes); 'Yenan' stands as juntong's period deviation.

延安大撤退.note: The CCP’s evacuation of its capital, Yan’an, before Hu Zongnan’s attack in March 1947.

建仁寺.note: The great Rinzai Zen monastery east of the Kamo, at the foot of Higashiyama.

弘法大師.note: Kukai (774-835), founder of Shingon esoteric Buddhism, held to lie not dead but in eternal meditation at Kōya-san, awaiting the future Buddha Maitreya.

张一麐.note: 张一麐 (1867–1943); Suzhou elder statesman, once a secretary to Yuan Shikai, later a patriotic notable.

张仁奎.note: Elder Green Gang figure; Du Yuesheng and many others were ranked below his generation.

张伯伦.note: Neville Chamberlain, British prime minister, whose Munich Agreement of September 1938 pressed Czechoslovakia to cede the Sudetenland to Germany.

张作霖.note: 1875-1928; the 'Old Marshal,' warlord of Manchuria, killed by the Japanese Kwantung Army in the Huanggutun bombing of 1928.

张发奎.note: Nationalist general who circulated a telegram mocking Wang's two-facedness.

张唯一.note: 1892–1955. A veteran of the Central Special Branch known in Pan Hannian’s Hong Kong circle as “the Old Master” (lao taiye); ran the inner office of the South China Intelligence Bureau.

张啸林.note: One of the ‘three big bosses’ of the Shanghai gangs, with Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng.

张嘉璈.note: Chang Kia-ngau (1889–1979), the banker and financial administrator.

张国焘.note: An early CCP leader who, during the Long March, split with the Central Committee over the line of march; later defected to the Kuomintang (1897–1979).

张垣.note: A literary name for Zhangjiakou (Kalgan), the Chahar gateway city; the form Chen favors in the Part-Four chapters. Introduced with Zhangjiakou in a note at its first appearance.

张大千.note: 1899–1983; one of the most celebrated modern Chinese painters.

张季鸾.note: Chief editorial writer of the Dagongbao (Ta Kung Pao), a celebrated political commentator.

张宗昌.note: 1881-1932; warlord of Shandong, the 'Dog-Meat General.' See the note in this section.

张执一.note: Zhang Zhiyi (1911–1983); head of the City Work Department of the CCP Shanghai Bureau, in charge of underground work in the city.

张放.note: The escort captain poisoned by Granny Xiong in the opening vignette (Prologue).

张敬尧.note: 1881–1933; Beiyang general and former military governor of Hunan, assassinated in Beiping in 1933.

张明达.note: A courier of the Nakanishi Kō cell who escaped the 1942 arrests; later wrote about the network under the name Fang Zhida (方知达).

张溥泉.note: Courtesy name of Zhang Ji (张继, 1882–1947), veteran Tongmenghui revolutionary and Nationalist elder.

张澜.note: 1872–1955. Chairman of the China Democratic League; in 1949 a vice-chairman of the Central People's Government.

张石川.note: 张石川 (1890–1953); pioneering Chinese film director and a founder of the Mingxing Film Company.

张继.note: A veteran Nationalist and member of the Central Standing Committee.

张群.note: 1889–1990; close associate of Chiang, foreign minister 1935–37; secretary-general of the Supreme National Defense Council.

张蔚林.note: Juntong radio officer turned secret Communist; member of Zhang Luping’s branch, executed 1945.

张露萍.note: 1921–1945. CCP agent who led the underground branch inside Juntong’s Chongqing radio headquarters; executed by the Nationalists in 1945.

张鼓峰.note: The Zhanggufeng / Lake Khasan border clash with the USSR, July–August 1938.

弥九郎.note: The childhood/common name of 小西行長 Konishi Yukinaga, kept in use by the Sakai merchants who had known him from boyhood; here in Kumobei's gossip.

弥五右衛門.note: Maki’s father, a good-natured Ikkō-sect peasant of the hamlet of Nagao; fifty-two in Tenshō 13. Not to be confused with Goemon (五右衛門): Yagoemon is 弥五右衛門.

当薬.note: The dried herb Swertia japonica, a bitter folk stomach remedy.

彭学沛.note: Vice-minister of Communications in the Nationalist government.

彭真.note: 1902–1997. Mayor of Beijing and head of the Party's political-legal work; purged in 1966 as first of the “Peng-Luo-Lu-Yang” clique.

影佐祯昭.note: 1893–1948. The Japanese army officer who ran the Ume Kikan, engineered Wang Jingwei’s defection, and served as the supreme military adviser of the Wang Jingwei regime.

後藤又兵衛.note: Retainer of the Kuroda, and one of the celebrated warriors of the age; died for the Toyotomi at the fall of Osaka in 1615.

後醍醐天皇.note: The fourteenth-century emperor whose brief Kenmu Restoration (1333) overthrew the Kamakura shogunate; Kusunoki Masashige was his most famous loyal general.

徐堪.note: 1888–1969; financial official, later minister of finance.

徐嫂.note: Xu Delin's wife. 嫂 (sao), literally “elder brother's wife,” is a familiar address for a married woman of one's own generation, here roughly “Mrs. Xu”; the form is kept. A fictional character; pinyin.

徐寿新.note: Alias Zhu Chengwo; chief communications inspector of the Shanghai District, shot at No. 76 on 25 Dec 1939. The reproduced Xu Wenqi essay memorializes him.

徐寿棪.note: Xu Shouxin's younger brother, a Juntong veteran; his letters recovered his brother's martyrdom for this book.

徐德林.note: A postman at the Jing'an office and a Communist courier, tortured to death by the Japanese; Zhongliang's father. A fictional character; pinyin.

徐恩曾.note: 1896–1985. Head of the Nationalist Zhongtong; a nephew-by-marriage of Chen Guofu and a member of the “CC Clique.” His memoir is quoted throughout this book.

徐文祺.note: A Shanghai District assistant secretary imprisoned with Xu Shouxin at No. 76; author of the reproduced memorial essay.

徐永昌.note: 1887–1959; general (courtesy name Ci-chen / 次宸); director of the Military Operations Board. The source's '次展 / 次辰' are misprints for 次宸.

徐谟.note: 1893–1956; vice-minister of Foreign Affairs who accompanied Trautmann and reported the mediation to the meeting; later a judge of the International Court of Justice.

御斎峠.note: 御斎峠 (usually Otodo-tōge) is glossed おとぎとうげ in the text, matching the chapter title おとぎ峠; site of Jūzō's grandfather's hermitage.

御陵衛士.note: ‘Guards of the Imperial Tomb’: the loyalist band Itō formed on breaking with the Shinsengumi in 1867, given the charge of tending Emperor Kōmei’s grave at Sennyū-ji.

御香宮.note: The Gokō-no-miya shrine at Fushimi; its wooded precinct became the Satsuma army's forward post in 1868, directly north of the Magistracy.

徳川.note: The Tokugawa house (Ieyasu's); named among the rumored authors of the fire.

忍び文字.note: 'Shinobi writing': the secret syllabic script ninja used among themselves. The chapter title; footnoted where the device is explained.

忍び熊手.note: A collapsible climbing-rake of jointed bamboo on a hemp cord that stiffens into a pole; a ninja tool, described in the text.

忍び組.note: The ‘Stealth Corps,’ the organized body of some two hundred Iga and Kōga ninja under Hanzō in Ieyasu’s service, whose unified command the author credits with Ieyasu’s edge at Nagakute.

忍者.note: The covert agents of Iga and Koga; rendered 'ninja' or 'shinobi' as the sentence wants.

忍術.note: The shinobi's craft of stealth, evasion, espionage and sabotage.

志愿军.note: The Chinese People's Volunteer Army sent to fight in the Korean War. Attested English name.

忘忧清乐集.note: A Song-dynasty classic of go; here it doubles as the key text of a cipher. Attested romanization.

忠义救国军.note: A Dai Li / Juntong-affiliated irregular force active in the lower Yangtze during the war; its Hengyang-region commander Zhou Kuilong held the couple (ch21). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: four books agree (the SACO-era standard English name); full translation glossed at first use.

快川.note: Kaisen Joki (d. 1582), Zen abbot of Erin-ji, burned to death with his monks by Nobunaga's men.

念仏.note: The invocation 'Namu Amida Butsu', central to Pure Land practice.

念流.note: Here the Maniwa Nen-ryū of Kōzuke, one of the oldest surviving sword schools; where Shichiri first trained.

怡和洋行.note: The British trading house Jardine, Matheson and Co. (Chinese hong-name Ewo). Book form "Jardine Matheson", per ch07/ch18; ch03 uses the colloquial "Jardine’s" in a factory list. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: modern standard form; 'Jardine, Matheson & Co.' only inside a period document that prints it.

恩智左近.note: A retainer of Kusunoki Masashige, remembered as a loyal lieutenant; Kondō casts Toshizō in the part.

息烽.note: A county in Guizhou; site of the Juntong's own detention camp for its own personnel.

恵林寺.note: The Takeda's devotional temple in Kai, burned with its monks in 1582.

惟任日向守光秀.note: Akechi Mitsuhide, who killed Nobunaga at the Honnō-ji; here under the name and court title Nobunaga had granted him.

惣五郎.note: The Sakai loafer (遊び人) from the Daimoku Hall who guides Jūzō to the pleasure quarter; a minor invented character.

惣兵衛.note: Ikedaya Sōbei, keeper of the inn; he died in prison after the affair.

愚园路.note: A fashionable road in western Shanghai; the site of Yang Yubo’s mansion.

愛宕山.note: Height above Kita-no-shō where Hideyoshi set his headquarters for the final assault.

愛染堂.note: A hall of Aizen Myō-ō in the ruined Tōdai-ji cloister; the scene of the killing.

愛染明王.note: The 'wisdom king' of passion, Rāgarāja; a patron of love.

懸巣ノ次郎.note: Matsukura's foster-retainer, found stabbed dead beneath the Great Buddha. 懸巣 = a jay.

戈登路.note: International Settlement street, printed in the source in Roman letters too; today Jiangning Road (江宁路).

我孫子村.note: Village on the outskirts of Sakai, Sōkyū's fief and foundry settlement.

戒光寺.note: A sub-temple within the grounds of Sennyū-ji, where Itō’s faction met.

战略间谍.note: A long-buried agent held in reserve for a strategic turning-point; see 冷藏间谋 “cold-storage spy.”

戴季陶.note: Real (1891-1949). KMT theorist of anti-communism ('Daiism'); reread Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles to exclude the Communists.

戴案.note: The Border Security’s name for the Hanzhong-class case, after Dai Li, whose Juntong system ran the agents.

戴笠.note: 1897–1946, head of the Nationalists' Military Statistics Bureau (军统/Juntong), the KMT secret service; Whampoa sixth class (did not graduate). Ordered and oversaw the couple's secret arrest (ch20–21).

戴藏宜.note: Son of Dai Li; the Dai and Wang families were once spoken of as prospective in-laws.

戸田采女正氏彬.note: Lord of the Ōgaki domain, a shogunal-loyalist han renowned for its gunnery ('Ōgaki of the guns'). Being ill, he left the field to his deputy Ohara Tesshin.

所司代.note: The Kyoto Deputy, the shogunate’s standing office for the government and policing of the capital, older and more regular than the Kyoto Protector under whom the Shinsengumi served.

手裏剣.note: The ninja’s throwing-blade; the eight-pointed happō-shuriken is thrown here in a rapid straight-line volley.

打狗队.note: A nickname for the Central Special Branch’s action squad (the “Red Squad”), which punished defectors and enemy agents; several later secret-service figures, Li Shiqun among them, had passed through it. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: lowercase descriptive (the formal handle is the Red Squad); zhou-enlai's capitalized form stands as its recorded deviation.

扬子公司.note: Kong Lingkan's Shanghai firm, a byword for wartime and postwar profiteering under the protection of H. H. Kung.

扬州.note: The Grand Canal city of Subei.

扬帆.note: 1912–1999. Chief of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau; arrested in 1954–55 in the “Pan-Yang case” and rehabilitated in the 1980s.

承禎入道.note: Later Buddhist name of Yoshikata / Hakkansai after his fall and tonsure in Kōga.

抗团.note: The standard abbreviation of the Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps (抗日杀奸团, NOTED ch02/ch11).

抗战夫人.note: A de facto second wife taken while separated from one's family by the war.

抗日杀奸团.note: A patriotic assassination group of young people in occupied North China.

抗日除奸队.note: 抗日除奸队, a resistance cell of the kind that hunted collaborators and turncoats in occupied Shanghai; here the unit to which Xiufen belongs. Rendered descriptively.

抜関斎.note: Buddhist name of Sasaki (Rokkaku) Yoshikata (六角義賢), last lord of the Sasaki of Ōmi; Kohagi's true father. Later took the further name 承禎入道 Jōtei.

抢救运动.note: The coercive spy-hunt of 1943 into which the Yan’an Rectification’s cadre-screening phase escalated; the euphemism “rescue” cast the purge as saving misled youths from espionage.

拉穆塞小组.note: Sorge’s Tokyo intelligence cell, from his radio code name “Ramsay”; the source also transliterates it 拉姓扎.

招商局.note: The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the handle; full 'the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company' at first use.

拝郷家嘉.note: A Shibata general (formal name Hisamitsu), killed by Fukushima Masanori at Shizugatake per the Taikōki; a namesake of the hero.

掏心战术.note: The code-name of the deep raid into the Communist-held triangle aimed at seizing the enemy's leadership at a stroke; the chapter title glosses it at title level.

提篮桥.note: Tilanqiao Prison (built 1901–03), known in English as Ward Road Gaol; after 1945 it held collaborators and Japanese war criminals. Historical.

摂津守.note: “Governor of Settsu”, a court title; borne here by Konishi Yukinaga.

摩利支天.note: Marīcī, the deva of the heat-shimmer; guardian deity of warriors and of the Iga/Kōga ninja. The Kōga byname of surpassing adepts.

摩利洞玄.note: The old Kōga master Gen'i owes his life to; born Ban Tōnai (伴藤内) of the Ban house, retired as 洞玄 Dōgen. Bears the Kōga byname 摩利/摩利支天 (Marishiten); called 甲賀ノ摩利 'Mari of Kōga'.

摩阿姫.note: Maeda Toshiie's daughter, a concubine of Hideyoshi known as Kaga-dono; the novel gives her the name Gō-hime, which properly belonged to another sister.

政友会.note: The Friends of Constitutional Government Party, a major pre-war Japanese political party.

敏体尼荫路.note: French Concession road, today's South Xizang Road. Book form 'Rue Montauban' matches ch08; historically this was Route Montigny (敏体尼 = Montigny) -- FLAG FOR B10 reconciliation.

教如.note: Kennyo’s son and the ‘new abbot,’ who held out at Ishiyama after his father left and was long estranged from him.

敢国神社.note: The ichinomiya (first shrine) of Iga province.

敦賀.note: A port town on the Sea of Japan, in Echizen (modern Fukui), where the Tengu Party was imprisoned and executed.

整风.note: The Yan'an Rectification, launched in 1942: Mao Zedong's campaign of ideological remolding and cadre screening.

整风运动.note: The Communist ideological campaign begun at Yan'an in 1942. Attested English name.

文化大革命.note: 1966–1976. The author uses the term in quotation marks throughout, marking the settled Party verdict that it was a catastrophe.

文禄・慶長の役.note: Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea, 1592 and 1597 (the Imjin and Jeongyu wars in Korean).

斎藤一.note: Historical, 1844–1915. Later captain of the Shinsengumi's Third Unit and one of its deadliest swordsmen; survived the wars, served as a Meiji policeman, and died in old age.

斎藤弥九郎.note: Master of the Renpeikan, the Shintō Munen-ryū hall reckoned one of the three great dōjō of Edo; Kondō's source of borrowed swordsmen.

斜塘镇.note: A small water-country town on the outskirts of Shanghai where Lin hides as a schoolteacher. Pinyin.

斤.note: A unit of weight, about 600 grams (a catty).

斧头帮.note: Shanghai assassins' gang; linked to the killing of the China Merchants director.

新井忠雄.note: An inspector of the Shinsengumi and one of Itō’s confidants from the Edo days; he left with Itō’s faction.

新保安.note: The walled town on the Ping-Sui line, southeast of Xuanhua, where Guo Jingyun's 35th Army was surrounded and destroyed between 6 and 24 December 1948.

新六军.note: An elite Nationalist army returned from Burma.

新兵衛.note: Tarao Doka's second son, seventeen, quick and handsome, the leader of the three Koga ninja sons at the seminary; hid the mission's sacred vessels at Oki-no-shima. A future antagonist of Goemon.

新华日报.note: The Communist Party’s newspaper in the Nationalist areas. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: transliterated masthead, majority; 'New China Daily' glossed once.

新四军.note: A Communist army operating in central-eastern China; nominally allied with the Nationalists against Japan. Standard English form.

新徳寺.note: The temple at Mibu that served as the Rōshigumi's headquarters, where Kiyokawa revealed his true design.

新徴組.note: The “Newly Levied Corps.” The rōnin who followed Kiyokawa back to Edo were reorganized under this name and set, under the Shōnai domain, to police the city; the corps lasted to the end of the shogunate.

新田義貞.note: The fourteenth-century commander who, for the emperor Go-Daigo, destroyed the Kamakura shogunate; victor at Bubaigawara in 1333.

新田革左衛門.note: A Shinsengumi corpsman who died soon after of wounds taken at the Ikedaya.

新艳秋.note: A celebrated Peking-opera actress of the female (dan) roles, performing at the Gengxin Stage on the night of Yu Yefeng's sanction.

新見錦.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction and an early officer of the corps; forced to commit seppuku in 1863. Reading from the source's furigana (にいみにしき).

新選組.note: The 'Newly Selected Corps,' the shogunate's Kyoto police militia of swordsmen, 1863–1869; the subject of the novel.

方君瑛.note: Elder sister of Fang Junbi and a fellow Tongmenghui revolutionary; took part in the 1910 plot against the Qing Prince Regent.

方君璧.note: 1898-1986; painter, wife of Zeng Zhongming; wounded in the Hanoi attack.

方広寺.note: Hideyoshi's Great Buddha temple in the capital; Kuroami's whetter-stall stands beside it. The Great Buddha itself was footnoted in ch03.

方志敏.note: 1899–1935; CCP leader of the Northeast Jiangxi soviet; his prison diary was among the papers kept in the Tongyi vault.

方柄忠.note: The handler who assigns Jiang the Gannan posting and the Wuhan detour.

於義丸.note: Ieyasu’s second son, given to Hideyoshi as adopted son and hostage; renamed Hashiba Hideyasu, later Yūki Hideyasu (1574–1607). (See the note at his adoption.)

施从滨.note: Division commander under Sun Chuanfang, executed by him at Bengbu; the killing his daughter Shi Jianqiao avenged in 1935.

施何成.note: A New Group One operative (aliases Bao Yueren, later Peng Jun); his letters supply several of the chapter's martyr cases.

施剑翘.note: Avenger who shot Sun Chuanfang dead in 1935; publicly pardoned.

施薬院全宗.note: Former Hiei monk turned Hideyoshi's physician and courtier; also called Maeda Tokuun. Cast by the Jesuits as the Taikō's procurer of women.

旅欧中国少年共产党.note: The European branch of the early Chinese Communist movement, founded in Paris in 1922. Attested English rendering.

旗本.note: A direct bannerman of the shogun, with the right of audience; a samurai of the Tokugawa house itself, ranked above the ordinary domain retainer.

旗袍.note: The close-fitting Chinese woman's dress (旗袍, qipao); ‘cheongsam’ is the established English form used throughout.

日本.note: 日本; Japan, named with England as America's two rivals in the East.

日本外史.note: Rai San’yō’s Unofficial History of Japan (1827), the stirring, imperial-centered history that did as much as any book to shape the loyalist feeling of the age. See ch12.

旭姫.note: Hideyoshi's half-sister (1543-1590), married to Ieyasu in 1586 to seal the alliance of the two houses.

明智光春.note: Mitsuhide's nephew; abandoned Azuchi and died at the fall of Sakamoto Castle.

明智光秀.note: Akechi Mitsuhide (1528?–1582), one of Nobunaga's chief generals; the man who would strike at Honnō-ji.

明里.note: The Shimabara courtesan said to have been Yamanami’s lover. The tradition is famous but late and unverified; see the note at first appearance.

春蟬.note: A courtesan of Yanagimachi; the informer Jūzō kills. Furigana はるぜみ.

智异.note: Zhao Cangbi’s coined term for the point-against-point contest of stratagems in covert struggle.

暨南大学.note: Overseas-Chinese university in Shanghai where Chen Gaoyong was a professor.

曲江.note: County town in northern Guangdong (present-day Shaoguan); wartime relief hub.

更新舞台.note: A Peking-opera theater on Newchwang Road in the International Settlement; the site of the Yu Yefeng sanction of January 1940.

曹锟.note: Real (1862-1938). President of the Republic 1923-24, deposed and placed under arrest in Feng Yuxiang's 1924 coup.

曾仲鸣.note: 1896–1939; Wang Jingwei's close aide, killed at Hanoi in the attack meant for Wang.

曾家岩.note: The Chongqing district where the Eighth Route Army office (the '八办') stood; site of the narrator's 1942 audience with Zhou Enlai (ch20–21).

曾泽生.note: 1902–1973. Yunnan-army general who led the 60th Army in revolt at Changchun in 1948; his troops became the PLA 50th Army.

曾澈.note: Secretary and later District chief of the Juntong's Tianjin organization, and head of the Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps; martyred at Beiping in 1940.

替死鬼.note: Literally a substitute-death ghost. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: default sense; keep the literal stand-in-for-the-dead image only where the ritual sense is live, with a note.

月真院.note: A sub-temple of Kōdai-ji; the Goryō-eji made it their headquarters, whence they were called the Kōdai-ji party.

有田.note: Arita Hachirō (有田八郎, 1884–1965), Japan's foreign minister 1936–40.

有田八郎.note: Japanese foreign minister at the time of Wang Jingwei's June 1939 Tokyo visit.

有馬.note: Christian domain in Hizen (Kyūshū); site of the first Japanese seminary.

服部半蔵.note: The historical Iga ninja who served Tokugawa Ieyasu; here recalled by Jūzō as the broker between the Tokugawa and the Iga gōshi. Footnoted at first appearance.

服部武雄.note: A man of Bushū and the finest blade among Itō's followers; he died fighting in the Aburanokōji affair.

望月亀弥太.note: Tosa loyalist, an associate of Sakamoto Ryōma; wounded at the Ikedaya, he cut his belly in the street.

望月刑部左衛門.note: Gyōbuzaemon Shigehisa (重久) of the Mochizuki house of Kōga; raised Kohagi and taught her the Kōga arts; died at Ishida Mitsunari's Kyoto mansion.

望龙门.note: The Chongqing site of the Juntong secret detention house where the narrator was held (ch21).

朝倉義景.note: Lord of Echizen destroyed by Nobunaga at Ichijōdani in 1573; his lands passed to Shibata Katsuie.

朝天门码头.note: Chongqing's principal wharf, at the tip of the peninsula where the Jialing meets the Yangtze.

朝鮮.note: Target of Hideyoshi's invasion; the campaign was footnoted in ch03.

木ノ本.note: Post-town below Shizugatake on the Hokkoku highroad, site of Hideyoshi’s forward headquarters.

木屋町.note: The street of taverns and inns along the Takase River; in these years a haunt of loyalist rōnin, backing onto the Chōshū mansion.

木曾義昌.note: Takeda vassal in Shinano whose secret defection to Nobunaga touched off the Takeda's final campaign.

木猿.note: Written 木さる in the ch04 title; 木猿 here. Her father wishes she had been a son.

木食応其.note: The ascetic-monk whose embassy won Hideyoshi's pardon for Mount Kōya and saved it from destruction.

本受寺.note: The small Sakai temple behind which Goemon and Maki keep house.

本圀寺.note: A temple on Horikawa used as the Kyōto quartering-ground of the Mito clan’s troops.

本多忠勝.note: Honda Heihachirō Tadakatsu (1548–1610), one of Ieyasu’s foremost generals, known by his deer-antler helmet-crest; at Nagakute he shadowed Hideyoshi’s whole army with six hundred men.

本所.note: A district on the east bank of the Sumida in Edo.

本能寺.note: The Kyoto temple where Oda Nobunaga was destroyed in 1582 by his own general Akechi Mitsuhide; by extension, in Rai San’yō’s poem and in Toshizō’s thought, the place where the true enemy is found to lie.

本良.note: The Tang soy-works clerk, beheaded by the Japanese with twelve other townsmen.

朱七.note: The water-bandit chief of the Xiangfu marsh.

朱升.note: The servant who killed the puppet Shanghai mayor Fu Xiao'an with an axe on 11 Oct 1940; central to ch28 Section 2. His assassination act was noted at ch04. Source spelling-variants (朱生, 朱升源) and the alias 陈中南 render inline.

朱子家.note: Pen name of Jin Xiongbai (金雄白); see that entry.

朱子桥.note: General Zhu Qinglan, a noted relief philanthropist of the Republican era.

朱学范.note: 1905–1996; postal-workers’ leader who rose through the Green Gang and the Nationalist labor apparatus, broke with the Kuomintang in 1948, and became a minister and vice-chairman of the NPC Standing Committee in the People’s Republic. Author of this article and calligrapher of the book’s title.

朱家骅.note: 1893–1963. Nationalist organization minister, rival of the CC Clique.

朱志尧.note: 1863–1955; the Catholic industrialist (Kiangnan Dock, machine works), co-founder of the Datong line.

朱怡贞.note: A Communist agent; Lin's former student and lover. Endearment 贞贞, Zhenzhen. Pinyin.

朱执信.note: Revolutionary and husband of Wang Jingwei's eldest sister; a fellow Tongmenghui founder.

朱承我.note: Alias of the martyr Xu Shouxin, taken to keep the memory of his late wife Zhu Cheng'e.

朱葆三.note: A prominent Ningbo-Shanghai comprador and financier.

朵云轩.note: The famous Shanghai studio for painting, calligraphy, and seal-carving (founded 1900). Attested romanization.

李亮.note: The everyday name of Li Zhengliang, director of the Akagi case.

李公朴.note: 1902–1946; educator, one of the Seven Gentlemen; assassinated at Kunming in 1946.

李启明.note: An intellectual cadre from Shanxi and son-in-law of Li Kenong; the youngest deputy head of the Border Security, later governor of Shaanxi. One of the author's interviewees.

李国杰.note: Real. Grandson of Li Hongzhang; principal of the 1933 China Merchants embezzlement case, sentenced to eight years.

李士珍.note: Whampoa graduate and police theorist, the strict team leader of the Honggongci training class; later a leading figure in the Nationalist police and a rival of Dai Li for its control.

李士群.note: 1905–1943. A former Communist who passed through the Nationalist and then the Japanese and Wang Jingwei secret services, becoming the dreaded chief of No. 76. Poisoned by the Japanese in 1943.

李大钊.note: 1889–1927; co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party. Seized from the Soviet embassy in Beijing and hanged on Zhang Zuolin’s orders in April 1927.

李完用.note: 1858–1926; the Korean prime minister who signed the 1910 treaty annexing Korea to Japan; a byword for a national traitor.

李宗仁.note: Guangxi Clique leader; later acting president of the Republic of China.

李少春.note: Li Shaochun (1919–1975); one of the great Peking-opera actors of the century; Gu Zhuxuan’s adopted son.

李得森.note: A Chinese member of Nakanishi Kō’s Nanjing network, arrested by the Japanese in 1942.

李德.note: Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), the German Comintern military adviser to the CCP and the only Westerner to make the Long March.

李春茂.note: Hanzhong-class liaison (aliases Li Changsheng, Li Jun); turned and taken into the Border Security.

李桂春.note: Li Guichun (1885–1962); Peking-opera actor known by the stage name ‘Xiao Dazi,’ father of Li Shaochun.

李正梁.note: Alias Li Liang; leader of the Third Action Brigade's Fourth Group, who directed the Akagi assassination.

李甫山.note: Longdong security-section chief who ran Wu Nanshan; later head of the Border Security office in Yan’an.

李白.note: 1910–1949. Communist radio operator in Shanghai, executed on the eve of the city's liberation; not to be confused with the Tang poet. His story inspired the film The Unfailing Radio Wave.

李石曾.note: 1881–1973; anarchist and Nationalist elder, with Wu Jingheng a leader of the Franco-Chinese work-study movement.

李祖夔.note: A former magistrate of Shanghai county.

李立三.note: 1899–1967; early Communist labor organizer, a leader of the May Thirtieth Movement and briefly the Party’s top leader (the ‘Li Lisan line,’ 1930).

李自成.note: 1606–1645. The northern-Shaanxi peasant rebel who overthrew the Ming.

李舜臣.note: Admiral of the Korean navy (1545-1598) and national hero; inventor of the armored turtle-ships that broke Japan's command of the sea.

李茂堂.note: 1904–1969. A lapsed early Communist who rose to head Zhongtong’s Shaanxi station-room and secretly returned to the CCP’s service.

李运昌.note: A Zunhua man and East-Hebei guerrilla chief in the war years, later a CCP general and Minister of Railways.

李鑫.note: A Shanghai Kang Corps action man who perished with his own bomb at the Jessfield Park Axis-recognition rally, August 1941.

李震.note: Minister of public security who died in 1973, officially a suicide, in a case never fully resolved.

李青天.note: Commander of the Korean Liberation Army; historical.

李鸿章.note: 李鸿章 (1823–1901); the late-Qing statesman who launched the self-strengthening state industries Wang Hefu cites as the beginning of Chinese industry.

李鼎铭.note: 1881–1947. Non-party gentry-assemblyman of the Border Region who proposed “crack troops and simple administration.”

杏春楼.note: A brothel in the county town where Old Mo is press-ganged into the Nationalist ranks.

村井貞勝.note: Nobunaga's shoshidai (military governor) of Kyoto; a patron of the Nanban-ji, killed defending Nobutada in 1582.

杜月笙.note: 1888-1951. Foremost of the Shanghai Green Gang 'three tycoons'; first introduced ch06. Pinyin form standard (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Yuesheng).

杜美路.note: A French Concession street, today's Donghu Road.

来島又兵衛.note: A Chōshū warrior famed for his valor, given command of the Saga (Tenryū-ji) force. He was killed at the Hamaguri Gate (ch. 25).

来迎寺.note: A temple at the edge of Tsuruga; the mass beheadings of the Tengu Party were carried out in its grounds.

杨云史.note: 杨云史 (1875–1941); poet, who served as a secretary to the warlord Wu Peifu.

杨复纲.note: Mr. Pan’s true name, revealed after his death; a martyr killed near Suqian in 1942. A fictional character; pinyin.

杨奇清.note: 1911–1978. Veteran CCP security officer and counter-espionage specialist; anti-traitor chief at the Eighth Route Army’s forward headquarters, later a vice-minister of public security.

杨度.note: 1875–1931; classical scholar who championed constitutional monarchy under Yuan Shikai, then reinvented himself—joining the Communist Party in secret in 1929 while serving as an adviser to Du Yuesheng. His CCP membership was made public only in 1975.

杨杏佛.note: Yang Quan (1893–1933); secretary-general of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights, assassinated 1933.

杨杰.note: 1889–1949. Nationalist general and military theorist, assassinated in Hong Kong on the eve of the new Political Consultative Conference.

杨柳青.note: The town on the northern reach of the Jin-Pu railway near Tianjin to which the Second Command Room fell back as the working district shifted ever northward.

杨淑勤.note: Qin Shuji's true wife and Party comrade, a PLA cadre; she signs Yanzhi's release and pronounces her Qin's lifelong stain. Formerly the sham 秦太太 (Mrs. Qin).

杨群.note: Chief of the security bureau in the Police Administration Department, Chongqing; a smooth, controlling policeman of thirty years and Tang Ya's former keeper. Fictional; pinyin.

杨虎.note: 1889–1966; former Songhu (Shanghai) garrison commander, notorious for his part in the 1927 anti-Communist purge; Tian Shujun was “of his household.”

杨虎城.note: The Shaanxi general who, with Zhang Xueliang, seized Chiang Kai-shek in the 1936 Xi'an Incident.

杭州.note: Zhejiang provincial capital on West Lake, where the author went into hiding in 1932–33.

東大寺.note: The great Nara temple; its colossal bronze Vairocana is the 'rain-soaked Buddha' of the chapter.

東雲大夫.note: A tayū of the Kizuya house in Shimabara; Toshizō’s partner on the one night the chapter turns on. Dayū is the title of the first rank of courtesan.

松倉蔵人/蔵人.note: The scarred leader in the Aizen-dō, who claims to be a rōnin of the Shibata house; Jūzō takes him for a broken Mino bandit and kills him. 蔵人 doubles as a court-office name, hence Jūzō's mockery.

松前伊豆守.note: The senior councillor (rōjū) Matsumae Takahiro, whom Kondō claims to have lobbied on the shogun's behalf.

松原庵星布.note: Real woman haiku poet (1732–1814) of a notable Hachiōji house; the ni of 星布尼 marks her a lay nun.

松原忠司.note: Historical Shinsengumi captain of the Fourth Unit, a master of the Sekiguchi school of jūjutsu; died in 1865.

松原通.note: An east-west street of the capital, running toward Kiyomizu.

松島肩衝.note: A celebrated shouldered tea-caddy; Sōkyū's gift of it to Nobunaga made his fortune.

松平上総介.note: As Shiba gives him: a collateral Tokugawa, of the line of Tadanaga, acting as a sponsor of the rōshi levy. A minor figure; reading of the title as the source gives it.

松平伊織.note: A hatamoto of eight hundred koku with a residence in Honjo, Edo; Osae’s late husband, married to her when she was seventeen. A minor figure; reading from the source’s furigana.

松平定敬.note: Lord of the Kuwana domain in Ise and, from 1864, Kyoto Shoshidai. He was the younger brother of the Kyoto Protector Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu; the two chief security offices of the capital were thus held by one family.

松平容保.note: Historical, 1836–1893. Lord of Aizu and, from 1862, Kyoto Protector (Kyoto Shugoshoku); under his patronage the Mibu corps became the Shinsengumi.

松平忠敏.note: A Kōbusho instructor placed in charge of the shogunate's rōshi levy of 1863. Reading from the source's furigana (ただとし).

松平慶永.note: Matsudaira Yoshinaga (Shungaku, 1828–1890), lord of Echizen Fukui, one of the leading reform-minded daimyō of the day and a voice for a union of court and shogunate.

松本良順.note: A Dutch-school physician, personal doctor to the shogun Iemochi, who befriended the Shinsengumi and later tended the dying Okita. After the Restoration, as Matsumoto Jun, he became Surgeon-General of the new army and a baron.

松林左馬助.note: The Kashima shrine-family swordsman credited with codifying the Kashima-ryū (a.k.a. Shinmei-ryū). Reading of the name not independently confirmed.

松永久秀/弾正久秀/久秀.note: The warlord who burned the Tōdai-ji Great Buddha in 1567; 弾正 (Danjō) is his court title. Died 1577.

松江.note: A county town southwest of Shanghai. Historical.

松江支队.note: A Communist-led guerrilla unit near Shanghai; Xiufen's husband was its political commissar. Fictional or semi-historical within the story.

松田重助.note: Higo loyalist, killed at the Ikedaya.

板倉周防守.note: Itakura Katsukiyo (1823–1889), a senior councilor (rōjū) of the shogunate.

板垣征四郎.note: Japanese general (1885–1948), Kwantung Army architect of the 1931 Manchurian seizure, war minister, later chief of staff of the China Expeditionary Army; hanged as a war criminal.

极司菲尔路.note: A road on the western edge of the Shanghai settlements; No. 76 became the notorious headquarters of the Wang puppet secret service.

林之江.note: A No. 76 executioner (with Wan Lilang) of Xu Shouxin; later turned back to the government and died in poverty at Hong Kong.

林小姐.note: Yanzhi's Shanghai neighbour, a foreign-firm manager's kept woman.

林康侯.note: One of the ‘three notables of Shanghai’ during the occupation.

林彪.note: 1907–1971. A leading Communist general and later marshal; named Mao Zedong's successor, he died fleeing China after an alleged coup attempt.

林怀部.note: 林怀部; Zhang Xiaolin's bodyguard, who shot him dead on 14 August 1940.

林柏生.note: An associate of Wang Jingwei who arranged the publication of the Yan Telegram at Hong Kong.

林楠笙.note: The protagonist; a Juntong agent. Pinyin.

林権助.note: Hayashi Gonsuke (Yasusada), the 63-year-old Aizu commissioner of artillery who commanded the Aizu contingent at Fushimi; killed in the fighting there.

林秀澄.note: Lieutenant-colonel, chief of the Special Higher Section of the Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie; the 'Section chief Lin' Chen knew only by surname.

枡屋.note: The tool-and-sundries shop that was the front for Furutaka’s arms depot.

枫林桥.note: Landmark on the road out to Longhua. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: pinyin, majority; the translated 'Maple Grove Bridge' stands as wang-yaqiao's recorded deviation.

柏原.note: Site of the Iga gōshi's last-stand fort in 1581.

柏木四郎兵衛.note: Karasumaru's father: an ex-Mori samurai turned Ikko-ikki commander at Toyama Castle, beheaded by an unknown ninja.

柘植清広.note: Also 柘植太郎清広. Named leader of the Iga league in the novel.

柯士甸道.note: 柯士甸道; Austin Road, Kowloon.

柳ケ瀬.note: Pass at the head of the Shizugatake front, gateway between Ōmi and Echizen.

柳余恨.note: Once the Jade-Faced Gentleman (玉面郎君); a swordsman ruined ten years ago, his face half sliced away, hands struck off at the wrist. Comes seeking his own death (ch02). See the note at ‘Love, from of old, leaves only regret behind.’

柳剛流.note: A school founded by Okada Sōemon, based at Warabi, notorious for shin-cutting strikes and for teaching the glaive alongside the sword.

柳町.note: The licensed pleasure quarter of the capital in this period, in Nakagyō.

柴田勝家.note: Nobunaga's senior general, lord of Kita-no-shō in Echizen; Hideyoshi's chief rival after 1582, whom he outmanoeuvred at Kiyosu and would destroy at Shizugatake.

柴田勝政.note: Younger brother of Sakuma Morimasa, holding the cutting near Shizugatake in Katsuie’s army.

柴田勝豊.note: Katsuie’s adopted son, made lord of Nagahama; resenting Katsuie’s favor to Morimasa, he defected to Hideyoshi in the twelfth month of 1582.

标金.note: 标金; bar gold of standard fineness traded for future delivery on the Shanghai exchange, the other great speculative market beside the bonds.

栖霞寺.note: A great Buddhist monastery northeast of Nanjing.

根岸友山.note: A wealthy Musashi headman and expel-the-barbarian sympathizer who enrolled in the Rōshigumi with a following of his own.

根来寺.note: The head temple of the Shingi Shingon warrior-monks in Kii, and a nest of gunners; Hideyoshi destroyed it in 1585.

根津一.note: 1860–1927. A Japanese army officer and educator who founded and long directed the East Asia Common Culture Academy in Shanghai.

桂小五郎.note: Historical, 1833–1877. Later known as Kido Takayoshi, one of the leaders of the Restoration.

桂林.note: Period English form. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: pinyin default; 'Kweilin' stands as juntong's period deviation.

桃井春蔵.note: Master of the Shigakukan, one of the three great dōjō of Edo. Reading from the source's furigana (もものい).

桐工作.note: The Kiri Kōsaku (桒工作), Japan’s most secret 1940 “peace” channel to Chongqing, run by Imai Takeo; 桒 is the paulownia (kiri).

桑名.note: A fudai domain in Ise, held by a branch of the Matsudaira; with Aizu it stood staunchly for the shogunate to the end.

桑山重晴.note: Held the Shizugatake position for Hideyoshi (styled Shuri-no-suke).

桥楼.note: Bridge House (桥楼), by the Sichuan Road bridge over Suzhou Creek: the Shanghai headquarters and torture-prison of the Kempeitai. Historical.

梁启超.note: Styled Rengong; reformist thinker and leader of the Emperor-Protection (Royalist) party, rival to the revolutionaries.

梁鸿志.note: 1882–1946; head of the Japanese-sponsored 'Reformed Government' at Nanjing (1938); executed as a traitor after the war.

梅乐斯.note: 1900–1961; U.S. Navy officer, head of the American side of the Sino-American Cooperation Organization.

梅思平.note: A negotiator of the secret 1938 Shanghai agreement for Wang Jingwei.

梅机关.note: The “Plum Agency” (Japanese Ume Kikan), the Japanese army’s special-service organ in Shanghai that engineered Wang Jingwei’s defection, under Lieutenant-General Kagesa Sadaaki.

梅花山.note: Real. Hill on Purple Mountain, Nanjing, over Sun Quan's tomb; plum-viewing ground planted from 1929. Noted ch26.

梶川景次.note: A master of the Shintō Munen-ryū with a training hall at Sakuramachi in Kōfu; a minor figure. Reading of the given name uncertain; romanization mine.

森蘭丸.note: Nobunaga's best-loved page and reputed boy-lover, who died with him at the Honno-ji; elder of the three Mori brothers (with Bomaru and Rikimaru).

森長可.note: Ikeda Tsuneoki’s son-in-law, lord of Kaneyama; killed at Nagakute.

椿弥十郎.note: The Chōshū samurai who distributed the domain's bill of denunciation against the Aizu lord Matsudaira Katamori.

楠正成.note: The fourteenth-century loyalist commander, byword for cunning generalship against the odds; claimed founder of the Kusunoki school of military science.

楯岡ノ道順.note: Legendary Iga jōnin (a.k.a. Momochi Sandayū); commander of the hundred-man shinobi corps.

榊原康政.note: One of Tokugawa Ieyasu's 'Four Guardians'; here the lieutenant whose letter of introduction sends Watanabe to Imai Sōkyū. Bare 康政 (Yasumasa) also used in narration.

榻榻米.note: 榻榻米, the Japanese straw-mat flooring, fitting the safe-house in the Japanese residents' quarter.

樊鹗.note: Master Fan the Elder, one of the Two Talents of the Northwest (西北双秀); his long tobacco-pipe strikes the body’s pressure-points. One of the Seven Heroes of the Marketplace (ch08).

権.note: An old temple servant of the Shōkōin, once rescued by Toshizō, who serves as his scout. Romanization from the source's furigana.

次郎左衛門.note: Bare name of Shimotsuge Jirōzaemon in narration; also styled 'the old man' / 'the Master' where the source uses 老人 / お師匠.

欧阳情.note: The reigning name on the flower-board of the Yiqing Court; Ouyang is a two-syllable surname, and her given name Qing means ‘passion’, chiming with the house’s own (‘Pleasing the Passions’) (ch05).

欧阳毅.note: 1910–2005. Head of the General Political Department’s Anti-Traitor Department, which handled the army-system agents; later a PLA lieutenant general.

歌乐山.note: A hill west of Chongqing; site of Xu Shiying's birthday banquet (ch20). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: Mount X pattern (as Mount Lu).

正光院.note: A field-temple with a graveyard near Bubaigawara, where Toshizō sets up his command post.

正則.note: Fukushima Masanori, a smith’s son raised by Hideyoshi; named here only as a foil for Gen’i’s obscure birth.

正定.note: The town reckoned the screen of Shimen, and the northern terminus of the Zheng-Tai railway.

正福寺.note: A poor Esoteric-sect temple at Azōda, near Ueno, that Lourenço turned into a crypto-Christian church; Hanzō worships there.

正言报.note: 正言报; a Shanghai newspaper run by Wu Shaoshu in the postwar takeover period.

武州多摩.note: The Tama district of Musashi Province (Bushū), the farming country west of Edo; the Shinsengumi's home ground.

武昌大学.note: The source's name for the university at Mount Luojia, whose canteen becomes the Japanese wounded-soldiers' hospital; the campus is National Wuhan University's.

武田信玄.note: The sixteenth-century warlord of Kai, whose tactics were handed down as the Kōshū school of military science.

武田勝頼.note: Last lord of the Takeda of Kai; destroyed by Nobunaga and Ieyasu in 1582.

武田耕雲斎.note: Historical, 1803–1865. A former chief councillor of the Mito domain who led the Tengu Party’s march on Kyoto and was beheaded, with his family, at Tsuruga. Not to be confused with the Shinsengumi’s Takeda Kanryūsai.

武田観柳斎.note: A jokin of the Shinsengumi, a rōnin of Izumo learned in warrior usage and military science; a flatterer whom Toshizō despised. He was exposed as a Satsuma informer and cut down within the corps in 1867.

武野紹鴎.note: 1502–1555; Sakai tea master who shaped the wabi style and taught both Sōkyū and Rikyū.

死间.note: Literally “dead agent”; one of the five kinds of spy in Sun Tzu’s Art of War, and Juntong’s term for agents planted to burrow into the Communist base areas.

段云鹏.note: The cat-burglar (“flying thief”) recruited by Nationalist intelligence; see also Chapter 11.

段祺瑞.note: 1865-1936; Beiyang premier and head of the Anhui clique. See the note in this section.

殷汝耕.note: 1885–1947; head of the Japanese-sponsored East Hebei regime; executed as a traitor after the war.

比叡山.note: Seat of the Tendai monastery Enryaku-ji, burned by Nobunaga in 1571.

毘廬遮那仏.note: The cosmic Buddha; the Tōdai-ji colossus is a Vairocana.

毛人凤.note: Dai Li's successor as head of the postwar secret service (the Baomiju).

毛内有之介.note: An inspector of the Shinsengumi (also known by the name Kenmotsu) who left with Itō’s faction.

毛利.note: The great western house of Mōri; one of the daimyō rumored to be behind the Jurakudai fire.

毛受勝介.note: Katsuie’s retainer who took his lord’s standard and name to die in his place at Hayashidani, covering Katsuie’s retreat.

毛森.note: Mao Sen (1908–1992); Juntong intelligence officer who became chief of the Shanghai police in the city’s last Nationalist months, notorious for repression.

民主联军.note: The “democratic” label taken by units that defected to, or fought alongside, the Communists in 1945–46, before the CCP called the fighting a “war of liberation.”

民报.note: The Tongmenghui's organ ('People's Journal'), on which Wang wrote as 'Jingwei.'

気組.note: The marshalling of spirit to overwhelm an opponent; the watchword of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

氰化钾.note: The fast-acting poison that gives the novella its title; carried by agents as a means of suicide on capture.

水原清.note: The Japanese reading of 水原清 is reconstructed; the man was a Japanese special agent posing as a “good devil” at Da’anzhuang.

水戸.note: A senior Tokugawa branch domain, and the intellectual seedbed of the revere-the-Emperor school; riven in these years by violent factional strife between its radicals (the Tengu Party) and conservatives.

水蛇帮.note: A band of river-pirates wiped out overnight by the Honest Monk (Prologue).

永井主水正尚志.note: Nagai Naomune (1816–1891), a senior shogunal official (here Grand Inspector). Mondo-no-shō is his court title. He led the 1865 embassy that interrogated Chōshū at Hiroshima.

永倉新八.note: Historical, 1839–1915. Held the full transmission of the Shintō Munen-ryū; survived the Restoration and left an inside memoir of the corps.

永安公司.note: Wing On Co., opened on Nanjing Road in 1918 facing Sincere; another of the 'four great' Shanghai department stores. ch05. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the handle; 'the Wing On Company' at first use.

汉中特训班.note: Juntong’s special training class near Hanzhong, run under the cover name “Tianshui Field Headquarters Guerrilla Cadre Training Class”; called the “Hanzhong class” (汉训班) for short.

汉奸.note: Literally a traitor to the Han, i.e. a collaborator with the Japanese; the postwar treason trials pursued them. Rendered 'traitor / collaborator' by context.

汉训班.note: Short form of the Hanzhong training class.

汉阳兵器厂.note: China's oldest modern ordnance works, at Hanyang; dismantled and shipped west ahead of the Japanese advance.

江东四杰.note: The four grand men Lu Xiaofeng humiliated with a stroke of the pen, left kneeling in the Peach Blossom Hall with mocking labels painted on their brows (ch02).

江南.note: Literally ‘south of the river’: the prosperous, cultured region south of the lower Yangtze.

江南造船厂.note: The Jiangnan (Kiangnan) Dock and shipyard in Shanghai.

江川.note: The hereditary intendant house at Nirayama, administering shogunal land.

江戸.note: Ieyasu's eastern seat, the future Tokugawa capital; here in a proleptic aside about Hattori Hanzō's later mansion.

江戸城.note: The half-ruined castle Ieyasu took as his seat on his transfer to the Kantō in 1590; the future Tokyo.

江湖.note: Literally ‘rivers and lakes’: the wandering world of martial artists, sects and outlaws that is the stage of all wuxia fiction. See the note at first appearance (Prologue).

江若水.note: The airfield's English interpreter in Gannan, who turns the Huaqing Pool bathhouse into a smugglers' club; executed. Fictional.

江青.note: 1914–1991. A Shanghai film actress and Mao Zedong's fourth wife; a leader of the Cultural Revolution and a member of the “Gang of Four.”

池步洲.note: 1908–2003. A Japan-trained Nationalist cryptanalyst who broke Japanese diplomatic ciphers; Chinese accounts credit him with forecasting a Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, a claim not independently corroborated abroad.

池田屋.note: The inn at the west end of Sanjō-kobashi, kept by one Sōbei, where the loyalists met and where Kondō’s party struck.

池田徳太郎.note: A Geishū (Hiroshima) rōnin of the Kiyokawa faction, active in the levying of the Rōshigumi.

池田恒興.note: Lord of Ōgaki, a foster-brother of Nobunaga’s (also called by his lay-monk name Shōnyū); his defection to Hideyoshi opened the Komaki campaign, and he died at Nagakute.

汤玉麟.note: 1871–1949; warlord governor of Rehe (Jehol), notorious for the opium trade. Attested form.

汪东兴.note: 1916–2015. Rose from Mao Zedong's Yan'an bodyguard to head of the Central Guard Bureau; a CCP vice-chairman in the years just after Mao's death.

汪伪政府.note: The Japanese-sponsored Reorganized National Government under Wang Jingwei (established Nanjing, 1940). Historical; 汪伪 = “Wang puppet.”

汪兆铭.note: The original name of Wang Jingwei (汪精卫); see that entry.

汪兆镛.note: Wang Jingwei's elder half-brother, a Guangxu provincial graduate and painter-chronicler of Lingnan; his stern tutor.

汪文惺.note: Wang Jingwei's eldest daughter, wife of He Wenjie.

汪时璟.note: North China's foremost economic collaborator; the Kang Corps' unfinished target (see Part One, ch06). Rendered Wang Shiying consistently across the book.

汪汉溪.note: 汪汉溪; the long-time manager of the Xinwenbao.

汪锦元.note: A secret Communist planted as a secretary at Wang Jingwei’s side, feeding the regime’s top secrets to the Pan Hannian network.

沈之岳.note: 1913–1994. Nationalist agent who infiltrated Yan’an; after 1949 rose to head Taiwan’s Investigation Bureau.

沈安娜.note: 1915–2010. The “red stenographer” who took down the Nationalists' confidential meetings for fourteen years; her husband Hua Mingzhi was her partner in the work.

沈崇.note: The Peking University student whose rape by U.S. Marines in December 1946 set off nationwide student protests.

沈近朱.note: The widowed art teacher Jiang Yongnan marries in Liyuan village. Fictional.

沖田総司.note: Historical, about 1842–1868. Died young of consumption; one of the most beloved figures of the Shinsengumi legend.

沙坪坝.note: A district of wartime Chongqing, thick with schools, offices, and government hostels.

沪江大学.note: A Baptist missionary university in Shanghai (Hujiang University). Attested English name.

河内.note: Province east of Ōsaka. Two referents: Hanoi in a Chinese/Vietnamese context; Kawachi province in a Japanese source. Both correct in their books.

油坂.note: A slope on the eastern edge of Nara where Jūzō takes an inn.

泉山.note: The maple-covered peak south of Higashiyama on which the Sennyū-ji stands; read Senzan (the mountain of 泉涌寺).

泉州.note: Izumi province (Senshū), in which Sakai lay.

泉涌寺.note: An ancient temple in Kyoto’s Higashiyama, mortuary temple of the imperial house.

法公董局.note: 法公董局; the Conseil d'administration municipale, governing body of the French Concession; its Chinese members were called 华董.

法印.note: “Seal of the Law”, the highest Buddhist priestly rank, also conferred by the court on distinguished laymen.

法大马路.note: A street in the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Jinling East Road; the address on the counter-notice.

法币.note: The Nationalist government's legal-tender paper currency (introduced 1935 in fact; the novel uses the term loosely).

法眼.note: “Eye of the Law”, the rank below Hōin, likewise granted to laymen of note.

法華宗.note: Nichiren Buddhism; Honno-ji was one of its temples.

法警.note: A court officer of the judicial police; here the corps also carries out the death sentences it guards.

泰山.note: The easternmost and most venerated of China’s five sacred peaks, in Shandong; watching the sunrise from its summit is an old pilgrimage (ch07).

泰顺茶庄.note: A tea shop used as a courier channel. A fictional front; pinyin.

洛克道.note: A street in Wan Chai, Hong Kong. Attested official English name.

洛阳.note: The ancient capital; in the peony legend Empress Wu Zetian banishes the flower to Luoyang, whence 'the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven' (Chapter 27).

洞玄.note: Bare name of Mari Dōgen, used throughout the narration.

津田算長.note: Head of the Suginobō of the Negoro-ji, who brought one of the first matchlocks from Tanegashima to Kishū.

洪帮.note: The other great Chinese secret-society tradition beside the Green Gang; weaker in Shanghai, stronger in the north.

洪涛.note: The swordsman called the Lightning Blade, killed by Ximen Chuixue (Prologue).

洪门.note: 洪门; the sworn-brotherhood secret society of south China. See the note at 'a Hongmen brother.'

活菩萨.note: An idiom of praise for a person of boundless mercy; here bitterly ironic. See the note at first appearance (Prologue).

派遣军.note: The Japan China Expeditionary Army, the umbrella command for Japanese forces in China, into which Jiang is conscripted as a colonial subject.

浄福寺.note: A temple giving its name to the street that bounded the Jurakudai on the west. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: Hepburn with macrons (lang-ja).

浅井長政.note: Lord of Odani Castle in Ōmi and Nobunaga's brother-in-law, turned enemy; besieged from 1570.

浅野長政.note: Asano Nagamasa (1547–1611), Hideyoshi's brother-in-law and one of the Five Commissioners; a protector of the mission, who led ten thousand men into Iga in the Tenshō war.

济州岛.note: The Korean island of Jiang Yongnan's birth.

浙江路.note: 浙江路; a Settlement road crossing Nanjing Road; older English Chekiang Road.

浜松.note: Ieyasu's castle town in Totomi, where Goemon is settled under the alias Saeki Dennai.

浦东.note: The east bank of the Huangpu; older English Pootung.

浪士組.note: The ‘corps of masterless men,’ levied by the shogunate in 1863 to go up to Kyoto ostensibly as the shogun's guard. Split by Kiyokawa's imperial gambit; the remnant that stayed in Kyoto became the Shinsengumi.

浮世橋.note: The vermilion bridge into the valley; furigana うきよばし. Named for the 'floating world'; to cross it is to leave the world of the living.

海关钟楼.note: The tower of the Maritime Customs House on the Bund, its Westminster-chiming clock (“Big Ching”) completed 1927. Historical.

海底.note: Juntong jargon (literally “sea bottom”) for the secret personal dossier each agent memorized—names, addresses, contacts, cipher, and oath—left on file at the training class.

海格路.note: Real. Avenue Haig (after Field Marshal Douglas Haig); today Huashan Road (华山路). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: concession street names keep their period foreign forms (shelf canon), pinyin glossed once.

海门.note: A county at the Yangtze mouth on the Beisha line.

涞水.note: The Hebei county and the campaign (the 涞水之役) in which the 35th Army bled, its commander and division commander took their lives, and the mass encoffining of the dead was carried out.

涪陵.note: A district on the Yangtze upstream of Chongqing, source of the local rice liquor in the bar's cocktail.

涿县.note: The county southwest of Beiping on the Ping-Han line where the First Command Room had its seat; the hub of section one and the place to which Fu Zuoyi's requisitioned coffins were sent.

淀君.note: Hideyoshi's favored concubine (Yodo-dono), daughter of Azai Nagamasa and niece of Nobunaga; mother of Tsurumatsu and, in 1593, of Hideyori. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: reader-facing English form; 'Yodo-gimi' stands as owls-castle's recorded deviation.

淀城.note: The castle Hideyoshi rebuilt for the Lady Yodo and their son southwest of Kyoto, fed by great river waterwheels; scene of Goemon's capture.

淑芬.note: Jiang Ruoshui's wartime wife, a painter of birds and flowers. Fictional.

淞沪会战.note: The battle of August–November 1937. Attested English name.

深津.note: A pupil of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, set to make fire during the ambush; a passing figure.

淳安.note: 淳安; a county in western Zhejiang.

清乡.note: 清乡 (qingxiang), the Japanese and Wang-regime campaign to pacify and control the countryside around occupied Shanghai.

清正.note: Katō Kiyomasa; here by his title Higo-no-kami. Footnoted at first appearance in ch04.

清水.note: Kiyomizu-dera, the great temple on the Higashiyama slope; its pagoda is the landmark seen from the fields.

清水宗治.note: Commander of Takamatsu Castle, who took his own life as the price of the Mori's peace with Hideyoshi.

清水董三.note: Secretary of the Japanese Foreign Ministry, part of the Wang Jingwei Tokyo party.

清河八郎.note: Historical, 1830–1863. A rural samurai of Shōnai in Dewa, a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept and strategist; conceived the Rōshigumi and tried to turn it to the imperial cause, and was cut down for it in 1863.

清洲.note: The Owari castle where Nobunaga's generals met in 1582 to settle the succession.

渡辺幸右衛門.note: The beat constable who, being on friendly terms with the corps, passed the tip to Mibu rather than to his own office. Romanization mine.

渡辺慧.note: The Kashima-school rōnin swordsman whom Kohagi bankrolls and sets against Jūzō; a fictional figure. The given name 慧 is left unglossed in the scan; the reading Satoru is a project call. Referred to in narration by the bare given name 慧.

港济公司.note: The opium-trafficking front company Du set up with Dai Li in 1939, with offices in Chongqing and Hong Kong, nominally under Gu Jiatang.

溥仪.note: 1906–1967. The last Qing emperor, installed by Japan as ruler of Manchukuo.

溪口.note: Chiang Kai-shek's native town in Fenghua, Zhejiang; the brigade's charge in the winter and spring of 1949 was to guard its outer ring.

滇越路.note: The French-built Yunnan–Vietnam (Kunming–Haiphong) railway, the route from Yunnan into Indochina.

滑竿.note: pole-slung carrying chair Adjudicated 2026-08-29: culture-specific item, italic romanization with a first-use gloss (the laohuzao pattern).

滝川一益.note: Senior Shibata-faction commander (styled Sakon-shōgen), daimyo of some 300,000 koku in Ise; struck first in the war and drew Hideyoshi’s Ise campaign.

滝川勝雄.note: Commander of Maruyama Castle in the novel; reading of 勝雄 not independently confirmed.

满洲国.note: The puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi; directed from emperor to premier by Japanese advisers.

满铁.note: The South Manchuria Railway Company, a vast Japanese “state-policy company” that ran the railways and much of the economy of the Northeast and doubled as a huge intelligence organ; its Research Department was a magnet for spies. Abbreviated 满铁 (Mantetsu).

满铁株式会社.note: The Japanese 'Mantetsu,' a vast semi-official enterprise and instrument of Japanese expansion in China.

滦榆游击总部.note: The Juntong guerrilla command for the Luan River and Shanhaiguan (Yuguan) region of East Hebei.

潘先生.note: The Communist handler over Zhou San and Su Lina in Shanghai. A fictional character; surname romanized. Distinct from Old Pan of The Rebel.

潘公展.note: Nationalist CC Clique figure and newspaperman in Shanghai.

潘新民.note: Old Pan's full name, given under interrogation; code name Index Finger. Pinyin.

潘汉年.note: 1906–1977. A literary man turned master of CCP intelligence and united-front work; deputy head of the Social Affairs Department, working from Hong Kong and Shanghai. Wrongly imprisoned as an “inner traitor” in 1955; rehabilitated in 1982.

澎湖.note: The Pescadores; the island group to which the brigade withdrew from Xiamen in September 1949 and where it was finally disbanded.

瀬木掃部.note: One of the hereditary priestly houses (shake) of the Rokusha Myōjin at Fuchū, in whose residence Rokusha Sōhaku lodged. Romanization mine.

炳华.note: The given name of Zhang Yanyuan (张炎元), an early Juntong figure; see that entry.

点穴.note: The wuxia trick of striking a specific acupuncture point to freeze the limb, seal off the voice, or immobilise the whole man. See the note at first appearance (ch02).

為三郎.note: Toshizō’s blind eldest brother, who took the poet-name Sekisui the Blind and was passed over for the headship of the house by the law of the day.

烏丸.note: A fat thirteen-year-old, orphan of an Ikko-ikki commander, Etegi's inseparable companion.

热河.note: Rehe (Jehol), the borderland province north-east of Beiping, invaded by the Kwantung Army in 1933. See the note at first appearance.

熊向晖.note: 1919–2005. The most celebrated of the Communists' deep-cover agents; secretary to Hu Zongnan for a decade and, later, a senior diplomat and deputy head of the Central Investigation Department.

熊坂長範.note: The giant bandit of medieval legend, a stock figure of the theater; see the note in the chapter.

熊姥姥.note: ‘Granny’ renders laolao (姥姥), a homely word for an old woman or grandmother; her surname is Xiong. The poisoner of the first vignette (Prologue).

爱丁堡大厦.note: An apartment building beside the Jing'an Temple; Lin's Shanghai residence. Rendered by the English place-name in the source.

片桐且元.note: One of the Seven Spears of Shizugatake; later steward of the Toyotomi house.

牛頭天王.note: The 'Ox-Head Heavenly King,' plague-warding deity of the Gion and Tennō shrines, whose talismans the waiwai-tennō sold.

牯岭.note: 牯岭 (also romanized Kuling); the hill-station atop Mount Lu (庐山) above Jiujiang, a summer retreat from the Yangzi heat.

特别第一区.note: The former German concession at Tianjin, taken back after the First World War.

特务.note: The word this chapter anatomizes. Originally a neutral term for “special-duty” military work, it became, in the mouths of both parties, the loaded word for the enemy's spies and secret police. Rendered by sense in this translation, and kept as tewu where the author discusses it as a word.

特务团.note: A combat unit directly under the Juntong, commanded by Wang Zhaohuai at Chongqing.

特务处.note: The covert-operations department of the Lixingshe, headed by Dai Li; the operational seed of the Juntong.

特务如麻.note: Kang Sheng’s image for the campaign’s hysteria: agents supposedly so numerous they were “thick as hemp.”

特工总部.note: The Wang regime's secret police, known from its address as 'No. 76.' Adjudicated 2026-08-29: closest to 特工 and attested; 'Secret Service Headquarters' stands as the-rebel's recorded deviation.

特种组织.note: The Leader's term for the older special services he had 'raised with his own hands over twenty years,' the Juntong foremost among them, whose decay he lamented at the opening of the Lizhi Class.
