特种部队.note: The new-pattern special force of the Pacification Corps; the same compound is glossed 'Special Forces' in the chapter that defines it (Part Four, chapter two).

特科.note: The CCP's clandestine intelligence and security service (中央特科), founded 1927 and active in Shanghai; here Yang Muci's and Lao Yu's organ. See the note at Chapter 4.

特高课.note: The Special Higher Police (Japanese Tokkō), Japan’s political and thought police, which ran surveillance on suspected subversives at home and in occupied territory.

牺盟会.note: The Sacrifice League for National Salvation (牧牙救国同盟会), an anti-Japanese mass body formed under Yan Xishan in Shanxi in 1936 and heavily penetrated by the Communists.

犬养健.note: Japanese politician of the Seiyūkai and son of former premier Inukai Tsuyoshi; Kagesa's aide in escorting Wang Jingwei from Hanoi.

犬养毅.note: Prime minister of Japan assassinated by naval officers in 1932; father of Inukai Ken.

狐狸精.note: In Chinese folklore a fox that has cultivated the power to take human shape, most often a beautiful woman, and bewitches men; in common speech, an insult for a seductress or husband-stealer, with the ghostly sense worn away. Distinct from the plain ‘little fox’ (小狐狸), which marks only slyness. See the note at first appearance (ch13, the Coda).

独孤一鹤.note: The present master of the Emei sword-sect and secret head of the Blue-Robe Tower; revealed to be Ping Duhe, one of the four traitor-ministers. Not to be confused with Dugu Fang, who shares the two-syllable surname Dugu but is his enemy (ch04).

独孤方.note: The Solitary Rider of a Thousand Li (千里独行), one of the strangest and most reclusive figures of the jianghu; a spectator, not an assassin, in Chapter 1’s three-against-two exchange. Dugu is a two-syllable surname.

独流.note: The Jin-Pu-line station where the assault team detrained and awaited orders; the Second Command Room's Second Group was seated there.

猿渡.note: The hereditary house of chief priests (gūji) of the Ōkunitama Shrine at Fuchū, documented from the fourteenth century.

猿田彦.note: The guiding deity of Japanese myth, shown as a long-nosed, red-faced figure; his mask (rubied here in the source as Sarudahiko) was one of those the waiwai-tennō wore.

玄武湖.note: Real. Lake against the northeastern wall of Nanjing.

玄武館.note: Chiba Shūsaku's Hokushin Ittō-ryū hall in Edo, greatest of the three great dōjō.

玉虫左大夫.note: A Sendai clansman and diarist (1823–1869); his intelligence-record Kanbu Tsūki preserves these figures. Also written 玉虫左太夫.

王一亭.note: 1867–1938 (born Wang Zhen); comprador, businessman, celebrated Shanghai-School painter and Buddhist-layman philanthropist; longtime chairman of the Flour Exchange.

王世英.note: 1905–1968. A Special Branch veteran who ran Communist intelligence and united-front work in the North; later a provincial governor, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

王伯群.note: Former Minister of Communications; owner of the Lane 1136 Yuyuan Road houses Wang Jingwei used.

王克敏.note: 1873–1945. Head of the Japanese-sponsored Provisional Government in North China.

王八.note: Coarse slang, literally ‘tortoise’: a scoundrel, and above all a cuckold. Kept romanised because the whole running gag of ch02 turns on the word. See the note at first appearance (ch02).

王叔铭.note: Nationalist air-force general; chief of the education section at the Air Force Officers' School.

王天木.note: A senior Juntong operative in North China; later, in the Hanoi affair and after, his loyalties became a matter of dispute.

王学文.note: 1895–1985. A Japan-trained Marxist economist and secret Communist who taught at the Japanese academy in Shanghai and later directed the Eighth Route Army’s enemy-army work and the Japanese Workers’ and Peasants’ School at Yan’an.

王宠惠.note: Styled Liangchou; jurist and Foreign Minister of the National Government.

王庆沱.note: The town some fifteen li west of Yangliuqing garrisoned by Zhu Zhankui's security corps; it fell to the bandit army on the night the assault team and the Second Command Room withdrew from it.

王懋功.note: 王懋功 (1891–1961); Kuomintang general, at this time chairman of Jiangsu Province.

王政復古.note: The Ōsei Fukko coup of Keiō 3/12/9 (3 January 1868): the shogunate and regency abolished, direct Imperial rule declared.

王新衡.note: A friend of Chiang Ching-kuo and figure in the Military Statistics Bureau.

王明.note: 1904–1974. Leader of the Moscow-trained “28 Bolsheviks” and the CCP’s representative to the Comintern; a rival to Mao whose successive “Left” and “Right” lines the author disparages.

王星文.note: Hanzhong agent (alias Wang Jiwu) at the Lu Xun Academy of Arts; turned by the Border Security.

王晓籁.note: A leading figure of the Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce.

王炎堂.note: Born Huang Jintang; entered the Social Affairs Department at fifteen and became an expert on the Nationalist secret services; later a deputy minister of the Central Investigation Department and one of the author's interviewees.

王珺.note: Social Affairs Department officer of the “Old Third Class” who traced the Second Bureau cell; later deputy minister of State Security.

王石坚.note: Chief of a large Communist intelligence network spanning the Northwest, North China, and the Northeast; his arrest in 1947, after a subordinate's betrayal, rolled up the whole system.

王禹卿.note: Partner and general manager of the Rong family's Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills; a director of the Shanghai Flour Exchange.

王芃生.note: Head of the Nationalist Institute for International Affairs, a noted intelligence analyst on Japan.

王超北.note: A Shaanxi native who built the Communists’ second, deep-buried Xi’an radio net—later the “Xi’an Intelligence Office”—which survived the breaking of Wang Shijian’s network in the civil war.

珊瑚坝.note: The airfield on a sandbar in the river at Chongqing, from which Wang flew out.

珍皇院.note: A half-ruined, landless temple in the Rokuhara district where the monk Gyōzan lodges travelers; evokes the real Rokudō-Chinnō-ji. Reading a project call.

珞珈山.note: The Wuhan University campus hill where the author met Guo Changlu. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: majority, and it is a hill; exception to the Mount X pattern.

珠光宝气阁.note: The seat of Yan Tieshan’s jewel empire; its name (‘the sheen of pearls, the glow of treasure’) gives Chapter 6 its title. Huo Tianqing is its steward (ch05).

理兵衛.note: Keeper of the Jōshūya inn at Fuda, the Tennen Rishin-ryū men's regular lodging. Romanization mine.

琉球.note: The island kingdom annexed by Japan in 1879, cited as the start of Japan's designs on China.

瑞金.note: The seat of the Central Soviet in Jiangxi, capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic.

甄别.note: The corrective phase from late 1943 in which the campaign’s cases were re-examined and most detainees cleared.

甘乃光.note: Nationalist official; the diarist 'Yongwu' consults him on Wang's flight.

生野.note: The silver-mining district in Tajima; furigana いくの.

田中义一.note: Japanese premier and foreign minister 1927–29; associated with the Jinan Incident and the alleged Tanaka Memorial.

田中光顕.note: Tanaka Mitsuaki (1843–1939), a Tosa loyalist who after the Restoration became a count and Imperial Household Minister; Shiba quotes his recollection of fearing the Shinsengumi.

田中土佐.note: Tanaka Tosa (Genba), a chief retainer of the Aizu domain during its years as Kyoto Protector; he died by his own hand at the fall of Aizu in 1868.

田中奏折.note: The alleged 1927 memorial of Tanaka Giichi on world conquest; generally regarded as a forgery.

田汉.note: 1898–1968; playwright and lyricist, author of the words of the PRC national anthem.

田沼玄蕃頭.note: Tanuma Okitaka (1834–1868), a junior councillor (wakadoshiyori) of the shogunate, grandson of the notorious minister Tanuma Okitsugu. He directed the harsh disposal of the surrendered Tengu Party at Tsuruga.

甲午战争.note: The war of 1894–95 in which Japan defeated Qing China.

甲州街道.note: One of the five great Tokugawa highways, running west from Edo through Fuchū toward Kōfu in Kai (Kōshū).

甲源一刀流.note: A sword school of the Chichibu country, founded 1776 by Henmi Tashirō; the school of Rokusha Sōhaku and, along the Kōshū Highway, the chief rival of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

甲賀.note: The neighboring ninja district in Ōmi.

甲賀三郎.note: Legendary founding ancestor of Kōga ninjutsu, hero of the medieval 甲賀三郎 tale.

甲賀文.note: Fictional Kōga calling-card: a single Sanskrit glyph on a slip, left as a ninja's greeting-token when entering another's territory.

甲陽鎮撫隊.note: The name (“Kōyō Pacification Corps”; Kōyō is a literary name for Kai province) given to the refitted Shinsengumi in the second month of Keiō 4 (1868), when the Tokugawa house sent it west to hold Kōfu Castle against the advancing new-government army.

申报.note: Shanghai's most famous daily newspaper (1872–1949); among the papers A-Chu lays out for Muci in Chapter 35. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: majority form, italic as a masthead; article per sentence.

申报馆.note: 申报馆; the office of the Shen Bao (Shun Pao), Shanghai's leading daily newspaper.

电子对抗.note: The author's term for the 1947 radio contest: interception, direction-finding, and radio-silence deception. Rendered "electronic warfare" though the technology of the day was radio, not electronics in the later sense.

界首.note: 界首; a town on the Henan–Anhui border, a wartime trans-shipment point between Nationalist and occupied territory.

白世维.note: Seventh-class academy graduate; the gunman who carried out the 1933 killing of Zhang Jingyao, the Beiping Station's first case.

白公馆.note: The household of the Fifth Concubine of the Bai family (白府五姨太), the concubine's sworn sister and protector; also rendered the House of Bai. Two referents: the SACO-era Baigongguan prison (keep the name) vs a fictional Bai family residence. Both correct in their books.

白区.note: Kuomintang-controlled territory, as opposed to the Red (soviet) areas; the author’s underground post was in the Shanghai white area. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: capitalized political geography, plural as the standard collective; glossed at first use.

白崇禧.note: 1893–1966. Muslim general of the Guangxi clique, nicknamed “Little Zhuge” for his generalship; deputy chief of the Nationalist general staff and later defense minister.

白毫寺.note: A temple on a hill at the eastern edge of Nara.

白泰来.note: Yanzhi's father, once the finest tailor in Xietang.

百乐门.note: The Paramount Ballroom, a famous Shanghai dance hall; here the house to which Young Tang is packed off. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the handle; 'the Paramount Ballroom' at first use.

百地三太夫.note: The most famous jonin of Iga; the Momochi fort where Tamo was maimed was of this house.

百地新之丞.note: An Iga gōshi of Tatsunokuchi, of the Momochi band.

皖南事变.note: The January 1941 Nationalist attack on the New Fourth Army headquarters in southern Anhui (literally “the Southern Anhui Incident”), which shattered the united front.

益田越中.note: A Chōshū elder councillor (karō) commanding the Yamazaki wing of the expedition.

益社.note: The disciple-fraternity Fan Shaozeng, this chapter's narrator, ran in Shanghai on the model of Du Yuesheng's Heng Society.

盛丕华.note: 1882–1961. Shanghai industrialist and democratic figure; after 1949 a deputy mayor of Shanghai.

監察.note: Kansatsu, the corps’s internal watch and intelligence officers, answering to the vice-commander.

真庭十郎左衛門.note: As Shiba gives him, the head of the Nen-ryū house at Maniwa and Chiba Shūsaku's antagonist in the Ikaho affair. The historical head of the Maniwa Nen-ryū was of the Higuchi family; Shiba names him from the school's seat.

真木和泉守.note: Maki Izumi (Yasuomi), a Shinto priest of Kurume and the most radical strategist of the loyalist cause; a chief planner of Chōshū's march on Kyoto. He died on Tennōzan (ch. 25).

真葛ヶ原.note: A moor at the western foot of Higashiyama, east of the capital, famed in poetry for its autumn bush-clover.

督邮街.note: The busiest night district of wartime Chongqing. Pinyin.

石友三.note: 1891–1940; a general notorious for switching sides repeatedly.

石坂周造.note: A defector from Hikone and follower of Kiyokawa; survived into the mid-Meiji years as a man of business, remembered as a pioneer of the Japanese petroleum trade.

石家庄.note: The Hebei rail-junction city, scene of the Communist siege and capture of November 1947; Chen more often calls it by its older name, Shimen.

石川五右衛門.note: The semi-legendary thief and shinobi who is the novel's hero; by tradition put to death by boiling in 1594.

石川数正.note: A senior retainer of Ieyasu’s who escorted Ogimaru to Hideyoshi; he later defected to Hideyoshi.

石库门.note: 石库门, the stone-framed-gate lane-house characteristic of Shanghai.

石田三成.note: Ishida Mitsunari (1560-1600), Hideyoshi’s ablest administrator and one of the Five Commissioners; led the western coalition against Ieyasu and was defeated at Sekigahara. Appears here by his court title Jibu-no-shōyū.

石田散薬.note: The Hijikata family's patent remedy for bruises and broken bones, made and peddled from the early eighteenth century until 1948.

石田村.note: Toshizō's birthplace in the Tama district of Musashi; now part of Hino, Tokyo.

石秀雪.note: The youngest of the Four Beauties of Emei; gentlest-seeming and hottest-tempered, she fights with a pair of short swords and dares, alone of the four, to love where she will. Hua Manlou catches her blades between two fingers, and she loses her heart to him (ch09).

石翠.note: Toshizō's eldest brother, blind from birth, who gave up the succession and lived by his arts — a shrewd, polished man. A historical figure (the eldest Hijikata brother); Sekisui is his elegant by-name.

石見守.note: The honorary provincial title Hattori Hanzō later took (Governor of Iwami).

石门.note: The older name of Shijiazhuang, used throughout this chapter.

砸烂公检法.note: The Cultural Revolution slogan against the legal apparatus; kept as a slogan and glossed.

磨擦.note: The standard term, on both sides, for Nationalist–Communist armed clashes 1939–1943; fan moca is “the struggle against friction.”

祁三益.note: Hanzhong-class demolition instructor sent to Yan’an as group liaison; turned by the Border Security and central to cracking the case.

祁先生.note: The Nationalist intelligence handler who first recruits Jiang, passing him the cyanide-filled coin. Fictional; pinyin.

祇園.note: The district below the Yasaka Shrine; not yet a quarter of teahouses in 1591, as the narration notes.

神保内蔵助.note: An elder councillor (karō) of the Aizu domain and its senior officer on the Kyoto command; full name Jinbō Kuranosuke Toshitaka. He would be made to take his own life in 1868, blamed for the Aizu retreat at Toba-Fushimi.

神道無念流.note: A widely practiced Edo sword school; Nagakura Shinpachi held its full transmission.

祥生汽车公司.note: A leading Shanghai taxi firm (Johnson Taxi), founded by Zhou Xiangsheng.

祥符荡.note: The reed-grown lake-marsh near Xietang, haunt of the water bandits (see note on 荡).

禁娱令.note: The wartime government's prohibition of dance halls and public amusements in the capital.

福原越後.note: A Chōshū elder councillor (karō) who led the Fushimi wing of the 1864 expedition. Wounded in the fighting, he was afterward ordered by his own domain to commit seppuku as one of the three councillors held responsible for the defeat.

福島正則.note: Also Fukushima Ichimatsu; foremost of the Seven Spears of Shizugatake and a lifelong Hideyoshi man.

福新.note: 福新面粉厂, the Rong family's Shanghai flour mill.

福煦路.note: A French Concession street, today's Yan'an Middle Road (eastern stretch).

福熙路.note: A French Concession boulevard, today's central Yan'an Middle Road. Attested French name.

福田理兵衛.note: A loyalist country samurai (gōshi) of Shimo-Saga who had earlier arranged the billeting of Chōshū troops at the Tenryū-ji. Romanization mine.

秀吉.note: Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), Nobunaga's foremost general and, after 1582, the unifier of Japan.

秀次.note: Hideyoshi's nephew and adopted heir, made Kampaku in 1591; forced to suicide in 1595.

秀芬.note: The widow of a killed guerrilla commissar, brought by Zhou San to keep house for Zhongliang. A fictional character; pinyin.

秀長.note: Hashiba (Toyotomi) Hidenaga (1540–1591), Hideyoshi’s younger half-brother and most trusted general; made governor of Kii and given the vanguard in the Kishū campaign of Tenshō 13. Titled Yamato Dainagon.

秀頼.note: Toyotomi Hideyori, Hideyoshi's son and heir, born to Yodo-gimi on the third day of the eighth month, Bunroku 2 (1593); infant name O-Hiroi. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: single-name convention for Toyotomi figures after a full first use (Toyotomi Hideyori).

租界.note: Render by referent: 'the Concessions' generically or for the French Concession; 'the Settlement' for the International Settlement specifically.

秦兆宽.note: A collaborator with the Wang Jingwei regime, general manager of the Dahua Trading Company and a Japanese liaison; Su Lina's target. A fictional character; pinyin.

秦启荣.note: A Shandong man of the sixth Whampoa class, named in Dai Li's directive to command the Tianjin-Pukou demolition brigade and organize the Qingdao action group.

秦太太.note: Qin Shuji's wife, who takes Yanzhi in without reproach.

秦平.note: Border Security field officer in Guanzhong and at the mail-inspection station.

秦树基.note: The Shanghai oil-painter Yanzhi loves and follows to the city.

秦桧.note: d. 1155; the Song chancellor who engineered the judicial murder of the general Yue Fei and made peace with the Jin; the archetypal Chinese traitor, whose kneeling iron effigy stands before Yue Fei's tomb at West Lake.

秦邦宪.note: Better known as Bo Gu (博古); one of the ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and de facto Party leader 1931–35.

秩父.note: The hill country of western Musashi; home ground of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū.

程一鸣.note: 1909–1998. Former Communist who headed Juntong’s Northwest District; long a deep CCP source.

程慕颐.note: Chief of Juntong’s Northwest Special Reconnaissance Station and deputy director of the Hanzhong class (cover name Cheng Yi); fled to Taiwan.

程益.note: Cover name of Cheng Muyi as director of the Hanzhong class.

程砚秋.note: 程砚秋 (1904–1958); one of the ‘Four Great Dan’ of Peking opera, founder of the Cheng school of dan roles.

種子ケ島.note: The island off southern Kyūshū where the matchlock is traditionally said to have reached Japan in 1543; the gun itself came to be called a tanegashima.

穆安素.note: 穆安素; an Italian lawyer of Shanghai, one of the foreign hostages at Lincheng.

穆欣.note: The Communist author of the 1979 booklet 'General Ji Hongchang,' which Chen quotes at length and disputes.

穴山梅雪.note: Takeda kinsman and general who defected to Nobunaga and Ieyasu as the house fell.

立水桥.note: The Daxing-county village, some thirty li north of Beiping's Andingmen, named for its cement bridge; scene of the October 1948 night battle between the local corps and the Communist militia.

章士钊.note: 1881–1973; scholar, lawyer, and sometime Beiyang education minister who named Du Yuesheng’s Heng Society; later a noted public figure in the People’s Republic.

章太炎.note: Given name Binglin; eminent classical scholar and revolutionary, editor-in-chief of the Min Bao, driven off by Wang.

童自重.note: A military-political adviser to the Wang regime; his Japanese army registry name is Uemura Kiyoshi (上村净). Assassinated at the Cathay Hotel. Pinyin.

竹ノ上人.note: The local nickname for the monk Gyōzan, who gazes at (and claims to become) the bamboo. 上人 (Shōnin) is an honorific for a holy monk.

竹叶青.note: A pale-green liquor of Shanxi: sorghum spirit steeped with bamboo leaves and herbs. See the note at the Shanglin Spring (ch05).

竹屋町.note: An east–west street in central Kyōto.

笠間喜十郎.note: An Echigo rōnin drawn into the ambush; he died of his wound days later, naming Itō as the man behind it.

筋違橋.note: A bridge on the road north of Fujinomori, where the Ōgaki troops caught the Chōshū column crossing.

筑波山.note: The twin-peaked mountain of Hitachi, long a sacred site, where the Tengu Party first rose in 1864.

策反.note: Inducing an enemy officer, unit, or garrison to defect. Rendered "turning" (and "turning work") throughout, distinct from ordinary united-front persuasion.

简二先生.note: The other of the Two Talents of the Northwest, sole heir to the Finger-Flicking art (弹指神通). One of the Seven Heroes of the Marketplace (ch08).

简照南.note: Founder of the Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Company.

築山どの.note: Ieyasu's principal wife and Nobuyasu's mother, accused of treasonous dealings with the Takeda and killed in 1579.

篠原泰之進.note: Eldest of Itō's followers, a rōnin of Kurume skilled in both the sword and jūjutsu; the one who warns Itō against trusting his own cleverness. Later a Kōdai-ji guardsman.

米沢藤次.note: A Chōshū samurai and Osae’s lover in Kyoto, through whom she passed shogunate-side intelligence.

粟田.note: Awata(guchi), the district at the eastern approach to the capital below Higashiyama; a scholar's academy there is the model for Kohagi's villa.

糖炒栗子.note: A common cold-weather street food. See the note at first appearance (Prologue).

納屋助左衛門.note: A great merchant of Sakai, later famed as Ruson (Luzon) Sukezaemon; Goemon robs his storehouse.

納屋宗次.note: Sakai merchant and tea man whose son-in-law and heir Sōkyū became.

細川.note: The Hosokawa house; another named in the same street rumor.

織田信孝.note: Nobunaga's ambitious concubine-born son (Sanshichi); Shibata's ally against Hideyoshi.

織田信長.note: The warlord whose 1581 invasion destroyed Iga; killed at the Honnō-ji in 1582.

織田信雄.note: Nobunaga's second surviving son, of the same mother as Nobutada; reckoned dull, made the young heir's guardian.

红十字会.note: The Red Cross; Jiang served with its Hankou branch before his arrest.

红旗党.note: The fabricated charge that an underground CCP organization was a Nationalist front “flying the red flag to oppose the red flag.”

红河大桥.note: The long road-and-rail bridge over the Red (Hong) River at Hanoi, the Pont Doumer (now Long Bien); scene of the failed car chase.

纪中原.note: Zhu Yizhen's controller and cover-husband; introduces himself as 'Old Ji.' Pinyin.

纳税华人会.note: 纳税华人会; the Chinese Ratepayers' Association of the French Concession, which elected Chinese members to the French Municipal Council.

绥靖.note: A Nationalist term for the 1946–49 civil war, casting the Communists as rebels to be pacified.

绥靖总队.note: In full the Ministry of National Defense Pacification Corps, the postwar special force raised for the 1946-49 campaign against the Communists; Chen commanded its First Brigade in the Beiping-Tianjin region.

维新政府.note: The Japanese-sponsored 'Reformed Government of the Republic of China' at Nanjing (Central China), headed by Liang Hongzhi.

绿兵船.note: The Maoxin/Fuxin mills' flour brand, taken as the exchange's benchmark grade; other mills' flour was discounted against it.

缪维.note: A Kang Corps operative killed with Huang Kezhong when their charge went off at Hongkou Park.

罗君强.note: Named in the 'Yongwu' diary; a figure in Wang Jingwei's Chongqing circle.

罗瑞卿.note: 1906–1978. First minister of public security of the People's Republic (from 1949); ranked Senior General in 1955. Brought down in December 1965 on the eve of the Cultural Revolution.

罗荣桓.note: Political commissar of the Communist Northeast field army, senior in the Party to Lin Biao; later a PLA marshal. Zheng Jiemin warns Chen to avoid his intervention.

罗青长.note: 1918–2014. A young Yan'an-trained intelligence officer and “living file,” aide to Zhou Enlai; later minister of the Central Investigation Department.

羅刹.note: A flesh-eating demon of Buddhist myth. Footnoted at first appearance.

羅刹谷.note: The chapter-title valley south of Higashiyama, its ruined Yakushi hall the rappa's muster-place. 羅刹 (rakshasa) footnoted at first appearance.

美专.note: The Shanghai Academy of Fine Arts, where Qin Shuji teaches oil painting (see note).

義仲.note: Minamoto (Kiso) no Yoshinaka, 1154–1184; the rough eastern warrior-cousin of Yoshitsune, briefly master of the capital before his fellow Minamoto destroyed him.

翁文灏.note: 1889–1971; geologist and Nationalist official, acting president of Tsinghua University in 1931 and later premier; returned to the mainland in 1951.

老号.note: The Border Security detainees held before the “Dai case” broke, mostly men merely suspected of being agents.

老实和尚.note: The ragged monk of the Prologue’s second vignette, so called because he cannot tell a lie; he destroyed the Water Snake Gang in a night. He resurfaces in ch05, mortified by his one dishonest deed.

老板娘.note: Zhu Ting’s wife; called only by this title (老板娘, ‘Boss’s Wife’) throughout, since her husband’s nickname is the Boss. A great beauty, and Lu Xiaofeng’s decoy for keeping Zhu Ting alive.

老潘.note: The Communist contact who reactivates Zhu Yizhen after Ji Zhongyuan's presumed death. Pinyin.

老莫.note: A boatman among the marsh bandits; becomes Yanzhi's right hand.

老金.note: The veteran bailiff who oversees the Chongqing executions and watches over Tang Ya. Fictional; “Old” renders the familiar prefix lao.

老闸捕房.note: 老闸捕房; the Louza (老闸) police station of the International Settlement, the very station whose men fired the shots of 30 May 1925. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: period romanization of the named station (shelf canon for concession-era names).

聂荣臻.note: 1899–1992. Commander of the Jin-Cha-Ji base area behind Japanese lines and later a marshal of the People's Republic.

联合准备银行.note: The North China puppet regime's central bank of issue (Federal Reserve Bank of China, 1938); Wang Shiying its governor. Distinct from the Wang regime's Central Reserve Bank (中央储备银行).

联络部.note: The Communist army organ for turning enemy troops, successively named the Destruction Department, Enemy Work Department, Nationalist-Army Work Department, and Liaison Department.

聚楽第.note: Hideyoshi's palace-villa in the capital (ch07's title, 聚楽). Footnoted at first appearance.

肤施县.note: The Nationalist name for the county containing Yan’an; its Nationalist “Fushi County Government” ran in parallel with the Communist “Yan’an County Government.”

胡主任.note: An officer of the Juntong headquarters inspectorate in Chongqing who sets Lin to watch Gu Shenyan. A fictional character; surname romanized.

胡均鹤.note: Chief of the Second Section of No. 76, later found to be a Communist as well.

胡士渊.note: Leader of the independent cell (aliases Hu Siyuan, Hu Yaonan, Hu Youlian) planted in the Military Commission’s Second Bureau.

胡底.note: 1905–1935. Killed on the Long March in Zhang Guotao's purge.

胡志明.note: Historical (1890–1969); Vietnamese revolutionary, later president of North Vietnam. Standard English form.

胡汉民.note: 1879–1936; a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek.

胡蝶.note: 1908–1989, the film star 'Butterfly Wu,' twice voted 'Queen of the Screen'; her lost wartime 'luggage' (largely smuggled goods) and her complaint to Dai Li triggered the couple's arrest (ch20–21).

胭脂.note: The protagonist; her given name is the ordinary word for rouge (see the first-appearance note).

脇坂安治.note: One of the Seven Spears of Shizugatake.

致公堂.note: The overseas Hongmen lodge network; Cantonese romanization.

臼杵.note: Town in Bungo; site of the Jesuit noviciate.

興正寺.note: A monzeki (imperially-connected) temple in Kyoto, next to the Nishi-Honganji; Kondō kept a rest-lodging at its lower villa.

舞林皇后.note: “Queen of the Dance World,” the title given the top dance-hostess, often by charity ballot.

良友.note: The famous illustrated pictorial of Republican Shanghai (1926–1945). Attested English title.

芥川.note: In the Nishinari district of Settsu; site of Nobunaga's field camp on his 1568 march to Kyoto.

花昌町.note: The site of the Shinsengumi’s last Kyoto barracks (also called Fudōdō-mura), near Samegai, Shichijō, and the Horikawa; no such place-name survives today. The source glosses the name kashō-chō.

花满楼.note: The name means ‘flowers fill the tower.’ See the note at his first appearance (Prologue).

芳駕籠.note: The palanquin-house by the Bukkō-ji gate. Apparently the novelist’s invention.

芹沢鴨.note: Historical, 1826/27–1863. A Mito man of the Shindō Munen-ryū, real name given variously as Kimura or Shimomura Tsuguji; first head of the Mibu corps, assassinated by the Kondō faction in the ninth month of 1863.

苏丽娜.note: A Communist agent married in cover to an army officer, later a dance-hostess. The modern-sounding given name 丽娜 (“Lina”) suits her cosmopolitan cover. A fictional character; pinyin.

苏堤.note: 苏堤; the willow-planted dyke across the West Lake, traditionally credited to the poet Su Shi. See the note in Fan Bowen's poem.

苏少卿.note: The name under which Su Shaoying passes himself off as the Yan household’s resident tutor and man of letters (ch07).

苏少英.note: Su the Second of the Three Heroes and Four Beauties of Emei (峨嵋三英四秀); a disciple of Dugu Yihe. His self-made Saber-and-Sword Double Kill could not save him from Ximen Chuixue’s blade (ch07).

苏浙行动委员会.note: 苏浙行动委员会; its Special Action Corps (别动队) was a Dai Li–organized irregular force raised in the 1937 Shanghai fighting.

若狭屋.note: The Yanagimachi brothel where Watanabe keeps a favorite; a minor invented setting.

英国.note: 英国; Britain, named with Japan as America's two rivals in the East. Britain for the state; England only where the source genuinely means England.

茂新.note: 茂新面粉厂, the Rong family's Wuxi flour mill, whose 'Green Warship' brand set the exchange's standard grade.

茨木.note: Town in Settsu, north-east of Ōsaka.

茨木屋.note: The sundries-wholesaler on Kawaramachi from whose upper floor the corps kept watch on the Masuya.

茶粥.note: Tea-gruel; see the note at its first mention.

荒尾精.note: 1859–1896. A Japanese army officer and pioneer of Japanese intelligence work in China, who opened the Hankou branch of the Rakuzendō pharmacy as a cover.

荒木流.note: A composite martial school of Kōzuke, taught iai among other arts; Shichiri Kennosuke's iai line.

荣宗敬.note: 1873–1938; with his brother Rong Desheng, builder of Republican China's largest private industrial group (the Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills and Shenxin cotton mills). Known as the 'Flour King.'

荣将军.note: A general of the Nationalist Ministry of National Defense's Operations Department; a Communist agent, his home name Liu Zongming. Surname romanized.

莫干山.note: The hill resort in Zhejiang where Du kept a villa.

莲花池.note: A Chongqing street corner with a Korean noodle shop, Jiang's planned rendezvous.

莲花湖.note: A lake near the Longsheng shop, where Jiang's body is to be “found.”

萧克.note: He Long's deputy as commander of the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army; the senior Communist commander in the Hebei-Rehe border region to whose forces Zhu Zhankui was sent after 1945.

萧焕文.note: The Hunan-born patriarch of the Xiao family, whose whole household served the Juntong; kept the Loyal Army's liaison.

萧秋雨.note: The Heartbreak Swordsman (断肠剑客); a scholarly-looking killer who kills to his own pleasure and quotes classical verse before the stroke (ch02). See the note at ‘Autumn wind, autumn rain.’

葉津子.note: The daughter of the Shiroko merchant Kadoya Kyuemon, sent to Ieyasu's bed on the night of his escape.

葛籠太郎兵衛.note: Jūzō's ailing father, killed in the invasion.

葛籠重蔵.note: 葛籠 is glossed つづら (Tsuzura) in the text; given name 重蔵 Jūzō. Referred to in narration as 重蔵.

董其昌.note: Ming-dynasty painter-calligrapher of tender grace, whose hand Wang's writing most resembled.

董显光.note: 1887–1971; Hollington Tong, US-trained journalist and the government's chief spokesman for foreign publicity.

蒋经国.note: Chiang Kai-shek’s son; the conventional Wade–Giles English form is used.

蒋鼎文.note: 1895–1974. A senior Whampoa-clique general and head of the Xi'an field headquarters; he carried out Chiang Kai-shek's order to kill Xuan Xiafu.

蒔田相模守広孝.note: Lord of Bitchū-Asao (ten thousand koku) and commander of the Kyoto Mimawarigumi. (The name is sometimes read Maita; the reading follows the source's own gloss.)

蒲生賢秀.note: Keeper of Azuchi, who spirited Nobunaga's family to safety at Hino after Honno-ji.

蓝小姐.note: A celebrated Shanghai socialite (交际花) who serves as Lin's assistant in the assassination attempt. Pinyin of her surname.

蓝衣社.note: Outsiders' name for the Lixingshe / Renaissance Society; glossed at its first appearance. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: the common handle; 'the Blue Shirt Society' at first use where the fuller form helps.

蓬莱.note: Hōrai (Chinese Penglai), the mythic island-mountain of the immortals; here evoked by the tower's shape. Footnoted.

蔡劲军.note: 1900–1985; Shanghai's chief of police / garrison figure in the mid-1930s.

蔡锷.note: 1882-1916; Yunnan general who launched the 1915 National Protection War against Yuan Shikai's monarchy. See the note in this section.

蔵縄手ノ鹿次.note: An Iga man cut down by his own comrades in the spring of 1591 for taking service with Katō Kiyomasa; reading of 鹿次 (Shishiji) not independently confirmed.

蕨.note: A post-town just north of Edo, in present-day Saitama; base of the Ryūgō-ryū.

藤ノ森.note: The district and shrine (Fujinomori-myōjin) south of Kyoto, on the Daibutsu highroad, where the Fushimi fighting opened.

藤吉.note: The manservant (komono) attending Toshizō on the rainy night of the ambush.

藤吉郎.note: The early name of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, when he was a lieutenant of Nobunaga.

藤堂平助.note: Historical, 1844–1867. A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū; later captain of the Shinsengumi’s Eighth Unit, killed at the Aburanokōji affair after joining Itō Kashitarō’s breakaway.

藤本安兵衛.note: A squad-leader of the Kyoto magistracy whose men gave chase at Yanagimachi.

藤林長門守.note: One of the two great jonin (upper ninja) masters of Iga.

蘇鉄.note: The sago palm (cycad), not native to Japan; the great specimen at Myokoku-ji is the subject of a Sakai legend.

虎徹.note: The prized blades of the Edo smith Nagasone Kotetsu. Kondō's famous ‘Kotetsu’ was, by most accounts, a forgery; see the note where he hunts for one.

虞洽卿.note: 1867–1945; a leading Shanghai comprador-businessman and community leader, honored as “the venerable Yu.” Chen cites him to refute a rumor that Dai Li had ordered his sanction.

虹口.note: 虹口; district of Shanghai north of Suzhou Creek, part of the International Settlement, with many Japanese residents and mills; older English Hongkew.

虹口公园.note: The park in the Hongkou district (今鲁迅公园), in the Japanese quarter of Shanghai; Zhongliang's last safe-house stands near it.

蛤御門.note: The Hamaguri-gomon, the 'Clam Gate,' one of the gates in the wall enclosing the Kyoto Imperial Palace. The battle about to be fought here gave the whole affair its name: the Hamaguri Gate Incident (Kinmon no Hen).

蝶恋花.note: An embroidery motif of butterflies among blossoms; also a classical song-lyric tune title.

行長.note: Bare name of Konishi Yukinaga (given as Yakurō Yukinaga / Settsu-no-kami Yukinaga).

衢地.note: From Sunzi's Art of War: a place where the roads of several regions meet, from which armies are readily moved.

袁世凯.note: President of the Republic of China 1912–16; recipient of Japan's Twenty-One Demands in 1915.

袁克定.note: Eldest son of Yuan Shikai, who drew Wang into secret talks with his father.

袁寒云.note: Yuan Kewen (袁克文), hao Hanyun; pinyin form used across the collection.

袁殊.note: 1911–1987. A left-wing writer and one of the war’s most tangled multiple agents—at once a Communist, a Nationalist Zhongtong man, and on the payroll of Japanese intelligence. Imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case.

袍哥.note: 袍哥; the ‘Gowned Brothers,’ the dominant secret-society brotherhood of Sichuan, analogous to the Green Gang and Hongmen of the lower Yangtze.

褚民谊.note: 1884–1946; a senior figure of the Wang Jingwei regime (deputy president of its Executive Yuan, then foreign minister); executed for treason after the war. New Group One planted an agent at his side.

西北特别侦察站.note: Juntong’s Xi’an-based station (西北特侦站 for short) directing the penetration of the Northwest base areas; headed by Cheng Muyi.

西南运输公司.note: A Nationalist wartime transport organ, with a Hong Kong branch, with which Dai Li had ties.

西尾寿造.note: Japanese general; inspector-general of education, made commander-in-chief of the China Expeditionary Army in September 1939.

西摩路.note: A road in the western International Settlement, today Shaanxi North Road (陕西北路). Zhongliang keeps his cigarette stall at a corner off it.

西柏坡.note: The Hebei village that served as the Communist central headquarters in 1948. Attested pinyin.

西郷吉之助.note: Saigō Takamori (1828–1877), the Satsuma leader — Kichinosuke was his everyday name — a chief architect of the Restoration and, later, of the Meiji state he then rebelled against and died fighting.

西里龙夫.note: A Japanese journalist and Common Culture Academy man who joined the Communist intelligence network in Nanjing; tried with Nakanishi Kō and freed in 1945.

西门吹雪.note: Ximen is a two-syllable Chinese surname; the given name Chuixue means ‘blowing snow.’ See the note at his first appearance (Prologue).

見廻組.note: The Kyōto Mimawarigumi, a patrol corps like the Shinsengumi but manned by direct shogunal retainers (hatamoto and gokenin), and so of higher formal standing.

覚鑁.note: The reforming monk of Mount Kōya (1095–1143) who founded the Negoro-ji; named in Maki’s lullaby.

角屋.note: A great ageya (house of assignation) in the Shimabara quarter, where guests were entertained by courtesans summoned from the tayū houses; the building survives in Kyoto.

角屋久右衛門.note: A merchant of Shiroko on Ise Bay, Hatsuko's father, who sheltered Ieyasu the night before he sailed for Mikawa.

講武所.note: The shogunate's own military academy in Edo, opened in 1856 to modernize the training of its retainers in swordsmanship, gunnery, and Western arms.

警政司.note: The police-administration bureau of the Ministry of the Interior, where Yang Qun heads the security bureau.

護王神社.note: A shrine facing the west side of the Kyoto Imperial Palace, dedicated to Wake no Kiyomaro; a landmark on the line of the Chōshū advance.

许广平.note: 1898–1968; educator and writer, wife of Lu Xun; editor of his Complete Works.

许建国.note: 1903–1965. Born Du Liqing; a veteran security officer, deputy head of the Border Security and later head of the Jin-Cha-Ji Social Affairs Department. Rendered “Du Liqing” where the book uses his original name.

许继慎.note: 1901–1931. Whampoa graduate and Red Army commander in the E-Yu-Wan base, executed in an internal purge after a Nationalist frame-up; later rehabilitated as a martyr.

调查统计局.note: The Military Affairs Commission bureau (1932) whose Second Department, under Dai Li, grew into the Juntong.

谢富治.note: 1909–1972. Minister of public security from 1959; a driver of the “smash the police, procuratorate, and courts” campaign, posthumously expelled from the Party in 1980.

谭延闿.note: Hunan military governor and Nationalist elder; first president of the Executive Yuan; signed the Wuhan order expelling Chiang in April 1927.

谭政文.note: 1910–1961. A Long March security cadre, deputy head of the Border Region Security Office; later a senior procuratorial official.

谭甫仁.note: Chairman of the Yunnan Revolutionary Committee, assassinated in 1970.

谷三十郎.note: Historical, died 1866. Master of the Tōhō Enshin-ryū of spear and sword at Osaka and Harada Sanosuke’s former teacher; later a Shinsengumi captain.

谷正纲.note: 谷正纲 (1902–1993); Kuomintang politician, later long the head of anti-Communist relief work on Taiwan.

谷正鼎.note: 1903–1974. CC-Clique figure, chief of the Nationalist Shaanxi provincial party headquarters.

豊玉.note: Toshizō’s haiku pen-name, known only to his intimates; see ch19.

豊臣秀吉.note: Ruler of Japan by 1591; the assassination target of the novel.

豊臣秀次.note: Hideyoshi's nephew and adopted heir, made kanpaku; forced to commit seppuku on Mount Kōya in 1595.

賤ケ岳.note: The ridge between Lake Biwa and Lake Yogo where Hideyoshi broke Katsuie in the fourth month of 1583; gave its name to the battle and the Seven Spears.

賤ケ岳の七本槍.note: The seven (in fact nine) young spearmen—Kiyomasa, Masanori and the rest—commended for valor at Shizugatake; a fixture of popular art.

费家村.note: A hamlet ten li outside Xietang where Yanzhi settles and lives out her days.

贺耀组.note: 1889–1961; the nominal director of the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, a figurehead while Dai Li ran its affairs as deputy director.

贺衷寒.note: 1900-1972; Whampoa 1st class, Blue Shirt political-warfare leader Adjudicated 2026-08-29: correct pinyin of 衷寒; 'He Zhongyan' was an error, recorded as wang-yaqiao's deviation.

赤備え.note: An akazonae, a unit armored and even armed all in red; Ii Naomasa’s was the most famous.

赤木亲之.note: Japanese deputy commissioner of the Shanghai Municipal Police, assassinated on Yuyuan Road, June 1941.

赤沢守人.note: A Chōshū man who quit his domain and was taken into the corps as an informer against it; his killing, in 1863, is the case of this chapter. Reading of the given name from the source’s furigana (もりと).

赵刚.note: ‘One Blade Quells the Nine Provinces,’ a hero murdered by Hong Tao; Ximen Chuixue avenges him although the two never met (Prologue).

赵去非.note: Border Security field-team head at Luochuan; later deputy governor of Heilongjiang and head of its public-security department.

赵君豪.note: 赵君豪; Shanghai journalist and editor of the Republican period.

赵圣.note: The working name of the Second Action Brigade's commander (real name Ji Zhencang, keyed); the man who reported the Zhang Xiaolin sanction. Rendered Zhao Sheng consistently.

赵大麻子.note: The dog-meat cook of the tavern called Yet Another Village, outside the town; his stew has no equal. Sikong Zhaixing wears his face in ch08.

赵家坟.note: The base village of the North-Suburb Mixed Group, at the northeastern corner of Beiping.

赵寿山.note: 1894–1965. Commander of the Northwestern Army's 38th Army, secretly guided by Mao Zedong; he defected to the Communists and became governor of Qinghai and then Shaanxi.

赵朴初.note: 1907–2000; Buddhist lay leader, poet, and relief organizer; secretly aided the Communist underground through Shanghai’s charitable and refugee bodies in the war years, and later headed the Buddhist Association of China.

赵理君.note: Acting chief of the Shanghai District and leader of its First Action Squad; on sick leave and transferred to Luoyang in 1939.

赵秀.note: Chief liaison for the Northwest Station’s Yan’an group; briefly turned, later fled back to Xi’an.

赵苍壁.note: 1916–1993. Border Security plainclothes-squad head sent to Longdong; later Minister of Public Security.

赵苍璧.note: 1916–1993. A northern-Shaanxi local cadre who rose through investigation work; minister of public security of the People's Republic from 1977 to 1983.

赵荣琛.note: 赵荣琛 (1916–1996); leading exponent of the Cheng school of Peking-opera dan roles.

越前.note: The old province along the Sea of Japan north of Lake Biwa, modern Fukui.

越後.note: Province on the Japan Sea coast; the far-off country of Jūzō's assumed identity.

越飞.note: Adolph Joffe, Soviet diplomat whose 1923 declaration with Sun Yat-sen framed the KMT-Soviet alliance.

足利義昭.note: The fifteenth and last Ashikaga shogun, installed by Nobunaga in 1568.

足利義輝.note: The thirteenth Ashikaga shogun (r. 1546–1565), a noted swordsman who studied under Bokuden; distinct from Yoshiaki, the last shogun.

跑反.note: A north-Shaanxi term for a whole population’s flight ahead of an oncoming army.

跑马厅.note: 跑马厅 (also 跑马场); the great racecourse of the International Settlement, off Bubbling Well Road (today People’s Square and People’s Park).

跑马地.note: A district of Hong Kong Island; its Chinese name means 'the racecourse ground.'

路透社.note: The British news agency; Lin's journalistic cover. Attested English name.

轻功.note: The martial art of lightness: moving as though almost weightless, to leap great distances or skim across water. See the note at first appearance (Prologue).

载沣.note: Prince Chun, the Prince Regent for the child Xuantong emperor; target of Wang's 1910 assassination attempt.

辣斐德路.note: French Concession road (Route Lafayette), today's Fuxing Middle Road.

辰吉.note: A young man of Renjaku who peddled horse-sandals at Hachiōji; a passing figure.

边保.note: Short form of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office (陕甘宁边区保安处); the region’s counter-espionage and public-security organ.

辻斬り.note: ‘Crossroads-cutting’: the testing of a blade, or of one's nerve, by cutting down a stranger on the road at night. Long a capital crime, it revived in the murderous mood of these years.

迎春阁.note: The best pleasure-house in Huangshi Town; see the note at first appearance (ch02).

近卫文麿.note: Prime Minister of Japan; issued the three statements of 1938 that Wang Jingwei answered.

近藤内蔵助.note: A rōnin of Enshū, late-eighteenth-century founder of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

近藤勇.note: Historical figure, 1834–1868. Head of the Tennen Rishin-ryū school of swordsmanship and, later, commander of the Shinsengumi.

近藤周斎.note: Historical. Third head of the Tennen Rishin-ryū (personal name Shūsuke; in retirement, Shūsai), who adopted the farm boy Katsuta and made him Kondō Isami, his heir.

近衛.note: The premier regent-house of the court nobility; here its Kyoto mansion, a landmark on the skyline.

还乡团.note: Landlord-led militias that returned with the Nationalist advance to retake land and take revenge on those who had carried out CCP land reform.

远藤.note: A Japanese general invoked in Jiang's cover story.

通济公司.note: The wartime trading company (c. 1943) fronted by Du for Dai Li, smuggling goods to and from the occupied areas under cover of Juntong privilege.

連雀.note: A village of the Tama country with no fencing hall, where Toshizō taught in the headman's miso storehouse.

逼供信.note: Mao’s three-word name for the purge method: coerce a confession, let the confession run wild, and believe it. First glossed at Chapter 1.

邓宝珊.note: 1894–1968. Nationalist general holding Yulin north of the Border Region; a friend of the Communists from Yan'an, he helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Beiping.

邓小平.note: 1904–1997. Here a mid-ranking political officer in Yan'an; after Mao Zedong's death, China's paramount leader and the architect of its “reform and opening.”

邓龙光.note: Cantonese Nationalist general, courted by Wang Jingwei for a South China regime but unmoved.

邵力子.note: 1882–1967; journalist and Nationalist official, later a peace envoy to the Communists.

邵范九.note: A cousin's nephew of the KMT elder Shao Lizi; sanctioned in November 1939 for going over to the puppets.

郑介民.note: Senior Nationalist intelligence chief; rose to full general.

郑学稼.note: Writer whose 1939 essay on Wang Jingwei (in The Spirit of the Age) Chen quotes.

郑文道.note: 1914–1942. Nakanishi Kō’s Chinese liaison; arrested by the Japanese gendarmerie in 1942, he took his own life to protect the network.

郭汝瑰.note: 1907–1997. Operations chief in the Nationalist Ministry of National Defense and a long-hidden Communist agent who fed the Communists top operational plans.

郭炳炎.note: A captured Nationalist colonel whom Jiang helps escape, later revealed as a powerful figure in the Zhongtong; Jiang's controller. Fictional; pinyin.

酒井兵庫.note: A veteran jokin of the Shinsengumi, put to death for desertion. See the note in the chapter for the disputed timing.

酒井忠次.note: One of Ieyasu's chief retainers; his silence before Nobunaga sealed Nobuyasu's fate.

里.note: A unit of distance, about 3.9 km (2.4 miles).

重光葵.note: Japanese diplomat, ambassador to the USSR at the time of the Zhanggufeng Incident.

重庆.note: The Nationalist wartime capital (the ‘great rear’). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: pinyin default, five books agree; 'Chungking' stands as juntong's period deviation.

重庆谈判.note: The peace talks of 28 August–10 October 1945, to which Mao Zedong flew in person; they produced the Double-Tenth Agreement.

重蔵.note: Bare given name of Tsuzura Jūzō, used throughout the narration.

野口健司.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction and an early Shinsengumi officer; died in 1864.

野老山.note: Tokoroyama Gokichirō, Tosa loyalist; wounded at the Ikedaya, he cut his belly before the locked Chōshū gate.

金九.note: Kim Ku (1876–1949), leader of the Korean independence movement and of the Provisional Government in exile; wounded in the 1938 Changsha shooting. Historical; attested Korean romanization.

金剛峯寺.note: The head temple of the Shingon school on Mount Kōya.

金森.note: Kanamori Hida-no-kami Yoshishige (1558-1615), a tea-connoisseur daimyō; the collector whose mansion Gohei raids.

金都大戏院.note: A cinema on Avenue Foch in Shanghai; the site of the military-police gunfight. Rendered by the theater's period English name.

金雄白.note: Journalist of the Wang Jingwei regime; wrote its history under the pen name Zhu Zijia.

金鹏王朝.note: The ancient kingdom whose name gives this volume its title, The Golden Roc Dynasty: a far realm overrun fifty years before the story, whose royal house bore the surname Shangguan. The jinpeng (金鹏) is the golden peng, the vast mythic bird of Chinese legend (ch04).

釜山城.note: Pusan (Busan), the first Korean fortress taken in the 1592 invasion. Added so the entry does not collide with 山城 (Yamashiro) as a substring.

鈴木三樹三郎.note: Itō Kashitarō's younger brother, who joined the corps with him. He later broke away with the Kōdai-ji faction, survived the Restoration, and lived to old age.

鉄扇.note: A folding fan with iron ribs (or a solid iron bar shaped like one), carried where a sword might give offense and used to parry or strike.

钱大钧.note: 钱大钧 (1893–1982); Kuomintang general, at this time mayor of Shanghai.

钱庄.note: 钱庄; a traditional Chinese private bank or money-shop, distinct from the modern 银行. The silk men's working credit runs through these houses, and it is a native-bank manager who will not stretch a point for Chen Junyi.

钱明.note: Real name Jing Ruonan; a Chinese liaison of the Nakanishi Kō cell and Zheng Wendao’s schoolmate.

钱永铭.note: 钱永铭, styled Xinzhi; the banker known throughout as Qian Xinzhi, general manager of the Bank of Communications.

钱益民.note: Investigation expert of the General Political Department’s Anti-Traitor Department, one of Yan’an’s “three great investigation experts.”

铁观音.note: A prized oolong tea from Anxi in Fujian; “Iron Goddess of Mercy.”

铁面判官.note: One of the two Blue-Robe Tower enforcers sent after Lu Xiaofeng in Chapter 1; his scarred face is said to have notched the blade that cut him. See the note at his first appearance (ch02).

铃木正男.note: The Japanese army surgeon who treats Lin in Hong Kong; addresses Lin as 'Pang-san.' Japanese reading.

锄奸.note: Literally “to hoe out the traitors.” The wartime CCP name for counter-espionage and anti-collaborator work; the army security departments were renamed Anti-Traitor Departments (锂奶部).

锄奸委员会.note: A mass body extending chujian (“rooting out traitors”) into a village-level surveillance network.

锄奸部.note: The renamed Eighth Route Army security department; kept parallel to the Anti-Traitor Committee (锂奶委员会).

镇反运动.note: The mass campaign of 1950–1953; see the footnote at its first appearance in this chapter.

镇江.note: The Yangtze city, Yang Guanbei's home.

長久手.note: The field east of present Nagoya where Ieyasu shattered Ikeda’s flanking column in the fourth month of Tenshō 12.

長宗我部元親.note: Lord of Tosa who had unified Shikoku; submitted to Hideyoshi in 1585 and was left Tosa alone.

長尾.note: Maki’s home hamlet, a league and a half up the Kishi River at the foot of Mount Tokika; a poor farming village on the border of the Kishū domain and the temple lands, where Goemon, Maki and Goichi take refuge.

長州.note: The Mōri domain of western Honshū, later the chief power of the anti-shogunal movement and the Shinsengumi's great enemy.

長曾我部.note: The Chōsokabe house of Tosa; here the Kyoto mansion (of 長曾我部宮内少輔, Chōsokabe Kunai-no-shōyū) whose back wall Jūzō vaults during the ambush.

長曾我部元親.note: The lord of Tosa who all but united Shikoku; sounded out by Ieyasu for the anti-Hideyoshi league.

長浜.note: Castle town on the east shore of Lake Biwa; Hideyoshi’s rear base in the Shizugatake campaign.

长安.note: The Tang capital (modern Xi'an), standing for the far-off imperial city in the tanci aria sung in Chapters 12 and 15.

长江.note: The conventional English form, used throughout.

関ヶ原.note: The 1600 battle that founded the Tokugawa shogunate.

関東.note: The eastern provinces, Ieyasu's domain of 2,550,000 koku.

関白.note: Imperial Regent, Hideyoshi's supreme office of state from 1585. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: traditional Hepburn (m before p), capitalized as the office.

阎又文.note: 1914–1962. A deep-cover Communist at Fu Zuoyi's side who helped bring about the surrender of Beiping; his identity was kept secret until 1992, long after his death.

阎宝航.note: 1895–1968. A Northeastern Christian educator and aide to Zhang Xueliang who became a secret Communist inside the Nationalist elite; his 1941 report of the date of the German invasion of the USSR is the intelligence coup of this chapter. Died in prison during the Cultural Revolution; posthumously decorated by Russia in 1995.

阎铁珊.note: The jewel magnate of Guanzhong, of the Yan house; revealed to be Yan Liben, one of the four traitor-ministers. It was he who sliced away half of Liu Yuhen’s face (ch04).

阎锡山.note: 阎锡山 (1883–1960), the militarist governor of Shanxi (the 'model governor'); in 1930 a leader of the anti-Chiang Northern coalition whose armies drive down the Tianjin–Pukou line in this chapter's war news.

阜丰.note: 阜丰面粉厂, a leading Shanghai flour mill, whose 'Red-and-Blue Cart' brand ranked with the Green Warship standard.

阮志中.note: Meng Annan's true Vietnamese name; his parents, followers of Ho Chi Minh, died in a French prison in Saigon. Vietnamese form (Nguyễn Chí Trung).

阳谋.note: Lit. “open/overt scheme,” coined as the mirror of 阴谋 yinmou “plot, conspiracy”: a design pursued in the open rather than in secret. Here it names the postwar contest in which each side maneuvered openly (the Chongqing talks) while racing for military position.

阿四.note: Qin Shuji's partner in the Fourth Avenue picture gallery.

阿弥陀ヶ峰.note: A peak of the Higashiyama range south-east of the capital; Hideyoshi would later be entombed on it.

阿英.note: Pen name of Qian Xingcun (1900–1977), writer and literary historian; ran the ‘Wind and Rain Bookroom’ hidden in the Tongyi Company.

陆伯鸿.note: 1875–1937; the Catholic industrialist and philanthropist, a papal knight; co-founder of the Datong line.

陆小凤.note: The protagonist. His given name, Xiaofeng, means ‘little phoenix’ and sounds like a woman’s name; the joke and the ‘four eyebrows’ riddle are noted at his first mention (Prologue).

陈公博.note: A close associate of Wang Jingwei who followed him into the collaborationist regime; later its head, executed 1946.

陈友仁.note: 1878–1944; foreign minister of the Wuhan Nationalist government; conventional English form retained.

陈嘉庚.note: 1874–1961. The pre-eminent overseas-Chinese leader of the South Seas, a Singapore rubber magnate and philanthropist; his 1940 visit to Yan'an turned him toward the Communists. Rendered in the Hokkien form by which he is universally known in English.

陈布雷.note: Chiang Kai-shek’s chief secretary and speechwriter; elder brother of Chen Xunshe.

陈明仁.note: 1903–1974. Nationalist general who beat back Lin Biao at Siping in 1947, then led his Central Army troops over to the Communists in Hunan in 1949 and became a PLA general.

陈春圃.note: A kinsman of Chen Bijun and an official in the Wang Jingwei regime.

陈果夫.note: 1892–1951. Elder of the CC Clique with his brother Chen Lifu.

陈树人.note: Nationalist elder and painter, cited on the causes of Wang's flight.

陈植琚.note: Xiao Shuying's husband; leader of the Dachang field group, blown to death by an enemy plane early in the war.

陈毅.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), PLA marshal, first mayor of Shanghai after 1949 and later foreign minister. Historical.

陈泊.note: Real name of Bu Lu, the “Red Sherlock Holmes.”

陈泰泞.note: The bald, self-effacing warehouse clerk at Shiliupu whom Qin Zhaokuan charges, in secret, with getting Su Lina safely out of Shanghai. A fictional character; pinyin.

陈济棠.note: 1890-1954; Guangdong warlord ("the King of the South"), led the 1936 Two Kwangs revolt against Chiang.

陈炯明.note: Guangdong warlord who rebelled against Sun Yat-sen in 1922.

陈焕章.note: Also known as Chen Tao. A Communist agent who, at Chen Geng’s direction, penetrated the puppet forces at Linfen and rose to hold, at once, major-general’s commissions from the Japanese-backed puppet army, from Juntong, and from Yan Xishan’s forces.

陈独秀.note: 1879–1942; first general secretary of the CCP, removed at the August Seventh Conference of 1927.

陈璧君.note: 1891–1959; Wang Jingwei's wife, a forceful political figure; imprisoned after the war.

陈科长.note: The public-security section chief who interrogates and at last releases Su Lina and Zhongliang after 1949. A fictional character; surname romanized. Distinct from Chen Taining and from Chen Yi.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001; Nationalist organization boss of the ‘CC Clique,’ firmly anti-Communist.

陈素农.note: Chen Sunong (1900–1983), a Whampoa graduate recorded as chief of staff of the 88th Division. A real officer.

陈群.note: Puppet politician; 'Chairman of Jiangsu Province' under the Wang regime, whose Yuyuan Road houses Wang used.

陈耀祖.note: Wang Jingwei's brother-in-law; wrote to Huang Yiguang urging him to join the 'Peace Movement.'

陈诚.note: 1898-1965; one of Chiang Kai-shek's most trusted generals and, at this time, Chief of the General Staff (Chen corrects here his fourth volume's misattribution of the post to Bai Chongxi, who was Minister of National Defense).

陈调元.note: Former chairman of the Anhui provincial government; his house at No. 76 Jessfield Road became a Wang-regime venue.

陈赓.note: Whampoa graduate and head of the intelligence (2nd) section of the Party’s Special Branch; later a PLA general.

陈铭枢.note: 陈铭枢 (1889–1965); Kuomintang general, a leader of the 1933 Fujian Rebellion.

陈龙.note: 1910–1958. From the Northeast anti-Japanese forces; Mao Zedong's guard at the Chongqing negotiations and a pioneer of Communist counter-espionage.

陕甘宁边区保安处.note: The Border Region government’s combined public-security and procuratorial organ, known for short as 边保 (Bianbao, the “Border Security”); the executing arm of Communist security work in Yan’an, and outwardly the government face of the Northwest Bureau’s Social Affairs Department.

陶德曼.note: Oskar Trautmann, German ambassador to China, whose winter-1937 mediation the quoted meeting record concerns (identified at ch13).

陶成章.note: Revolutionary who, with Zhang Taiyan, set up the rival Restoration Society (Guangfuhui).

陶联芳.note: A New Group One member, buried alive by the puppet Huzhou Station after being caught re-linking with the Bureau.

陶铸.note: Senior Communist official, another victim of the Cultural Revolution.

隆盛参茸行.note: A Shapingba shop dealing in ginseng and deer-antler, a front for a Japanese intelligence station. Fictional.

隼人.note: Toshizō’s late father, and also the hereditary given name borne by the head of the Hijikata house.

雑賀.note: Saiga (Saika) in Kishu, home of a famed league of gunsmiths and mercenary gunners, a hub of the arms trade.

雑賀崎.note: The cape south of Wakayama to which the name Saiga later shrank; Maki’s people were of the old, wider Saiga of the lower Kino.

雨花台.note: The Terrace of Raining Flowers, a hill south of Nanjing long used as an execution ground.

雲兵衛.note: The young ex-sailor and one-time balladeer in Matsukura's band; Jūzō spares and conscripts him.

霍休.note: The richest man under heaven, who lives as a reclusive, cranky old man (‘old Huo’) in a hut on the mountainside; revealed to be Shangguan Mu, one of the four ministers entrusted with the Golden Roc’s treasure, and the secret source of his own vast fortune (ch03–ch04).

霍天青.note: Steward of Yan Tieshan’s Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour; a master of very high martial generation who serves Yan because Yan once saved his life in the Qilian Mountains (ch05).

霞飞将军.note: The French mail steamer on which Chen sailed from Hong Kong to Shanghai.

霞飞路.note: A main thoroughfare of the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Central Huaihai Road.

青云客栈.note: The inn where Lu Xiaofeng is putting up when the Blue-Robe Tower’s enforcers find him (ch02).

青天白日满地红.note: The national flag of the Republic of China, flown also by Wang Jingwei's collaborationist regime.

青岛.note: Shandong port city, host of the Fifth National Bar Association congress (1933).

青帮.note: 青帮; the great secret-society brotherhood of the lower Yangtze and Shanghai. Rendered ‘Green Gang’ across the collection.

青干班.note: The youth-cadre training course (青年干部训练班) at Liyuan village.

青年军.note: The Nationalist corps of educated volunteers raised in 1944.

青木关.note: A place west of Chongqing where the released couple settled 1945 (ch21).

青枫.note: The Taoist abbot of the Green Wind Temple and Huo Tianqing’s friend over the chessboard; bought by Huo Xiu to bear false witness that Huo Tianqing had died by his own hand, and burned with his temple soon after (ch12).

青红帮.note: The Green Gang (青帮) and the Hong/Red Gang (洪帮), the great secret-society brotherhoods of Republican Shanghai; Young Tang names them as A-Chu's likely enemies after the hospital bombing.

青葉の冠者.note: ‘The Green-Leaf Page,’ the refined cover-name Hanzō gave a cold-natured Kōga lower ninja of the Tarao; Goemon’s contact on the Osaka assignment.

青蓮院.note: A monzeki (imperial-abbot) temple at the northern foot of Higashiyama.

青衣楼.note: A vast, tightly-run criminal organisation: a hundred and eight towers, a hundred and eight men to each, whose portraits hang in a First Tower whose location no one knows. Its enforcers come for Lu Xiaofeng in ch02. See the note on the number 108. The Tower is Gu Long’s invention.

青风观.note: The Taoist temple on the front of Huo Xiu’s mountain, where Huo Tianqing’s body is found; its abbot is the Taoist Qingfeng (青枫), whose name chimes with the temple’s (both sound Qingfeng). Huo Xiu burns it to the ground to destroy the one witness to his lie (ch12).

静安寺.note: The Jing'an (Bubbling Well) Temple, which gave its name to Bubbling Well Road; the district around it, where the narrator and Helen breakfast (ch29).

静安寺路.note: The concession-era English name of 静安寺路 (today Nanjing West Road, 南京西路). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: five books and the shelf canon for concession street names; pinyin glossed once.

静安邮政所.note: The neighborhood post office where Xu Delin and Zhongliang serve. Fictional workplace; named for the Jing'an district.

静海.note: The Hebei county on the northern reach of the Jin-Pu railway where the Second Command Room was seated.

革水蜘蛛.note: A ninja flotation device (mizugumo, 'water-spider'): a deerskin float that turns the wearer into a one-man raft. The fiction's own furniture; described in the text.

韩国临时政府.note: The Korean government-in-exile, based in wartime Chongqing.

韩家潭.note: A lane in Beiping's Eight Great Hutongs pleasure quarter.

韩练成.note: 1908–1984. A Nationalist general who secretly served the Communists from within; later a PLA lieutenant general.

韮山.note: A seat in Izu of the Egawa house, hereditary shogunal intendants.

音無川.note: The thin stream running through Rakshasa Valley to the Kamo; furigana おとなしがわ. The name means 'the soundless river'.

音羽ノ城戸.note: Iga genin; historically the marksman who ambushed Nobunaga at the Aekuni Shrine.

頼山陽.note: Historical, 1780–1832. Confucian historian and poet, author of the Nihon Gaishi, whose romantic, imperial-centered narrative of Japanese history deeply shaped late-shogunate loyalism.

顕如.note: The abbot of the Hongan-ji (1543–1592) who led the Ikkō league through the long war against Nobunaga and, at Ishiyama’s fall, withdrew into Kishū.

顺义.note: The county north of Beiping where the assault team, in the autumn of 1948, seized a puppet county commissar and broke up an arms-repair shop at Niulanshan.

顾兰君.note: A 1930s Shanghai film actress; Chen rented her former apartment on Seymour Road.

顾孟余.note: A leading figure of Wang's faction who declined to follow him to Nanjing.

顾慎言.note: Lin's superior and the director of studies of his training class. Pinyin.

顾祝同.note: 1893–1987; Kuomintang general, commander of the Third War Zone.

顾竹轩.note: Jiangsu-born gang figure who dominated Zhabei; two articles here treat his rise and his cover for revolutionary work.

顾顺章.note: Head of the Party’s Special Branch whose 1931 defection to the Kuomintang gravely wrecked the Shanghai underground.

顾鳌.note: 1879–1949; a Beiyang-era politician styled a ‘meritorious servant of the Hongxian’ monarchy; here one of Du's opium-smoking retainers, called ‘Secretary Gu.’

風間五平.note: 風間 glossed かざま (Kazama); 五平 Gohei.

飛火野.note: A meadow in the Kasuga precinct of Nara.

飞凤针.note: Princess Danfeng’s signature hidden weapon: poisoned needles said to close the throat at the first touch of blood. Xue’er accuses her cousin of using them on Liu Yuhen (ch06).

食指.note: Old Pan's code name; literally the index finger (the 'eating finger'). Rendered by sense.

香取.note: The great shrine of Shimōsa, across the river from Kashima; the other cradle of the classical sword schools.

香港.note: British colony; seat of the Party’s Southern Bureau.

馬印.note: A commander’s tall field standard; Katsuie’s was a golden gohei, Hideyoshi’s the golden gourd.

馬庭.note: The seat of the Maniwa Nen-ryū in Kōzuke (Jōshū), present-day Gunma.

馬関.note: The old name for the strait and port at Shimonoseki, the western mouth of the Inland Sea, in Chōshū territory.

駿河.note: Coastal province east of Kai; on the Tōkaidō.

马公.note: The main harbor town of Penghu (the Pescadores), where the brigade went ashore in September 1949.

马关条约.note: The 1895 treaty ending the first Sino-Japanese War.

马寅初.note: Economist, later famous for advocating population control.

马文瑞.note: 1912–2004. Longdong prefectural party secretary who took Wu Nanshan in; himself once wrongly arrested in the northern-Shaanxi purge. Later a vice-chairman of the CPPCC National Committee.

马斯南路.note: Real. Rue Massenet, after the composer Jules Massenet; today Sinan Road (思南路). The recognition-signal address. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: French Concession streets keep their Route/Avenue period forms (shelf canon).

马林.note: Henk Sneevliet ('Maring'), early Comintern representative to China.

马树礼.note: Ma Shuli (1909–2006); Nationalist journalist and politician, later secretary-general of the Kuomintang’s Central Committee in Taiwan.

马步芳.note: The Nationalist Muslim warlord of Qinghai.

马汉三.note: 1903–1948. Senior Juntong officer; later executed by the Nationalists over the missing “Nine-Dragon Sword.”

马秀真.note: The eldest of the Four Beauties of Emei; tall, with a pair of long phoenix eyes and a killing air even as she smiles. She leads the four in the bath-house interrogation of Lu Xiaofeng (ch09).

马行空.note: Chief armsman of the Allied Escort Houses of Guanzhong, styled the Divine Dragon in the Clouds. An old wound from Huo Tianqing’s palm halved his skill, so he leans on the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour (ch07).

马连良.note: 1901–1966. Celebrated Peking-opera actor of the old-man (laosheng) roles.

马锡武.note: The book prints 马锡武; the documented judge is 马锡五 (1899–1962), same romanization, whose plain, investigative “Ma Xiwu adjudication method” became a CCP model.

驼峰.note: The Allied airlift route over the eastern Himalayas from India to Nationalist China after the Burma Road was cut.

高台寺.note: A temple in Kyoto’s Higashiyama; the Goryō-eji fixed their headquarters at its sub-temple Gettsuin, whence they were also called the Kōdai-ji party.

高宗武.note: A Nationalist diplomat who conducted the secret 1938 Shanghai talks with Japan on Wang's behalf; later broke with him.

高山右近.note: The most famous of the Christian daimyo; chose exile over apostasy, dying in Manila in 1615.

高崇武.note: So printed in the source; the man is the documented Gao Zongwu (高宗武), who with Tao Xisheng exposed the draft Japan–Wang Jingwei treaty in the January 1940 “Gao-Tao incident.”

高崇民.note: 1891–1971. A leading Northeastern patriot who founded the Northeast Salvation Association; a bridge between the Communists and the Northeastern and Northwestern armies before the Xi'an Incident.

高幡不動.note: A temple of Fudō Myō-ō in the Tama country of Bushū, near Hijikata’s home village of Ishida; the family kept ties to it.

高松城.note: Bicchū Takamatsu, flooded by Hideyoshi in 1582; the siege broke off at word of Nobunaga's death.

高树勋.note: Former Northwest Army general who defected with the New 8th Army at Handan on 30 October 1945.

高树勋运动.note: Mao’s slogan-campaign, named for Gao Shuxun’s October 1945 defection, urging Nationalist troops to revolt rather than fight the civil war.

高槻.note: Takayama Ukon's castle town between Kyoto and Osaka, where the seminary was rebuilt after Azuchi.

高瀬川.note: Not a river but a shallow canal, dug in the early seventeenth century to carry cargo boats (takasebune) between Kyoto and Fushimi; its west bank was lined with the Kyoto mansions of the domains.

高野山.note: Mount Kōya, the monastic center of Shingon Buddhism, where Kobo Daishi is held to sit in eternal meditation.

高麗.note: 高麗 (Kōrai/Koryŏ), an older name for Korea; used in Jūzō's aside. The standard rendering for 朝鮮 elsewhere is also Korea.

鬼子母神.note: The child-guarding goddess Hariti, once a child-devouring ogress, converted by the Buddha; shown with a pomegranate.

魏道明.note: Styled Bocong; a Nationalist official who asked Chen after Wang's movements.

鲁大师.note: Zhu Ting’s master in the maker’s art and a descendant of Lu Ban; now dead, leaving Zhu Ting the first hand under heaven at the making of hidden contrivances (ch12).

鲁班.note: The legendary master carpenter and engineer of the state of Lu in the fifth century BCE, patron deity of builders and craftsmen; Zhu Ting’s art of contrivances descends from him. See the note at his first mention (ch12).

鲁迅.note: Pen name of Zhou Shuren (1881-1936); author of The True Story of Ah Q; the central figure of essay 3.

鲍罗廷.note: Mikhail Borodin, the chief Soviet (Comintern) adviser to the Nationalist Party in the 1920s.

鲶鱼.note: Zhongliang's code name after he takes over Zhou San's work (鲶鱼, “catfish”); he plays on it in English with Father Kruger.

鳥居喜八郎.note: A Kōga middle-rank shinobi of Ōhara; father of Torii Moriichirō.

鳥居守一郎.note: Nineteen, eldest of the three Koga seminary pupils; sallow, thick-fleshed, flighty, and the most cruel of them. A future antagonist of Goemon.

鴨川.note: The river running north to south through the eastern side of Kyōto. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: capital R in the English name.

鴻池.note: The greatest merchant-and-banking house of Osaka, financiers to daimyo and shogunate alike.

鴻池善右衛門.note: The head, by hereditary name, of the Kōnoike house, the greatest merchant-bank of Osaka (see ch15). It bankrolled Kondō in return for the corps’s protection against loyalist extortion.

鷹司屋敷.note: The Kyoto residence of the Takatsukasa regental house, on the palace's edge, where Kusaka Genzui and Terashima Chūzaburō died.

鸡鸣寺.note: Real. Temple by the Nanjing city wall, passed on the drive.

鹿儿岛.note: City and bay at the southern tip of Kyushu, Japan, where the navy rehearsed the Pearl Harbor attack. Attested.

鹿島.note: The great shrine of Hitachi and the sword tradition that grew from its shrine-families; paired with Katori as the twin fountainheads of Japanese swordsmanship.

黄克忠.note: A Kang Corps action man (also recorded as Huang Ruitang); took part in the Tōwa Theater bombing and died at Hongkou Park.

黄克诚.note: Huang Kecheng (1902–1986); then a senior commander of the New Fourth Army in the Subei base area, later a general of the People’s Liberation Army and a leading Party figure.

黄兴.note: Styled Kexing; co-founder with Sun Yat-sen of the Tongmenghui and chief military leader of the 1911 revolution.

黄包车.note: The man-pulled two-wheeled cab of Republican Shanghai.

黄埔军校.note: Conventional English form (Whampoa). Adjudicated 2026-08-29: full form at first use, 'Whampoa' as the handle thereafter.

黄埔江.note: The river running through Shanghai (source 黄埔 for the standard 黄浦).

黄复生.note: Originally Shuzhong; Wang Jingwei's co-conspirator in the 1910 attempt on the Prince Regent, imprisoned with him.

黄庭坚.note: Huang Tingjian (1045–1105), Song-dynasty poet and one of the great masters of calligraphy. Historical.

黄楚九.note: 黄楚九 (1872–1931); the entrepreneur who founded the Great World amusement hall and dealt in patent medicines. See the note at ch15.

黄浦江.note: The river through Shanghai; A-Chu’s men dump the kidnappers’ bodies in it. Adjudicated 2026-08-29: 'the Huangpu River' at first use, 'the Huangpu' thereafter; both attested, one policy.

黄涵之.note: 黄涵之 (1875–1961); Shanghai Buddhist layman and philanthropist, an associate of Guan Jiongzhi.

黄炎培.note: 1878–1965. Educator and founder of the China Democratic National Construction Association; a frequent guest of Du's who did wartime liaison work.

黄石镇.note: The town north of the Dragon-Soaring Inn to which the Blue-Robe Tower riders chase their quarry (ch02); rendered by its literal pinyin (‘Yellow-Stone Town’), a fictional locale.

黄郛.note: The diplomat (courtesy Yingbai) who acted for He Yingqin at Beiping in the early 1930s as chairman of the Executive Yuan's Beiping Political Affairs Reorganization Committee.

黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession patrol house; Chiang Kai-shek was once his disciple.

黄雍.note: Courtesy name Jianqiu; a first-class Whampoa graduate who took Chen in at Nanjing and recommended him into the work.

黎广文.note: Meng Annan's cover name in postwar Shanghai, working as an editor at the French Photo Agency; Zhu Yizhen passes in cover as his wife, Mrs. Li. Pinyin.

黒田官兵衛.note: Hideyoshi's ablest strategist; later took the monastic name Josui.

黒谷.note: The Kurodani precinct (the temple Konkai Kōmyō-ji), on the eastern hills of Kyoto, which served as the Aizu domain's Kyoto headquarters.

黒阿弥.note: Full form 佐那具ノ黒阿弥, Sanagu-no-Kuroami.

龙云.note: The semi-autonomous governor of Yunnan, forced out by Chiang in October 1945.

龙华.note: District in the southern outskirts of Shanghai; site of the Kuomintang Garrison Command’s prison and execution ground.

龙潭.note: The 1927 battle where Sun Chuanfang was routed.

龙翔客栈.note: The busy inn where the Blue-Robe Tower’s decoy-search for Lu Xiaofeng opens Chapter 1.

洪秀全.note: 1814–1864. Leader of the Taiping Rebellion; the “Heavenly King.” Isaacs’s spelling “Hung Tsui-chuen” is idiosyncratic; standard Wade-Giles is Hung Hsiu-ch’üan. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Hung Tsui-chuen” in its text.

曾国藩.note: 1811–1872. Hunan official whose provincial army broke the Taiping Rebellion; pillar of the landed gentry. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Tseng Kuo-fan” in its text.

光绪.note: The Guangxu Emperor (reigned 1875–1908), who backed the 1898 reforms and was placed under palace arrest by the Empress Dowager until his death. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Kwang Hsu” in its text.

慈禧.note: Cixi (1835–1908), the Empress Dowager who dominated the Qing court for nearly half a century; crushed the 1898 reforms and later backed the Boxers. Isaacs names her only by title. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “the Empress Dowager” in its text.

王莽.note: c. 45 BCE–23 CE. Usurped the Han throne and ruled as the Xin dynasty (9–23 CE), decreeing a nationalization of land. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Wang Mang” in its text.

王安石.note: 1021–1086. Song chief councillor whose New Policies (from 1069) included state farm loans and price stabilization. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Wang An-shih” in its text.

陈翰笙.note: 1897–2004. Marxist economist whose village surveys of the 1920s–30s Isaacs draws on for his picture of the agrarian crisis. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chen Han-seng” in its text.

彭湃.note: 1896–1929. Organizer of China’s first mass peasant associations, at Haifeng; shot by the Kuomintang in 1929. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Peng Pai” in its text.

陈廉伯.note: Compradore of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation who financed the Canton Merchants’ Volunteers against the Kuomintang in 1924. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chen Lim-pak” in its text.

杨希闵.note: Yunnanese general whose mercenary army held Canton until routed by the Kuomintang in 1925. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Yang Hsi-min” in its text.

刘震寰.note: Kwangsi general allied with Yang Hsi-min in Canton; expelled with him in 1925. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Liu Chen-han” in its text.

张静江.note: 1877–1950. Financier, bankroller of Sun’s revolution and Chiang’s patron and mentor; briefly chairman of the Kuomintang Central Executive Committee. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chang Ching-chiang” in its text.

郭松龄.note: 1883–1925. General under Chang Tso-lin who mutinied against him in November 1925 and was captured and shot. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Kuo Sung-lin” in its text.

伍朝枢.note: 1887–1934. Nationalist foreign minister at Canton and later ambassador to the United States; son of the diplomat Wu Ting-fang. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “C. C. Wu” in its text.

许崇智.note: 1886–1965. Commander of the Cantonese Army; implicated in the 1925 murder of Liao Chung-kai and driven from Canton, clearing a military rival from Chiang’s path. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Hsu Chung-shih” in its text.

高语罕.note: 1888–1948. Communist and member of the Kuomintang Supervisory Committee; the “Tuan Chi-jui” remark quoted here was his. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Kao Yu-han” in its text.

李之龙.note: 1897–1928. Communist head of the Canton Naval Bureau and nominal object of the March 20 coup; executed by the Nationalists in 1928. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Li Chih-lung” in its text.

谭平山.note: 1886–1956. Founder of the Chinese Communist Party and its senior figure inside the Kuomintang; minister of agriculture at Wuhan in 1927, later a founder of the “Third Party.” This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Tang Ping-shan” in its text.

钮永建.note: Veteran Kuomintang operative and Chiang Kai-shek’s chief agent in Shanghai, holding a mandate from party headquarters at Canton. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Niu Yung-chien” in its text.

蔡元培.note: 1868–1940. Eminent educator, chancellor of Peking University in the May Fourth era and founder of the Academia Sinica; one of the Kuomintang’s “four elders.” This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Tsai Yuan-pei” in its text.

李宝章.note: Commander of the Shanghai garrison for the warlord Sun Chuang-fang; ran the white terror against the workers in early 1927 before defecting to Chiang Kai-shek. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Li Pao-chang” in its text.

米夫.note: 1901–1939 (pseudonym of M. A. Fortus). Soviet China specialist and rector of the Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow; Stalin’s instrument in the Chinese party. Shot in the purges. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “P. Mif” in its text.
