徐谦.note: 1871–1940. Christian and Western-trained jurist, twice minister of justice, and a left-Kuomintang leader at Wuhan; fled to Hong Kong after the Wuhan collapse. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “George Hsu-chien” in its text.

向忠发.note: 1880–1931. Hupeh boatmen’s and labor organizer who became the nominal general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party in 1928; arrested and shot in Shanghai in 1931. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Hsiang Chung-fah” in its text.

许克祥.note: 1890–1964. Kuomintang regimental commander at Changsha who launched the Horse Day coup of May 21, 1927 against the Hunan mass organizations, opening the rural terror. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Hsu Keh-chang” in its text.

何键.note: 1887–1956. Hunanese general who became the province’s military governor after the 1927 terror and a byword for anti-Communism; his regime executed Mao Tse-tung’s wife, Yang Kai-hui, in 1930. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Ho Chien” in its text.

苏兆征.note: 1885–1929. Seamen’s-union leader of the Hong Kong and Canton–Hong Kong strikes and chairman of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions; minister of labor in the Wuhan government. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Hsu Chao-jen” in its text.

朱培德.note: 1888–1937. Yunnanese general commanding the Third Army and governing Kiangsi, whose 1927 purge of the Communists was comparatively bloodless — he had them escorted out rather than shot. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chu Pei-teh” in its text.

张太雷.note: 1898–1927. A founder of the Communist Youth League who led the Canton Commune of December 1927 and was killed in it — the highest-ranking Communist to die in the risings of 1927. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chang Tai-lei” in its text.

彭德怀.note: 1898–1974. One of the ablest Red commanders, later a marshal and China’s defense minister; disgraced in 1959 for challenging Mao over the Great Leap famine, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Peng Teh-huai” in its text.

张闻天.note: 1900–1976. Pen name Lo Fu. One of the Moscow-trained leaders; became the party’s general secretary in 1935 and later a senior diplomat, purged with Peng Teh-huai in 1959. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Lo Fu” in its text.

太平天国.note: The “Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace,” the Taiping regime (1851–1864); its rebellion was among the deadliest wars in history. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Taiping” in its text.

义和团.note: The “Boxers United in Righteousness,” the martial-arts movement behind the anti-foreign Boxer Rising of 1900. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “I Ho Chuan” in its text.

天地会.note: The “Heaven and Earth Society,” sworn brotherhoods with an anti-Manchu, “restore the Ming” tradition. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Triads” in its text.

新青年.note: The magazine Chen Tu-hsiu founded in 1915, central organ of the New Culture Movement. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “New Youth” in its text.

商团.note: The British-backed Canton merchant militia crushed by the Kuomintang in 1924. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Merchants’ Volunteers” in its text.

安福系.note: The pro-Japanese faction that controlled the Peking government in 1918–20. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Anfu clique” in its text.

第二国际.note: The pre-1914 federation of socialist parties, whose collapse into wartime nationalism prompted the founding of the Comintern. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Second International” in its text.

西山会议派.note: The right-wing Kuomintang faction that met in the Western Hills outside Peking in November 1925 to demand expulsion of the Communists and dismissal of Borodin. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Western Hills Conference group” in its text.

孙文主义学会.note: A right-wing anti-Communist body of 1925, strong among the Whampoa cadets, that claimed to defend Sun’s doctrine against Communist influence. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Sun Yat-senist Society” in its text.

商务印书馆.note: Founded in Shanghai in 1897, China’s largest publishing house and a landmark of the Chapei district; its workforce made it a labor stronghold and, in the 1927 rising, a fortified strongpoint. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Commercial Press” in its text.

中华苏维埃共和国.note: The federation of rural soviet base areas proclaimed at Juichin (Ruijin) in Kiangsi on November 7, 1931, with Mao Tse-tung as chairman; broken by Chiang’s fifth campaign and abandoned in the retreat of 1934. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chinese Soviet Republic” in its text.

八路军.note: The name under which the Red Army was folded into the Nationalist forces in September 1937 for the war with Japan; under Chu Teh’s command the main Communist force in the north. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Eighth Route Army” in its text.

救国会.note: The broad patriotic movement of the mid-1930s pressing for a united front against Japan; Nanking jailed seven of its leaders (the “Seven Gentlemen”) in November 1936. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “National Salvation Association” in its text.

满洲.note: The northeastern region, homeland of the Manchus; contested by Russia and Japan and seized by Japan in 1931. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Manchuria” in its text.

云南.note: The far-southwestern province bordering French Indochina; a base of the militarists Isaacs describes. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Yunnan” in its text.

成都.note: Capital of Szechwan province in the west. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Chengtu” in its text.

沙面.note: The small British-and-French concession island at Canton; focus of the 1925 boycott. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Shameen” in its text.

沙基.note: The Canton bund where British and French troops shot down marchers on June 23, 1925. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Shakee” in its text.

河南.note: North-central province, site of the February 1923 railway massacre at Chengchow (Zhengzhou). This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Honan” in its text.

安徽.note: Lower-Yangtze province; Chen Tu-hsiu’s home. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Anhwei” in its text.

清.note: The Manchu dynasty (1644–1912), China’s last. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Ch‘ing” in its text.

明.note: The last Han-Chinese dynasty (1368–1644) before the Manchu conquest. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Ming” in its text.

汉.note: China’s second imperial dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE); also the name of the majority Chinese people. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Han” in its text.

唐.note: The dynasty of 618–907, a cultural high point. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “T‘ang” in its text.

宋.note: The dynasty of 960–1279; setting of Wang An-shih’s reforms. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “Sung” in its text.

公行.note: The Canton guild of licensed merchants that monopolized trade with Westerners before 1842. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “co-hong” in its text.

两.note: A Chinese unit of silver by weight (customs tael about 37.8 g), not a coin; used for large sums. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “tael” in its text.

担.note: A unit of weight; Isaacs notes one picul equals 133⅓ pounds (about 60 kg). This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “picul” in its text.

辫子.note: The shaved forehead and braid imposed on Chinese men by the Manchus; cutting it off was an act of rebellion. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “queue” in its text.

厘金.note: The internal transit tax (1853–1931) levied on goods in movement at local barriers. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “likin” in its text.

县.note: A county, the basic unit of local administration. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “hsien” in its text.

亩.note: A Chinese unit of land area, about one-sixth of an acre (roughly 0.07 hectare); fifteen mow make a hectare. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “mow” in its text.

红胡子.note: “Red beards” — the traditional armed bandit bands of Manchuria (Isaacs spells it “hunghudtze”); many turned to anti-Japanese guerrilla resistance after 1931. This annotated English edition of Isaacs prints the Wade-Giles form “hunghutze” in its text.
